  • (C2) Local Lipschitz condition: For any \(\theta_1\) and \(\theta_2\) in a neighborhood of the true parameter \(\theta_0\), there exists a measurable envelope function \(\dot{\psi}(x)\) with \(P[\dot{\psi}(X)]^2 < \infty\) such that:

\[ \|\psi_{\theta_1}(x) - \psi_{\theta_2}(x)\| \le \dot{\psi}(x) \|\theta_1 - \theta_2\| \]
  • (C3) Moment and differentiability conditions: Assume \(P\|\psi_{\theta_0}\|^2 < \infty\), and the map \(\theta \mapsto P \psi_\theta\) is differentiable at the zero \(\theta_0\), with non-singular derivative matrix \(V_{\theta_0}\):
\[ V_{\theta_0} := \left. \frac{\partial}{\partial \theta} P[\psi_\theta(X)] \right|_{\theta = \theta_0} \]
  • (C4) Consistency: The estimator satisfies \(P_n \psi_{\hat{\theta}_n} = o_P(n^{-1/2})\) and \(\hat{\theta}_n \xrightarrow{p} \theta_0\).

Then the estimator satisfies asymptotic normality:

\[ \sqrt{n}(\hat{\theta}_n - \theta_0) = -V_{\theta_0}^{-1} \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} \sum_{i=1}^n \psi_{\theta_0}(X_i) + o_P(1) \xrightarrow{d} N\left(0, V_{\theta_0}^{-1} P \psi_{\theta_0} \psi_{\theta_0}^T (V_{\theta_0}^{-1})^T\right) \]

docs.title: 5.2 Empirical Processes and Donsker Classes
docs.text:
To rigorously prove the asymptotic normality of M-estimators and Z-estimators, we need tools from empirical process theory.

  • Basic setup: Let \(X_1, \dots, X_n\) be random samples from an unknown distribution \(P\) on a measurable space \((\mathcal{X}, \mathcal{A})\). Define the empirical distribution measure:
\[ P_n = n^{-1} \sum_{i=1}^n \delta_{X_i} \]
  • Operator notation: For a measurable function \(f: \mathcal{X} \mapsto \mathbb{R}\), we denote the expectation under \(P_n\) and \(P\) respectively as:
\[ P_n f = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n f(X_i), \quad P f = \int f dP \]
  • Empirical process linear functional: Define the empirical process acting on a function \(f\) as:
\[ \mathbb{G}_n f = \sqrt{n}(P_n f - P f) = \sqrt{n}\left( \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n f(X_i) - E f(X) \right) \]

Definition 12.4 (Donsker Class of Functions)

A measurable function class \(\mathcal{F}\) is called a P-Donsker class if, for all \(f \in \mathcal{F}\), the sequence \(\mathbb{G}_n f\) converges weakly in \(\ell^\infty(\mathcal{F})\) (the space of bounded linear functionals) to a tight limiting Gaussian process.

  • Robust Lipschitz Donsker criterion: Let \(\mathcal{F} = \{f_\theta : \theta \in \Theta\}\) be a function class indexed by a bounded subset \(\Theta \subset \mathbb{R}^d\). If there exists a measurable function \(m(x)\) such that \(f_\theta(x)\) satisfies a global Lipschitz condition:
\[ |f_{\theta_1}(x) - f_{\theta_2}(x)| \le m(x) \|\theta_1 - \theta_2\|, \quad \forall \theta_1, \theta_2 \in \Theta \]

and if \(P|m|^r < \infty\) for some \(r > 0\), then \(\mathcal{F}\) is P-Donsker.

docs.title: 5.3 Key Random Function Lemma
docs.text:
Lemma 12.6 (van der Vaart Lemma 19.24)

Assume the following conditions hold:

  • (a) \(\mathcal{F}\) is a P-Donsker measurable function class.

  • (b) \(\{\hat{f}_n\}\) is a sequence of random functions taking values in \(\mathcal{F}\) and converging in \(L_2(P)\) to some deterministic function \(f_0\):

\[ \int (\hat{f}_n(x) - f_0(x))^2 dP(x) = P(\hat{f}_n - f_0)^2 \xrightarrow{p} 0 \]

Then:

\[ \mathbb{G}_n(\hat{f}_n - f_0) \xrightarrow{p} 0 \quad \text{and} \quad \mathbb{G}_n \hat{f}_n \xrightarrow{d} \mathbb{G}_P f_0 \] Extension of Lemma 12.6 to Z-Estimators (click to expand)

In the framework of the theorem, we set \(\hat{f}_n := \psi_{\hat{\theta}_n}\) and \(f_0 := \psi_{\theta_0}\). By the Lipschitz condition:

\[ P(\psi_{\hat{\theta}_n} - \psi_{\theta_0})^2 \le P(\dot{\psi})^2 \|\hat{\theta}_n - \theta_0\|^2 \rightarrow 0 \]

When \(\hat{\theta}_n \xrightarrow{p} \theta_0\) and the envelope moment condition \(P(\dot{\psi})^2 < \infty\) holds, the above condition is satisfied. Therefore, because \(\mathcal{F} = \{\psi_\theta : \theta \in \Theta\}\) is P-Donsker, Lemma 12.6 directly implies:

\[ \mathbb{G}_n(\hat{f}_n - f_0) = \sqrt{n}(P_n \psi_{\hat{\theta}_n} - P \psi_{\hat{\theta}_n}) - \sqrt{n}(P_n \psi_{\theta_0} - P \psi_{\theta_0}) \xrightarrow{p} 0 \]

Rearranging gives:

\[ \sqrt{n}(P_n \psi_{\hat{\theta}_n} - P \psi_{\hat{\theta}_n}) = \sqrt{n}(P_n \psi_{\theta_0} - P \psi_{\theta_0}) + o_P(1) \]

The proof is complete. \(\square\)

docs.title: 5.4 Complete Proof of Theorem 12.5
docs.text:
Asymptotic expansion proof of Theorem 12.5 (click to expand)

From the derivation in Section 5.3, we have established the asymptotic equivalence of the empirical process:

\[ \mathbb{G}_n \psi_{\hat{\theta}_n} - \mathbb{G}_n \psi_{\theta_0} = \mathbb{G}_n(\psi_{\hat{\theta}_n} - \psi_{\theta_0}) \xrightarrow{p} 0 \quad \text{--- (12.13)} \]

Meanwhile, expand the definition of the empirical process: \(\mathbb{G}_n \psi_{\hat{\theta}_n} = \sqrt{n}(P_n \psi_{\hat{\theta}_n} - P \psi_{\hat{\theta}_n})\). Since \(\theta_0\) is the true population zero satisfying \(P \psi_{\theta_0} = 0\), we can rewrite the above as:

\[ \mathbb{G}_n \psi_{\hat{\theta}_n} = \sqrt{n}(P_n \psi_{\hat{\theta}_n} - P \psi_{\hat{\theta}_n}) = \sqrt{n} P_n \psi_{\hat{\theta}_n} + \sqrt{n}(P \psi_{\theta_0} - P \psi_{\hat{\theta}_n}) \]

By the approximate zero condition (C4), \(\sqrt{n} P_n \psi_{\hat{\theta}_n} = o_P(1)\). Substituting this yields:

\[ \mathbb{G}_n \psi_{\hat{\theta}_n} = \sqrt{n}(P \psi_{\theta_0} - P \psi_{\hat{\theta}_n}) + o_P(1) \quad \text{--- (12.14)} \]

Combining (12.14) with (12.13), we can eliminate the empirical linear term at the estimator location:

\[ \mathbb{G}_n \psi_{\theta_0} = \mathbb{G}_n \psi_{\hat{\theta}_n} + o_P(1) = \sqrt{n}(P \psi_{\theta_0} - P \psi_{\hat{\theta}_n}) + o_P(1) \]

Next, perform a first-order Taylor expansion of the deterministic expectation function \(P \psi_\theta\) around \(\theta_0\):

\[ \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} \sum_{i=1}^n \psi_{\theta_0}(X_i) + o_P(1) = -\sqrt{n} \left. \frac{\partial}{\partial \theta} P \psi_\theta(X) \right|_{\theta = \theta_0} (\hat{\theta}_n - \theta_0) + \sqrt{n} o_P(\|\hat{\theta}_n - \theta_0\|) \]

Substituting the matrix \(V_{\theta_0}\):

\[ \sqrt{n} V_{\theta_0}(\hat{\theta}_n - \theta_0) = -\mathbb{G}_n \psi_{\theta_0} + \sqrt{n} o_P(\|\hat{\theta}_n - \theta_0\|) \quad \text{--- (12.15)} \]

Because the central limit theorem (CLT) guarantees \(\mathbb{G}_n \psi_{\theta_0} = O_P(1)\), equation (12.15) implies stochastic boundedness: \(\sqrt{n} \|V_{\theta_0}(\hat{\theta}_n - \theta_0)\| = O_P(1)\). Using non-singularity of the matrix:

\[ \sqrt{n} \|\hat{\theta}_n - \theta_0\| \le \|V_{\theta_0}^{-1}\| \sqrt{n} \|V_{\theta_0}(\hat{\theta}_n - \theta_0)\| = O_P(1) + o_P(\sqrt{n} \|\hat{\theta}_n - \theta_0\|) \]

This proves the \(\sqrt{n}\)-consistency, i.e., \(\sqrt{n} \|\hat{\theta}_n - \theta_0\| = O_P(1)\).

Substituting this rate back into the remainder term in (12.15), the higher-order term becomes \(o_P(1)\):

\[ \sqrt{n}(\hat{\theta}_n - \theta_0) = -V_{\theta_0}^{-1} \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} \sum_{i=1}^n \psi_{\theta_0}(X_i) + o_P(1) \]

Finally, applying the multivariate central limit theorem and Slutsky's theorem yields the asymptotic normality. \(\square\)

docs.title: 6. Asymptotic Normality of M-Estimators
docs.text:
Analogous to Z-estimators, we can establish asymptotic normality of M-estimators by imposing smoothness and differentiability conditions on the criterion function.

Theorem 12.6 (Asymptotic Normality of M-Estimators)

Assume the following standard conditions hold:

  • Measurability: For each \(\theta\) in the open parameter space, the map \(x \mapsto m_\theta(x)\) is measurable, and \(\theta \mapsto m_\theta(x)\) is differentiable at the true point \(\theta_0\) for \(P\)-almost every \(x\), with first derivative (score function) denoted \(\dot{m}_{\theta_0}(x)\).

  • Lipschitz condition: There exists a square-integrable control function \(\dot{m}(x)\) (\(P[\dot{m}(X)]^2 < \infty\)) such that in a neighborhood of \(\theta_0\):

\[ |m_{\theta_1}(x) - m_{\theta_2}(x)| \le \dot{m}(x) \|\theta_1 - \theta_2\| \]
  • Moment and second-order differentiability: Assume the map \(\theta \mapsto P m_\theta\) admits the following second-order Taylor expansion at the global maximizer \(\theta_0\):
\[ P m_\theta = P m_{\theta_0} + \frac{1}{2}(\theta - \theta_0)^T V_{\theta_0}(\theta - \theta_0) + o(\|\theta - \theta_0\|^2) \]

where the symmetric Hessian matrix \(V_{\theta_0}\) is non-singular:

\[ V_{\theta_0} = \left. \frac{\partial^2}{\partial \theta^2} P[m_\theta(X)] \right|_{\theta = \theta_0} \]
  • Consistency and approximate maximization rate: The estimator satisfies \(P_n m_{\hat{\theta}_n} \ge \sup_\theta P_n m_\theta - o_P(n^{-1})\) and \(\hat{\theta}_n \xrightarrow{p} \theta_0\).

Then the M-estimator satisfies asymptotic normality:

\[ \sqrt{n}(\hat{\theta}_n - \theta_0) = -V_{\theta_0}^{-1} \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} \sum_{i=1}^n \dot{m}_{\theta_0}(X_i) + o_P(1) \xrightarrow{d} N\left(0, V_{\theta_0}^{-1} P \dot{m}_{\theta_0} \dot{m}_{\theta_0}^T V_{\theta_0}^{-1}\right) \]

docs.title: 7.1 Asymptotic Distribution of the Sample Median (via M-Estimation Theory)
docs.text:
The sample median can be obtained by maximizing the following criterion function:

\[ \theta \mapsto -\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n |X_i - \theta| \]

Assume the population distribution function \(F(x)\) is differentiable at the true population median \(\theta_0 = F^{-1}(1/2)\), and its density satisfies \(f(\theta_0) > 0\).

We use the centered M-estimation function: \(m_\theta(x) = |x - \theta| - |x|\). By the triangle inequality, for any \(\theta_1, \theta_2\):

\[ ||x - \theta_1| - |x - \theta_2|| \le |\theta_1 - \theta_2| \]

This shows the function satisfies a Lipschitz condition controlled by a constant, where \(\dot{m}(x) \equiv 1\), which obviously satisfies the square-integrability condition.

Moreover, this map is differentiable almost everywhere except at \(x = \theta\), with first derivative (score function):

\[ \dot{m}_{\theta_0}(x) = -\text{sign}(x - \theta_0) \]

Its squared expectation is:

\[ E(\dot{m}_{\theta_0}(X))^2 = E(\text{sign}^2(X - \theta_0)) = 1 \]

Using integration by parts, we can derive the analytic form of the deterministic objective function:

\[ P m_\theta = E(m_\theta(X)) = \int |x - \theta| dF(x) - \int |x| dF(x) \] \[ = \theta F(0) + \int_{(0, \theta]} 2(\theta - x) dF(x) - \theta(1 - F(0)) = 2\int_0^\theta F(x) dx - \theta \]

Taking first and second derivatives of the objective function:

\[ \frac{d P m_\theta}{d \theta} = 2F(\theta) - 1, \quad \frac{d^2 P m_\theta}{d \theta^2} = 2f(\theta) \]

Therefore, the second-order matrix evaluated at \(\theta_0\) is \(V_{\theta_0} = 2f(\theta_0)\).

Since the asymptotic variance takes the sandwich form \(V_{\theta_0}^{-1} P[\dot{m}_{\theta_0} \dot{m}_{\theta_0}^T] V_{\theta_0}^{-1} = \frac{1}{(2f(\theta_0)) \cdot 1 \cdot (2f(\theta_0))} = \frac{1}{4f^2(\theta_0)}\), substituting into Theorem 12.6 directly yields the classic asymptotic normality result for the median:

\[ \sqrt{n}(\hat{\theta}_n - \theta_0) \xrightarrow{d} N\left(0, \frac{1}{4f^2(\theta_0)}\right) \]

docs.title: 7.2 Nonlinear Least Squares Estimation
docs.text:
Suppose observed samples \((X_1, Y_1), \dots, (X_n, Y_n)\) consist of covariates \(X\) and response \(Y\), with data generating mechanism:

\[ Y = f_{\theta_0}(X) + e, \quad E(e|X) = 0, \quad \text{Var}(e|X) = \sigma^2(X) < \infty \]

The nonlinear least squares estimator (LSE) minimizes the sum of squared residuals:

\[ \hat{\theta}_n = \arg\min_\theta \sum_{i=1}^n (Y_i - f_\theta(X_i))^2 \]

This is equivalent to a special M-estimator with loss function \(m_\theta(x, y) = -(y - f_\theta(x))^2\). The limit of the empirical objective function under the law of large numbers is:

\[ \theta \mapsto P m_\theta = -E(Y - f_\theta(X))^2 = -E[Y - f_{\theta_0}(X) + (f_{\theta_0}(X) - f_\theta(X))]^2 \] \[ = -E(f_{\theta_0}(X) - f_\theta(X))^2 - E e^2 \quad \text{--- (12.16)} \]

From (12.16), if the model satisfies an identifiability condition (i.e., \(\theta \ne \theta_0 \implies P(f_\theta(X) \ne f_{\theta_0}(X)) > 0\)), then the true parameter \(\theta_0\) is indeed a global maximizer of the objective function, guaranteeing consistency of the estimator.

Now we verify the key Lipschitz condition for asymptotic normality:

\[ |m_{\theta_1}(x,y) - m_{\theta_2}(x,y)| = |(y - f_{\theta_1}(x))^2 - (y - f_{\theta_2}(x))^2| \] \[ = |f_{\theta_1}(x) - f_{\theta_2}(x)| \cdot |2y - f_{\theta_1}(x) - f_{\theta_2}(x)| \]

Assume the regression function is well-behaved in first order: \(|f_{\theta_1}(x) - f_{\theta_2}(x)| \le g(x) \|\theta_2 - \theta_1\|\), and the function values are uniformly bounded \(|f_\theta(x)| \le c(x)\). Then we can construct a square-integrable global Lipschitz envelope:

\[ \dot{m}(x,y) := g(x)[2|y| + 2c(x)] \]

Perform a Taylor expansion of the objective function (12.16) to obtain the Hessian matrix \(V_{\theta_0}\):

\[ P m_\theta = P m_{\theta_0} - \int [f_\theta(x) - f_{\theta_0}(x)]^2 \rho(x) dx \] \[ = P m_{\theta_0} - \int [(\theta - \theta_0)^T \dot{f}_{\theta_0}(x) + o(\|\theta - \theta_0\|)]^2 \rho(x) dx \] \[ = P m_{\theta_0} - \frac{1}{2}(\theta - \theta_0)^T \left[ 2 \int \dot{f}_{\theta_0}(x) \dot{f}_{\theta_0}^T(x) p(x) dx \right] (\theta - \theta_0) + o(\|\theta - \theta_0\|^2) \]

Thus, the Hessian matrix and the corresponding first-order score function are:

\[ V_{\theta_0} = -2 P(\dot{f}_{\theta_0} \dot{f}_{\theta_0}^T), \quad \dot{m}_{\theta_0}(x,y) = 2(y - f_{\theta_0}(x)) \dot{f}_{\theta_0}(x) = 2 e \dot{f}_{\theta_0}(x) \]

Plugging into the asymptotic normality formula for M-estimators, under the assumption of independence between the error \(e\) and covariates \(X\), the middle sandwich matrix simplifies to:

\[ V_{\theta_0}^{-1} P(\dot{m}_{\theta_0} \dot{m}_{\theta_0}^T) V_{\theta_0}^{-1} = [2P \dot{f}_{\theta_0} \dot{f}_{\theta_0}^T]^{-1} \cdot 4 P(e^2 \dot{f}_{\theta_0} \dot{f}_{\theta_0}^T) \cdot [2P \dot{f}_{\theta_0} \dot{f}_{\theta_0}^T]^{-1} \] \[ = [P \dot{f}_{\theta_0} \dot{f}_{\theta_0}^T]^{-1} E(\sigma^2(X)) [P \dot{f}_{\theta_0} \dot{f}_{\theta_0}^T]^{-1} \]

This determines the asymptotic distribution of the nonlinear least squares estimator.

docs.title: 7.3 Binary Regression Model
docs.text:
Suppose observed samples \((X_1, Y_1), \dots, (X_n, Y_n)\), where \(X_i\) is a \(k\)-dimensional covariate vector and \(Y_i \in \{0, 1\}\) is a binary response variable, with conditional probability model:

\[ P_\theta(Y_i = 1 | X_i = x) = \Psi(\theta^T x) \]

Here \(\Psi: \mathbb{R} \mapsto [0, 1]\) is a known continuously differentiable monotonic link function.

  • Logistic Regression: Take \(\Psi(t) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-t}}\).

  • Probit Model: Take \(\Psi(t) = \Phi(t)\) (standard normal distribution function).

The maximum likelihood estimator for this model maximizes the conditional log-likelihood function:

\[ \theta \mapsto \prod_{i=1}^n p_\theta(Y_i | X_i) := \prod_{i=1}^n \Psi(\theta^T X_i)^{Y_i} (1 - \Psi(\theta^T X_i))^{1 - Y_i} \]

To ensure identifiability of the parameter, we require that the covariates are non-degenerate, i.e., the distribution of \(X_i\) does not concentrate on any \((k-1)\)-dimensional affine subspace of \(\mathbb{R}^k\). To this end, we assume the range of \(X_i\) is bounded and the matrix \(E X X^T\) is non-singular.

Differentiating the log-likelihood gives the corresponding Z-estimator score equation:

\[ \psi_\theta(x, y) := \dot{l}_\theta(y|x) = \frac{y - \Psi(\theta^T x)}{\Psi(\theta^T x)[1 - \Psi(\theta^T x)]} \Psi'(\theta^T x) x \]

When the parameter \(\theta\) varies over a compact set, this score function is uniformly bounded in \((x,y)\), so the conditions are naturally satisfied. Compute the corresponding Fisher information matrix:

\[ I_\theta = E \left[ \frac{\Psi'(\theta^T X)^2}{\Psi(\theta^T X)[1 - \Psi(\theta^T X)]} X X^T \right] \]

Applying the asymptotic normality theorem for Z-estimators, the maximum likelihood estimator converges to the following normal limiting distribution:

\[ \sqrt{n}(\hat{\theta}_n - \theta) \xrightarrow{d} N(0, I_\theta^{-1}) \]

docs.title: Chapter 12: M-Estimators and Z-Estimators (Part II)
docs.text: In the previous part, we discussed the consistency and asymptotic normality of standard M-estimators and Z-estimators. In practical statistical modeling, we often encounter situations involving nuisance parameters or requiring iterative algorithms (such as the Newton-Raphson method) to obtain solutions. This part delves into Z-estimators with estimated parameters and one-step estimators.

docs.title: 8. Estimators with Estimated Nuisance Parameters
docs.text:
Suppose the samples \(X_1, \dots, X_n \sim i.i.d.\ F_{(\theta, \eta)}\), where:

  • \(\theta\) is the parameter of interest.
  • \(\eta\) is an unknown nuisance parameter.

Typically, we need to substitute an estimator of \(\eta\) (denoted \(\hat{\eta}_n\)) into the Z-estimating equation:

\[ P_n \psi_{(\theta, \eta)} \Rightarrow P_n \psi_{(\theta, \hat{\eta}_n)} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \psi_{(\theta, \hat{\eta}_n)}(X_i) = 0 \]

This is essentially a two-step procedure: first estimate \(\eta\), then treat it as a "known" parameter and solve for \(\theta\) in the equation.

docs.title: 8.1 Motivating Example: Missing Response Regression
docs.text:
Consider the regression model:

\[ y_i = m_{\theta_0}(x_i) + \epsilon_i, \quad E(\epsilon_i | x_i) = 0 \]

Assume the response \(y_i\) is subject to missingness. We define an indicator variable: \(R_i = 1\) if \(y_i\) is observed; \(R_i = 0\) if \(y_i\) is missing.

Missing at Random (MAR) Assumption: Assume the missingness mechanism satisfies:

\[ P(R_i = 1 | x_i, y_i) = P(R_i = 1 | x_i) = \omega_{\eta_0}(x_i) \]

where \(\omega_{\eta_0}(\cdot)\) is called the missing propensity function. Here we assume it follows a parametric binary regression model.

  • Meaning of MAR: Given \(X_i\), the missing indicator \(R_i\) and the true response \(y_i\) are conditionally independent.

  • This missingness mechanism is called ignorable missing at random, because as long as we observe \(x_i\), the missing \(y_i\) does not introduce additional bias for inference.

How to estimate the target parameter \(\theta\)?

Method 1: Least squares estimation (LSE) using only the observed data (i.e., \(R_i = 1\))

The objective function is:

\[ LS_n(\theta) = \sum_{i=1}^n R_i (y_i - m_\theta(x_i))^2 \]

Taking derivatives gives the score equation:

\[ \frac{\partial LS_n(\theta)}{\partial \theta} = -2 \sum_{i=1}^n R_i (y_i - m_\theta(x_i)) \frac{\partial m_\theta(x_i)}{\partial \theta} = 0 \quad \text{--- (8.13)} \]

At the true parameter \(\theta_0\), using \(E(\epsilon_i | x_i) = 0\) and under the MAR assumption:

\[ E \left\{ R_i (y_i - m_{\theta_0}(x_i)) \frac{\partial m_{\theta_0}(x_i)}{\partial \theta} \right\} = E \left\{ \epsilon_i \frac{\partial m_{\theta_0}(x_i)}{\partial \theta} \omega_{\eta_0}(x_i) \right\} = 0 \]

Thus, under certain regularity conditions, the least squares estimator obtained by solving (8.13) is consistent and asymptotically normal (AN).

Method 2: Inverse Probability Weighted Estimation (IPW)

By weighting (8.13) with the true missing propensity \(\omega_{\eta_0}(x_i)\), we obtain the IPW score equation:

\[ \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{R_i (y_i - m_\theta(x_i)) \frac{\partial m_\theta(x_i)}{\partial \theta}}{\omega_{\eta_0}(x_i)} = 0 \quad \text{--- (8.14)} \]

Taking expectations also verifies unbiasedness:

\[ E \left\{ \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{R_i (y_i - m_\theta(x_i)) \frac{\partial m_\theta(x_i)}{\partial \theta}}{\omega_{\eta_0}(x_i)} \right\} = E \left\{ \epsilon_i \frac{\partial m_{\theta_0}(x_i)}{\partial \theta} \right\} = 0 \]

Question: Which estimator is more efficient (i.e., has smaller asymptotic variance): the estimator ignoring missing values (8.13) or the IPW estimator (8.14)?

docs.title: 8.2 Binary Likelihood Estimation of the Nuisance Parameter
docs.text:
In practice, \(\eta_0\) is usually unknown. We can estimate it by maximizing the binary likelihood function:

\[ L_n(\eta) = \prod_{i=1}^n \omega_\eta^{R_i}(x_i) (1 - \omega_\eta(x_i))^{1 - R_i} \]

The log-likelihood function is:

\[ l_n(\eta) = \sum_{i=1}^n \{ R_i \log \omega_\eta(x_i) + (1 - R_i) \log(1 - \omega_\eta(x_i)) \} \]

Differentiating and setting to zero yields \(\hat{\eta}\):

\[ \frac{\partial l_n(\eta)}{\partial \eta} = \sum_{i=1}^n \left\{ \frac{R_i}{\omega_\eta(x_i)} - \frac{1 - R_i}{1 - \omega_\eta(x_i)} \right\} \frac{\partial \omega_\eta(x_i)}{\partial \eta} = 0 \Rightarrow \hat{\eta} \]

Then, (8.14) becomes an equation with an estimated nuisance parameter:

\[ \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{R_i (y_i - m_\theta(x_i)) \frac{\partial m_\theta(x_i)}{\partial \theta}}{\omega_{\hat{\eta}}(x_i)} = 0 \quad \text{--- (8.15)} \]

Counterintuitive conclusion: Chen, Leung and Qin (2008) proved that the \(\theta\) obtained from equation (8.15) using the estimated parameter \(\hat{\eta}\) is asymptotically more efficient than the \(\theta\) obtained from equation (8.14) using the true known parameter \(\eta_0\)!

docs.title: 8.3 Nonparametric Estimation of the Missing Propensity
docs.text:
Assuming the parametric model \(P(R_i = 1 | x_i) = \omega_{\eta_0}(x_i)\) may be too restrictive. We can consider a nonparametric form:

\[ P(R_i = 1 | x_i, y_i) = P(R_i = 1 | x_i) = \omega(x_i) \]

The missing propensity \(\omega(\cdot)\) can be estimated via kernel smoothing methods (e.g., the Nadaraya-Watson estimator):

\[ \hat{\omega}_h(x) = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n K\left(\frac{x - x_i}{h}\right) R_i}{\sum_{i=1}^n K\left(\frac{x - x_i}{h}\right)} \]

where \(K\) is a kernel function (symmetric probability density function) and \(h\) is the smoothing bandwidth. We require that as \(n \rightarrow \infty\), \(h \rightarrow 0\) and \(nh \rightarrow \infty\). Its expectation is essentially a weighted average of the weights at the sample points:

\[ E(\hat{\omega}_h(x)) = E \left( \sum_{i=1}^n E \left( \frac{K\left(\frac{x - x_i}{h}\right)}{\sum K\left(\frac{x - x_j}{h}\right)} R_i \Big| x_1, \dots, x_n \right) \right) = E \left( \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{K\left(\frac{x - x_i}{h}\right)}{\sum K\left(\frac{x - x_j}{h}\right)} \omega(x_i) \right) \]

It can be shown that if we choose an appropriate bandwidth \(h \approx O(n^{-\frac{1}{4+d}})\) (where \(d\) is the dimension of \(x\)), then:

\[ \sqrt{nh^d} (\hat{\omega}_h(x) - \omega(x)) \rightarrow N(\mu, v^2) \quad (x \in \mathbb{R}^d) \]

docs.title: 9. Asymptotic Theorem for Z-Estimators with Estimated Parameters
docs.text:
Theorem 8.13 (Asymptotic Expansion for Two-Step Z-Estimators)

For every \(\theta\) in an open subset of \(\mathbb{R}^k\) and every \(\eta\) in a metric space, let \(x \rightarrow \phi_{\theta, \eta}(x)\) be a \(\mathbb{R}^k\)-valued measurable function, such that: the class of functions \(\{\phi_{\theta, \eta} : \|\theta - \theta_0\| < \delta, d(\eta, \eta_0) < \delta\}\) is Donsker for some \(\delta > 0\); and \(P\|\phi_{\theta, \eta} - \phi_{\theta_0, \eta_0}\|^2 \rightarrow 0\) as \((\theta, \eta) \rightarrow (\theta_0, \eta_0)\).

Assume \(P\phi_{\theta_0, \eta_0} = 0\), and the map \(\theta \rightarrow P\phi_{\theta, \eta}\) is differentiable at \(\theta_0\) (uniformly in \(\eta\) in a neighborhood of \(\eta_0\)), with a nonsingular derivative matrix \(V_{\theta_0, \eta}\), and \(V_{\theta_0, \eta} \rightarrow V_{\theta_0, \eta_0}\) as \(\eta \rightarrow \eta_0\).

Furthermore, if there exist consistent estimators \((\hat{\theta}, \hat{\eta}) \xrightarrow{p} (\theta_0, \eta_0)\) satisfying \(\sqrt{n}\mathbb{P}_n\phi_{\hat{\theta}, \hat{\eta}} = o_p(1)\), then:

\[ \sqrt{n}(\hat{\theta}_n - \theta_0) = -V_{\theta_0, \eta_0}^{-1} \sqrt{n} P\psi_{\theta_0, \hat{\eta}_n} - V_{\theta_0, \eta_0}^{-1} \mathbb{G}_n\psi_{\theta_0, \eta_0} + o_P(1 + \sqrt{n}\|P\psi_{\theta_0, \hat{\eta}_n}\|) \]

Remarks on Theorem 8.13:

  1. The drift term on the right-hand side, \(-V_{\theta_0, \eta_0}^{-1} \sqrt{n} P\psi_{\theta_0, \hat{\eta}_n}\), arises because we have additionally estimated the nuisance parameter \(\eta\).
  2. Here \(\eta\) can be an infinite-dimensional functional parameter (not just a scalar or vector parameter).

  3. Under certain smoothness conditions, this extra drift term can be approximated by a Taylor expansion using the Delta method:

    \[ P\psi_{\theta_0, \hat{\eta}_n} = P\psi_{\theta_0, \eta_0} + \frac{\partial P\psi_{\theta_0, \eta_0}}{\partial \eta} (\hat{\eta}_n - \eta_0) + o_p(\hat{\eta}_n - \eta_0) \]

  4. Orthogonality: If the target parameter and the nuisance parameter satisfy an (approximate) orthogonality condition, i.e., the cross partial derivative is 0 (\(\frac{\partial P\psi_{\theta_0, \eta_0}}{\partial \eta} = 0\)), then the error in estimating the nuisance parameter \(\hat{\eta}_n\) will not affect the first-order asymptotic distribution of \(\hat{\theta}_n\) (the drift term vanishes).

docs.title: 9.1 Example: Symmetric Location Model
docs.text:
Suppose \(X_1, \dots, X_n \sim i.i.d.\ F\), and the distribution \(F\) is symmetric about the true location parameter \(\theta_0\). We want to estimate \(\theta_0\), but the scale parameter \(\sigma\) is unknown. Let \(x \rightarrow \psi(x)\) be an antisymmetric odd function.

Consider the following Z-estimating equation (with \(\hat{\sigma}\) being a consistent estimator of \(\sigma\)):

\[ \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \psi\left( \frac{X_i - \theta}{\hat{\sigma}} \right) = 0 \]

Since \(F(\cdot)\) is symmetric about \(\theta_0\) and \(\psi(\cdot)\) is an odd function, under the true parameter, the expectation is zero for any scale estimator \(\hat{\sigma}\):

\[ P\psi_{\theta_0, \hat{\sigma}} = \int \psi\left( \frac{x - \theta_0}{\hat{\sigma}} \right) dF(x) = 0, \quad \forall \hat{\sigma} \]

Therefore, by Theorem 8.13, since the drift term is zero, we obtain:

\[ \sqrt{n}(\hat{\theta}_n - \theta_0) = -V_{\theta_0, \eta_0}^{-1} \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} (\mathbb{P}_n\psi_{\theta_0, \eta_0} - P\psi_{\theta_0, \eta_0}) + o_p(1) \]

This means that the estimation procedure is asymptotically equivalent to using the true \(\eta_0\). In this model, the estimation error of \(\hat{\sigma}\) does not appear in the first-order asymptotic expansion.

docs.title: 10. One-step Estimator
docs.text:
In many complex models, the exact root of the Z-estimating equation \(\Psi_n(\theta) = 0\) can be very difficult to obtain (e.g., multiple local extrema, high nonlinearity).

We can improve the estimation by performing one optimization step based on an initial estimator \(\tilde{\theta}_n\). This is exactly the idea of the Newton-Raphson algorithm.

Consider a first-order Taylor expansion around \(\tilde{\theta}_n\):

\[ \Psi_n(\tilde{\theta}_n) + \dot{\Psi}_n(\tilde{\theta}_n)(\theta - \tilde{\theta}_n) = 0 \quad \text{--- (8.16)} \]

We obtain a one-step update of \(\tilde{\theta}_n\):

\[ \hat{\theta}_n = \tilde{\theta}_n - \dot{\Psi}_n^{-1}(\tilde{\theta}_n) \Psi_n(\tilde{\theta}_n) \quad \text{--- (8.17)} \]
  • Usually, we can choose a computationally easy but inefficient \(\sqrt{n}\)-consistent estimator as the initial value \(\tilde{\theta}_n\) (e.g., method of moments estimator). We will see that the one-step estimator \(\hat{\theta}_n\) achieves exactly the same asymptotic efficiency as the fully iterated Z-estimator that would otherwise be difficult to compute.

docs.title: 10.1 Regularity Conditions
docs.text:
Uniform convergence condition: For any constant \(M\) and a given nonsingular matrix \(\dot{\Psi}_0\), we have:

\[ \sup_{\sqrt{n}\|\theta - \theta_0\| < M} \|\sqrt{n}(\Psi_n(\theta) - \Psi_n(\theta_0)) - \dot{\Psi}_0 \sqrt{n}(\theta - \theta_0)\| \xrightarrow{P} 0 \quad \text{--- (8.18)} \]

where \(\dot{\Psi}_0\) is the limit matrix of the derivative \(\dot{\Psi}_n(\theta)\) as \(\theta \rightarrow \theta_0\).

In practice, we can replace the empirical derivative in (8.17) with any consistent estimate matrix \(\dot{\Psi}_{n,0}\) (satisfying \(\dot{\Psi}_{n,0} \xrightarrow{p} \dot{\Psi}_0\)):

\[ \hat{\theta}_n = \tilde{\theta}_n - \dot{\Psi}_{n,0}^{-1} \Psi_n(\tilde{\theta}_n) \quad \text{--- (8.19)} \]

Theorem 8.14 (Asymptotic Equivalence of One-step Estimators)

Assume the central limit theorem holds: \(\sqrt{n}\Psi_n(\theta_0) \xrightarrow{d} Z\), and condition (8.18) above is satisfied. For any \(\sqrt{n}\)-consistent initial estimator \(\tilde{\theta}_n\) and a derivative estimator satisfying \(\dot{\Psi}_{n,0} \xrightarrow{p} \dot{\Psi}_0\), the one-step estimator \(\hat{\theta}_n\) constructed by (8.19) satisfies:

\[ \sqrt{n}(\hat{\theta}_n - \theta_0) = -\dot{\Psi}_0^{-1} \sqrt{n} \Psi_n(\theta_0) + o_p(1) \quad \text{--- (8.20)} \]

This means the one-step estimator has exactly the same asymptotic distribution as the true Z-estimator.

Proof of Theorem 8.14 (click to expand)

Starting from the one-step update formula (8.19), multiply both sides by \(\sqrt{n}\dot{\Psi}_{n,0}\) to obtain:

\[ \dot{\Psi}_{n,0} \sqrt{n}(\hat{\theta}_n - \theta_0) = \dot{\Psi}_{n,0} \sqrt{n}(\tilde{\theta}_n - \theta_0) - \sqrt{n}\Psi_n(\tilde{\theta}_n) \]

Rewrite by subtracting \(\Psi_n(\theta_0)\):

\[ = \dot{\Psi}_{n,0} \sqrt{n}(\tilde{\theta}_n - \theta_0) - \sqrt{n}\{\Psi_n(\tilde{\theta}_n) - \Psi_n(\theta_0)\} - \sqrt{n}\Psi_n(\theta_0) \]

Since the initial estimator is \(\sqrt{n}\)-consistent, i.e., \(\sqrt{n}(\tilde{\theta}_n - \theta_0) = O_p(1)\), we can choose a large enough \(M\) such that \(P(\sqrt{n}\|\tilde{\theta}_n - \theta_0\| < M)\) is arbitrarily close to 1. Therefore, by condition (8.18), on the neighborhood where this probability tends to 1:

\[ \sqrt{n}\{\Psi_n(\tilde{\theta}_n) - \Psi_n(\theta_0)\} = \dot{\Psi}_0 \sqrt{n}(\tilde{\theta}_n - \theta_0) + o_p(1) \]

Substituting this expression into the previous equation:

\[ \dot{\Psi}_{n,0} \sqrt{n}(\hat{\theta}_n - \theta_0) = \dot{\Psi}_{n,0} \sqrt{n}(\tilde{\theta}_n - \theta_0) - \dot{\Psi}_0 \sqrt{n}(\tilde{\theta}_n - \theta_0) + o_p(1) - \sqrt{n}\Psi_n(\theta_0) \]

Factor and combine terms:

\[ = (\dot{\Psi}_{n,0} - \dot{\Psi}_0) \sqrt{n}(\tilde{\theta}_n - \theta_0) - \sqrt{n}\Psi_n(\theta_0) + o_p(1) \]

Since \(\dot{\Psi}_{n,0} - \dot{\Psi}_0 = o_p(1)\) and \(\sqrt{n}(\tilde{\theta}_n - \theta_0) = O_p(1)\), their product is \(o_p(1)\):

\[ = o_p(1) \cdot O_p(1) - \sqrt{n}\Psi_n(\theta_0) + o_p(1) = -\sqrt{n}\Psi_n(\theta_0) + o_p(1) \]

Finally, applying Slutsky's lemma (multiply on the left by \(\dot{\Psi}_{n,0}^{-1}\), which converges in probability to \(\dot{\Psi}_0^{-1}\)), we directly obtain:

\[ \sqrt{n}(\hat{\theta}_n - \theta_0) = -\dot{\Psi}_0^{-1} \sqrt{n} \Psi_n(\theta_0) + o_p(1) \]

The proof is complete. \(\square\)

Additional remarks: If \(\Psi_n(\theta) = \mathbb{P}_n \psi_\theta\), then under the conditions of Theorem 8.11 (standard Z-estimator asymptotic normality), condition (8.18) is naturally satisfied, with \(\dot{\Psi}_0 = V_{\theta_0}\); under the conditions of van der Vaart (1998) Theorem 5.41, this condition also holds, with \(\dot{\Psi}_0 = P\dot{\psi}_{\theta_0}\).

docs.title: 10.2 Example: One-step Estimator for the Cauchy Location Model
docs.text:
Let \(X_1, X_2, \dots, X_n \sim i.i.d.\ F\), with probability density function given by the Cauchy distribution:

\[ p_\theta(x) = \frac{1}{\pi(1 + (x - \theta)^2)} \]

The score function is:

\[ \dot{l}_\theta(x) = \frac{\dot{p}_\theta(x)}{p_\theta(x)} = \frac{2(x - \theta)}{1 + (x - \theta)^2} \]

For large \(x\), the score function \(\dot{l}_\theta(x) \sim \frac{1}{x}\), so it has finite Fisher information: \(E(\dot{l}_\theta^2(X)) < \infty\). Since this equation has multiple roots, directly finding the global maximum likelihood estimator (MLE) via numerical optimization is very difficult.

A safer strategy is to use the one-step estimator: Take the sample median as the initial estimator \(\tilde{\theta}_n\) (the median is a stable \(\sqrt{n}\)-consistent estimator), then perform a single Newton step on the score equation near it. This ensures the asymptotic efficiency of the estimator (equivalent to the MLE) while avoiding the computational pitfalls of multiple roots.

docs.title: 10.3 Example: One-step Estimator for a Mixture Model
docs.text:
Suppose the observed data come from a mixture of two location-scale models:

\[ X_1, X_2, \dots, X_n \sim i.i.d.\ pF_1 + (1-p)F_2 \]

where:

\[ f_1(x) = f\left( rac{x - \mu}{\sigma} ight) rac{1}{\sigma} \quad ext{and} \quad f_2(x) = g\left( rac{x - u}{ au} ight) rac{1}{ au} \]

Here, \((\mu, u)\) are location parameters, \((\sigma, au)\) are scale parameters. The parameter vector is \( heta = (\mu, \sigma, u, au, p)\). The mixture density is:

\[ f(x) = p f\left( rac{x - \mu}{\sigma} ight) rac{1}{\sigma} + (1-p) g\left( rac{x - u}{ au} ight) rac{1}{ au} \]

The likelihood function is:

\[ L_n( heta) = \prod_{i=1}^n \left\{ p f\left( rac{X_i - \mu}{\sigma} ight) rac{1}{\sigma} + (1-p) g\left( rac{X_i - u}{ au} ight) rac{1}{ au} ight\} \]

If we set the parameter \(\mu = X_1\) and let \(\sigma ightarrow 0\) (i.e., let the first distribution collapse onto the first data point), one term in the likelihood tends to infinity. This causes the entire likelihood function to become unbounded:

\[ \sup L_n( heta) = \infty \]

This is known as the unbounded likelihood problem. Standard MLE cannot be used directly.

One-step strategy: Since the likelihood function does not have a finite global maximum, we start from another stable estimator. First, obtain method of moments estimators \(\hat{ heta}_{me}\) by matching the first five moments. This estimator is consistent and does not depend on the shape of the likelihood. Then, using \(\hat{ heta}_{me}\) as the starting point, perform a single-step maximization or a Newton step nearby to obtain an asymptotically efficient and statistically well-behaved optimal estimator.

docs.title: Chapter 8: Moment Estimation and Generalized Method of Moments (ME & GMM)
docs.text: In statistical inference, Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) is the gold standard for parameter estimation. However, MLE strongly depends on a full parametric specification of the data distribution. When the exact form of the distribution is unknown, or only partial moment conditions are known, we need other estimation methods. This chapter introduces Moment Estimation (ME) and the Generalized Method of Moments (GMM), which is extremely important in econometrics and statistics.

docs.title: 1. Moment Estimator (ME)
docs.text:
Let \(X_1, ..., X_n \stackrel{i.i.d}{\sim} F_\theta\), where \(\theta_0\) is the true parameter. Given a set of known functions \(f_1, ..., f_k\).

The population moments are defined as:

\[ E_\theta f_j(X) = \int f_j(x) dF_\theta(x), \quad j=1, ..., k \]

The most classical choice is \(f_j(x) = x^j\). Let the vector \(f = (f_1, ..., f_k)^T\).

Definition 12.1 (Moment Estimator, ME)

Match the sample moment \(\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n f(X_i)\) with its corresponding population moment:

\[ P_n f := \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n f(X_i) \stackrel{\text{match}}{=} e(\theta) := E_\theta f(X) := P_\theta f \]

If \(e(\theta)\) is one-to-one, then the moment estimator can be expressed explicitly as \(\hat{\theta}_n = e^{-1}(P_n f)\).

If the inverse map \(e^{-1}\) is differentiable and the second moment \(E_{\theta_0} f(X)f^T(X) < \infty\) (which guarantees the asymptotic normality of \(P_n f\)), then \(\hat{\theta}_n\) is also asymptotically normal.

Theorem 12.1 (Central Limit Theorem for Moment Estimator )

If \(e(\theta) = P_\theta f := E_\theta f(X)\) is one-to-one on an open set \(\Theta \subset \mathbb{R}^k\), continuously differentiable at \(\theta_0\) with non-singular Jacobian matrix \(e'(\theta_0)\), and \(P_{\theta_0} \|f\|^2 < \infty\).

Then \(\hat{\theta}_n\) exists with probability approaching 1 (wpa 1) and satisfies asymptotic normality:

\[ \sqrt{n}(\hat{\theta}_n - \theta_0) \xrightarrow{d} N\left(0, [e'(\theta_0)]^{-1} (E_{\theta_0} ff^T - E_{\theta_0} f E_{\theta_0} f^T) ([e'(\theta_0)]^{-1})^T \right) \]

To prove this theorem, we need the Inverse Function Theorem:

Lemma 12.1 (The Inverse Function Theorem)

Let \(A\) be an open set in \(\mathbb{R}^n\); \(g: A \mapsto \mathbb{R}^n\) is continuously differentiable at \(a\), and differentiable in a neighborhood of \(a \in A\). If the Jacobian matrix \(Dg(x) := \partial g(x) / \partial x^T\) is non-singular at \(a\).

Then there exists a neighborhood \(U\) of \(a\) and an open set \(V\) in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) such that \(g: U \mapsto V\) is one-to-one; and the inverse function \(g^{-1}: V \mapsto U\) exists, is continuously differentiable, and satisfies:

\[ Dg^{-1}(y) := \partial g^{-1}(y) / \partial y^T = (Dg(x))^{-1} \] Proof of Theorem 12.1 (click to expand)
  • Continuous differentiability at \(\theta_0\) implies differentiability in a neighborhood of \(\theta_0\) and continuity of \(\theta \mapsto e'_\theta\).
  • Non-singularity of \(e'_\theta\) implies it is also non-singular in some neighborhood of \(\theta_0\).
  • Therefore, by the Inverse Function Theorem, there exist an open neighborhood \(U\) of \(\theta_0\) and an open neighborhood \(V\) of \(P_{\theta_0}f\) such that \(e: U \mapsto V\) is a diffeomorphism (one-to-one) with differentiable inverse \(e^{-1}: V \mapsto U\).
  • By the Law of Large Numbers (LLN), \(\mathbb{P}_n f \equiv \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n f(X_i) \xrightarrow{a.s.} e(\theta_0) \in V\). Hence, wpa 1 \(\mathbb{P}_n f \in V\), which implies \(\hat{\theta}_n = e^{-1}(\mathbb{P}_n f)\) exists wpa 1. Then by the continuous mapping theorem:
\[ \hat{\theta}_n := e^{-1}(\mathbb{P}_n f) \xrightarrow{a.s.} e^{-1}(e(\theta_0)) = \theta_0 \]
  • By the Central Limit Theorem (CLT), the sequence \(\sqrt{n}(\mathbb{P}_n f - P_{\theta_0} f)\) satisfies asymptotic normality.
  • Finally, applying the Delta Method completes the proof: multiplying by the Jacobian matrix \((e^{-1}(x_0))' = (e'(\theta_0))^{-1}\) yields the final asymptotic variance.

docs.title: 2. Examples of Moment Estimation and Exponential Family
2.1 Example: Moment Estimation of the Beta Distribution
docs.text:
Let \(X_1, X_2, ..., X_n\) be a random sample from a Beta distribution with density \(f(x; \alpha, \beta) = \frac{1}{B(\alpha, \beta)} x^{\alpha-1} (1-x)^{\beta-1}\), where \(x \in (0,1)\), parameters \(\alpha > 0, \beta > 0\).

The population moments are:

\[ \mathbb{E}X^k = \frac{1}{B(\alpha, \beta)} \int x^{\alpha+k-1} (1-x)^{\beta-1} dx = \frac{B(\alpha+k, \beta)}{B(\alpha, \beta)} = \prod_{r=0}^{k-1} \frac{\alpha+r}{\alpha+\beta+r} \]

Matching the first two moments:

\[ \overline{X} = \frac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta}, \quad \overline{X^2} = \frac{\alpha(\alpha+1)}{(\alpha+\beta)(\alpha+\beta+1)} \]

Solving gives the moment estimators:

\[ \hat{\alpha} = \overline{X} \left[ \frac{\overline{X}(1-\overline{X})}{\overline{X^2} - \overline{X}^2} - 1 \right], \quad \hat{\beta} = (1-\overline{X}) \left[ \frac{\overline{X}(1-\overline{X})}{\overline{X^2} - \overline{X}^2} - 1 \right] \]

The asymptotic distribution can be obtained by computing the Jacobian matrix and the covariance matrix in the theorem, yielding \(\sqrt{n}(\hat{\theta}_n - \theta) \Rightarrow N(0, \Sigma)\).

docs.title: 2.2 Exponential Family
docs.text:
Assume \(X_1, ..., X_n \sim F_\theta\), and the density belongs to an exponential family:

\[ p_\theta(x) = c(\theta)h(x)\exp\{\theta^T t(x)\} \]

The log-likelihood is \(l_\theta(x) = \log c(\theta) + \log h(x) + \theta^T t(x)\). The score function is \(\dot{l}_\theta(x) = \frac{\dot{c}(\theta)}{c(\theta)} + t(x) = t(x) - E_\theta t(X)\) (since \(E \dot{l}_\theta(X) = 0\) implies \(\dot{c}(\theta)/c(\theta) = -E_\theta t(X)\)).

Therefore, the Maximum Likelihood Estimator (MLE) is essentially a Moment Estimator (ME):

\[ \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n t(X_i) = E_\theta t(X) = e(\theta) \]

If \(e(\theta)\) is continuously differentiable and \(E_\theta \|t(X)\|^2 < \infty\), then \(\hat{\theta}_{mle} = \hat{\theta}_{me}\), and:

\[ \sqrt{n}(\hat{\theta}_{me} - \theta) \rightarrow N\left(0, [(e'(\theta))^{-1}] var_\theta(t(X)) [(e'(\theta))^{-1}]^T \right) = N(0, I_\theta^{-1}) \]

where \(I_\theta\) is the Fisher information matrix \(I_\theta = var(\dot{l}_\theta(X))\).

Limitations of Moment Estimation: 1. The statistical efficiency of ME is usually lower than that of MLE. 2. ME can be semiparametric, while MLE must be fully parametric. 3. The choice of "moments" to match is somewhat ad-hoc.

docs.title: 3. Generalized Method of Moments (GMM)
docs.text: MLE requires a full distributional specification of the model (e.g., joint density, conditional density). GMM, proposed by Hansen (1982), generalizes moment estimation and does not require specifying the distribution density, only moment constraints. This makes GMM very attractive for models with infinite-dimensional nuisance parameters (semiparametric).

docs.title: 3.1 Setup and Examples
docs.text:
Let \(\{w_i\}_{i=1}^n\) be i.i.d. random variables in \(\mathbb{R}^m\), \(g(w_i; \theta) \in \mathbb{R}^r\) be a known \(r\)-dimensional function, and parameter \(\theta \in \Theta \subset \mathbb{R}^p\). Assume there exists a unique true parameter \(\theta_0 \in \Theta\) such that:

\[ E\{g(w_i; \theta_0)\} = 0 \]
  • Just-identified: When \(r = p\) (number of moment conditions equals number of parameters), statisticians usually directly solve the equation \(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n g(w_i, \theta) = 0\).
  • Over-identified: When \(r > p\), the system of equations cannot be solved exactly; this is common in econometrics and requires GMM.

Example 1: Parametric Regression Data \(\{w_i = (Y_i, X_i)\}_{i=1}^n\). Model \(Y_i = m(X_i, \theta) + \epsilon_i\), with \(E(\epsilon_i | X_i) = 0\). The least squares score function is \(g(w_i, \theta) = \frac{\partial m(X_i, \theta)}{\partial \theta}(Y_i - m(X_i, \theta))\). Here \(r = p\), can be solved directly.

Example 2: Poisson Regression Suppose count data \(Y_i\) satisfy \(E(Y_i | X_i) = \mu(X_i, \theta)\) and \(Var(Y_i | X_i) = \mu(X_i, \theta)\). We can combine information from both the mean and variance to construct an over-identified score function:

\[ g(w_i, \theta) = \begin{pmatrix} g_1(w_i, \theta) \\ g_2(w_i, \theta) \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \frac{\partial \mu(X_i, \theta)}{\partial \theta}(Y_i - \mu(X_i, \theta)) \\ a(X_i, \theta) \{[Y_i - \mu(X_i, \theta)]^2 - \mu(X_i, \theta)\} \end{pmatrix} \]

This uses more information and is more efficient than using only the mean.

docs.title: 3.2 Definition of GMM Estimator
docs.text:
Definition 12.2 (GMM Estimator)

Given \(g(w_i; \theta)\) satisfying \(E g(w_i; \theta_0) = 0\). The GMM estimator \(\hat{\theta}_{GMM}\) is defined as minimizing the following quadratic form:

\[ \hat{\theta}_n = \arg\min_{\theta \in \Theta} \left( \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n g(w_i, \theta) \right)^T \hat{W}_n \left( \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n g(w_i, \theta) \right) \]

where \(\hat{W}_n\) is an \(r \times r\) nonnegative definite weight matrix satisfying \(\hat{W}_n \xrightarrow{p} W_0 > 0\), with \(W_0\) deterministic and possibly depending on \(\theta_0\).

For identification, we assume \(\theta_0\) is the unique parameter such that \(E g(w_i; \theta) = 0\). Because \(W_0 > 0\), \(\theta_0\) is also the unique minimizer of the objective function \(E\{g^T(w_i; \theta)\} W_0 E\{g(w_i; \theta)\}\).

docs.title: 4. Asymptotic Normality of GMM
docs.text:
Assumptions: (i) \(g(w, \cdot)\) is continuously differentiable at the interior point \(\theta \in Int(\Theta)\). (ii) \(G_0 = E\left( \frac{\partial g(w, \theta_0)}{\partial \theta^T} \right)_{r \times p}\) exists and has full column rank (rank \(p\)).

Theorem 12.2 (Asymptotic Normality of GMM)

Under conditions ensuring \(\hat{\theta}_n \rightarrow \theta_0\), we have:

\[ \sqrt{n}(\hat{\theta}_n - \theta_0) \xrightarrow{d} N\left(0, (G_0^T W_0 G_0)^{-1} G_0^T W_0 \Lambda_0 W_0 G_0 (G_0^T W_0 G_0)^{-1} \right) \]

where by the Central Limit Theorem, \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} \sum_{i=1}^n g(w_i, \theta_0) \rightarrow N(0, \Lambda_0)\), with \(\Lambda_0 = Var\{g(w_i; \theta_0)\}\).

Proof of Asymptotic Normality (click to expand)

From the definition that \(\hat{\theta}_n\) minimizes the quadratic form, the first-order condition (FOC) is:

\[ \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{\partial g^T(w_i, \hat{\theta}_n)}{\partial \theta} \hat{W}_n \left( \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n g(w_i, \hat{\theta}_n) \right) = 0 \quad \cdots (1) \]

(Note the matrix calculus rule: \(\frac{\partial g^T W g}{\partial \theta_i} = 2 \frac{\partial g^T}{\partial \theta_i} W g\).)

Perform a Taylor expansion of \(g(w_i, \hat{\theta}_n)\) in (1) around the true parameter \(\theta_0\):

\[ \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{\partial g^T(w_i, \hat{\theta}_n)}{\partial \theta} \hat{W}_n \left\{ \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n g(w_i, \theta_0) + \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{\partial g(w_i, \hat{\theta}_n^*)}{\partial \theta^T} (\hat{\theta}_n - \theta_0) \right\} = 0 \quad \cdots (2) \]

where \(\hat{\theta}_n^*\) lies between \(\theta_0\) and \(\hat{\theta}_n\). Since \(\hat{\theta}_n \rightarrow \theta_0\), by the Law of Large Numbers the gradient matrices converge in probability:

\[ \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{\partial g^T(w_i, \hat{\theta}_n)}{\partial \theta} \xrightarrow{p} G_0^T, \quad \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{\partial g^T(w_i, \hat{\theta}_n^*)}{\partial \theta} \xrightarrow{p} G_0^T \]

Since \(\hat{W}_n \rightarrow W_0\), from (2) we obtain:

\[ (G_0^T W_0 G_0)(\hat{\theta}_n - \theta_0) = -G_0^T W_0 \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n g(w_i, \theta_0) \{1 + o_p(1)\} \]

Let \(A_0 = G_0^T W_0 G_0\), multiply both sides by \(\sqrt{n}\):

\[ \sqrt{n}(\hat{\theta}_n - \theta_0) = -A_0^{-1} G_0^T W_0 \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} \sum_{i=1}^n g(w_i, \theta_0) + o_p(1) \]

Since \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} \sum_{i=1}^n g(w_i, \theta_0) \xrightarrow{d} N(0, \Lambda_0)\), we finally obtain:

\[ \sqrt{n}(\hat{\theta}_n - \theta_0) \xrightarrow{d} N(0, A_0^{-1} G_0^T W_0 \Lambda_0 W_0 G_0 A_0^{-1}) \]

The proof is complete.

docs.title: 5.1 Optimal Weight Matrix
docs.text:
The efficiency of the GMM estimator depends on the choice of the weight matrix \(\hat{W}_n\) (converging to \(W_0\)). Which is best?

If we choose \(W_0 = \Lambda_0^{-1}\), the middle term in the asymptotic variance becomes \(G_0^T \Lambda_0^{-1} \Lambda_0 \Lambda_0^{-1} G_0 = G_0^T \Lambda_0^{-1} G_0\), and the asymptotic variance simplifies to:

\[ Avar(\hat{\theta}_{GMM}) = A_0^{-1} = (G_0^T \Lambda_0^{-1} G_0)^{-1} \]

Hansen (1982) showed that for any \(W_0 > 0\):

\[ (G_0^T W_0^{-1} G_0)^{-1} (G_0^T W_0 \Lambda_0 W_0 G_0) (G_0^T W_0^{-1} G_0)^{-1} \ge (G_0^T \Lambda_0^{-1} G_0)^{-1} \]

Therefore, \(W_0^* = \Lambda_0^{-1}\) is the optimal weight matrix.

docs.title: 5.2 Two-step GMM Estimation
docs.text:
To obtain the optimal GMM estimator, a two-step procedure is commonly used:

  • Step 1: Construct an initial estimator \(\tilde{\theta}\) using any positive definite weight matrix (e.g., \(\hat{W}_n = I_r\)).

  • Step 2: Estimate the covariance matrix using the initial estimator to obtain the optimal weight matrix:

    \[ \hat{W}_n^* = \hat{\Lambda}^{-1} = \left( \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n g(w_i; \tilde{\theta}) g^T(w_i; \tilde{\theta}) \right)^{-1} \]

Re-estimate using \(\hat{W}_n^*\) to get the efficient GMM estimator \(\hat{\theta}_{GMM}^*\).

docs.title: 6. Hypothesis Testing and the Sargan-Hansen Test
6.1 Sargan-Hansen Test (Overidentification Test)
docs.text:
For over-identified models (\(r > p\)), we need to test whether the moment conditions themselves are valid, i.e., test \(H_0: E g(w_i; \theta_0) = 0\). Using the optimal GMM estimator \(\hat{\theta} = \hat{\theta}_{GMM}^*\), the objective function satisfies:

\[ T_n(\hat{\theta}) = n^{-1/2} \sum_{i=1}^n g^T(w_i; \hat{\theta}) \hat{W}_n^* n^{-1/2} \sum_{i=1}^n g(w_i; \hat{\theta}) \xrightarrow{d} \chi^2_{r-p} \]
  • Rejection rule: If \(T_n(\hat{\theta}) > \chi^2_{r-p, 1-\alpha}\), reject the null hypothesis.
  • In this context, \(\hat{\theta}_{GMM}\) is also called the minimum chi-square estimator.

docs.title: 6.2 Tests of Parameter Hypotheses
docs.text:
For testing \(H_0: c(\theta_0) = 0\), where \(c(\theta) \in \mathbb{R}^Q\) and \(Q \le p\):

  • Wald test:

    \[ c^T(\hat{\theta}) (\hat{V}(\hat{\theta}))^{-1} c(\hat{\theta}) \xrightarrow{d} \chi^2_Q \]

    where \(\hat{V}(\hat{\theta}) = var(c(\hat{\theta}))\).

  • Distance Discrepancy Test:

    \[ \tilde{T}_n = \frac{1}{n} \left[ \sum_{i=1}^n g^T(w_i; \tilde{\theta}_n) \hat{W}_n^* \sum_{i=1}^n g(w_i; \tilde{\theta}_n) - \sum_{i=1}^n g^T(w_i; \hat{\theta}_n) \hat{W}_n^* \sum_{i=1}^n g(w_i; \hat{\theta}_n) \right] \xrightarrow{d} \chi^2_Q \]

    where \(\tilde{\theta}_n\) is the restricted GMM estimator under the constraint \(c(\theta) = 0\).

docs.title: 7. An Important Feature of GMM: More Moment Conditions Increase Efficiency
docs.text:
If we have \(r\) restrictions, does adding more moment conditions improve efficiency? Consider \(g(w, \theta) = (g_{(r-1)}^T(w, \theta), g_r(w, \theta))^T\).

The asymptotic variance based on the \(r\)-dimensional condition is: \(V_r = [E\left(\frac{\partial g^T}{\partial \theta}\right) E^{-1}(gg^T) E\left(\frac{\partial g}{\partial \theta}\right)]^{-1}\). The asymptotic variance based on the \((r-1)\)-dimensional condition is: \(V_{r-1} = [E\left(\frac{\partial g_{(r-1)}^T}{\partial \theta}\right) E^{-1}(g_{(r-1)} g_{(r-1)}^T) E\left(\frac{\partial g_{(r-1)}}{\partial \theta}\right)]^{-1}\).

Important Feature

\[ V_r \le V_{r-1} \]

Hence, GMM with \(r\) restrictions is at least as efficient as GMM with \(r-1\) restrictions.

Proof of the Feature (click to expand)

At \(\theta = \theta_0\), partition the covariance matrix:

\[ E(gg^T) = \begin{pmatrix} E(g_{(r-1)} g_{(r-1)}^T) & E(g_{(r-1)} g_r^T) \\ E(g_{(r-1)}^T g_r) & E(g_r^2) \end{pmatrix} := \begin{pmatrix} A & B \\ B^T & C \end{pmatrix} \]

Using the partitioned matrix inversion formula, let the Schur complement be \(D = C - B^T A^{-1} B\):

\[ \begin{pmatrix} A & B \\ B^T & C \end{pmatrix}^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix} A^{-1} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix} A^{-1}B \\ -I \end{pmatrix} D^{-1} (B^T A^{-1}, -I) \]

This can be written compactly as:

\[ (E(gg^T))^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix} (E(g_{(r-1)} g_{(r-1)}^T))^{-1} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} + H \]

where \(H \ge 0\) (positive semidefinite). Substitute this into the quadratic form of the information matrix:

\[ V_r^{-1} = \left( E\left(\frac{\partial g_{(r-1)}^T}{\partial \theta}\right), E\left(\frac{\partial g_r^T}{\partial \theta}\right) \right) \left\{ \begin{pmatrix} (E(g_{(r-1)} g_{(r-1)}^T))^{-1} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} + H \right\} \begin{pmatrix} E\left(\frac{\partial g_{(r-1)}}{\partial \theta}\right) \\ E\left(\frac{\partial g_r}{\partial \theta}\right) \end{pmatrix} \]

Expanding gives:

\[ V_r^{-1} = E\left(\frac{\partial g_{(r-1)}^T}{\partial \theta}\right) (E(g_{(r-1)} g_{(r-1)}^T))^{-1} E\left(\frac{\partial g_{(r-1)}}{\partial \theta}\right) + \tilde{H} = V_{r-1}^{-1} + \tilde{H} \]

Because \(\tilde{H} \ge 0\), we have \(V_r^{-1} \ge V_{r-1}^{-1}\), i.e., \(V_r \le V_{r-1}\). This is the appeal of GMM: by adding valid moment conditions in certain directions, the asymptotic variance can be reduced.

docs.title: 1.1 Core Idea
docs.text:
In statistics, many estimands of interest are not expectations of a single observation, but rather expectations of a function of several independent observations:

\[ \theta(P) = E h(X_1, \dots, X_m), \quad X_i \stackrel{iid}{\sim} P \]

A U-statistic estimates this quantity by averaging the function \(h\) over all distinct \(m\)-tuples in the sample.

Applications:

  • Classical statistics: Unbiased sample variance, Gini mean difference, Kendall's tau, Mann-Whitney/Wilcoxon statistic.

  • Statistical inference: Asymptotic variance estimation, confidence intervals, permutation tests, rank tests.

  • Modern machine learning: AUC/ranking problems, kernel two-sample tests based on MMD, independence tests based on HSIC, scalable incomplete U-statistics.

docs.title: 1.2 Intuition: Averaging over all subsamples
docs.text:
Suppose we have a simple unbiased estimator that uses only \(m\) observations:

\[ h(X_1, \dots, X_m), \quad E h(X_1, \dots, X_m) = \theta \]

In a sample of size \(n\), there are many subsets of size \(m\). Instead of choosing just one subset, we average over all such subsets:

\[ U_n = \binom{n}{m}^{-1} \sum_{1 \le i_1 < \dots < i_m \le n} h(X_{i_1}, \dots, X_{i_m}) \]

Intuitive explanation: Given an unordered sample, averaging the naive estimator over all possible relabelings removes the artificial randomness introduced by choosing a particular subsample. This typically reduces variance while maintaining unbiasedness.

docs.title: 1.3 Example: Sample variance
docs.text:
Variance can be written as a two-sample functional:

\[ \sigma^2 = \frac{1}{2} E(X_1 - X_2)^2 \]

Thus, the unbiased sample variance can be expressed as:

\[ \binom{n}{2}^{-1} \sum_{1 \le i < j \le n} \frac{(X_i - X_j)^2}{2} = \frac{1}{n-1} \sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar{X}_n)^2 \]
  • Our commonly used formula for sample variance is not an ad hoc formula.
  • It is actually the complete average of the unbiased estimator \(\frac{(X_1 - X_2)^2}{2}\) based on two observations.

docs.title: 2. The Principles of Mathematical Statistics Behind U-statistics
docs.text: The original reason for introducing U-statistics was not just "stability through averaging"; it is a classic construction in mathematical statistics.

docs.title: 2.1 Starting Point: Estimable functional
docs.text:
If there exists a measurable function \(h\) such that:

\[ \theta(P) = E_P h(X_1, \dots, X_m) \]

where \(X_1, \dots, X_m \stackrel{iid}{\sim} P\), then the parameter \(\theta = \theta(P)\) is called an estimable functional of degree \(m\). In this case, \(h(X_1, \dots, X_m)\) is the naive unbiased estimator of \(\theta\) based on only \(m\) observations.

  • If \(m=1\), the most natural estimator is the sample mean of \(h(X_i)\).
  • If \(m \ge 2\), the sample contains many equally valid \(m\)-subsamples.
  • The U-statistic is essentially the Rao-Blackwellized version of the naive estimator, removing the arbitrariness of subsample selection.

docs.title: 2.2 Examples of Estimable Functionals
docs.text: Degree Functional \(\theta(P)\) Unbiased kernel \(h\) Interpretation 1 \(\mu = EX\) \(h(x) = x\) Many nonlinear parameters are essentially expectations, but expectations based on several independent copies. 1 \(EX^r\) \(h(x) = x^r\) U-statistics are the natural unbiased extension of sample means for such functionals. 2 \(\mu^2\) \(h(x_1, x_2) = x_1 x_2\) 2 \(\sigma^2\) \(h(x_1, x_2) = (x_1 - x_2)^2 / 2\) 2 \(F(t)^2\) \(h(x_1, x_2) = \mathbb{I}(x_1 \le t)\mathbb{I}(x_2 \le t)\) 2 \(\mathbb{P}(X < Y)\) \(h(x, y) = \mathbb{I}(x < y)\) Two-sample

docs.title: 3. Sufficient Statistics and the Rao-Blackwell Principle
3.1 Unordered Sample as a Sufficient Statistic
docs.text:
Let the order statistic (or, when ties may exist, the unordered sample/empirical measure \(P_n\)) be:

\[ T = (X_{(1)}, \dots, X_{(n)}) \]
  • For i.i.d. samples from any distribution \(P\), the unordered sample \(T\) is sufficient for \(P\).
  • Equivalently, given \(T\), the remaining randomness is just the random assignment of labels to the observations.
  • This conditional label distribution is free of \(P\): all label permutations are equally likely (accounting for multiplicities if ties exist).

docs.title: 3.2 Rao-Blackwell Principle
docs.text:
If \(A\) is an unbiased estimator, then the conditional expectation \(E(A|T)\) remains unbiased, and:

\[ Var\{E(A|T)\} \le Var(A) \]

Thus, conditioning on the unordered sample removes label noise without changing the target of estimation.

docs.title: 4. Key Identity: Conditional Expectation Constructs the U-statistic
docs.text:
Start from the naive unbiased estimator:

\[ A = h(X_1, \dots, X_m), \quad E A = \theta \]

Given the unordered sample \(T\), the first \(m\) labels are drawn uniformly without replacement from \(\{1, \dots, n\}\). Therefore:

\[ E\{h(X_1, \dots, X_m) | T\} = \frac{(n-m)!}{n!} \sum_{(i_1, \dots, i_m): \text{distinct}} h(X_{i_1}, \dots, X_{i_m}) \] \[ = \binom{n}{m}^{-1} \sum_{1 \le i_1 < \dots < i_m \le n} h^{sym}(X_{i_1}, \dots, X_{i_m}) \]

If the kernel \(h\) is symmetric, then this is exactly the U-statistic:

\[ U_n = \binom{n}{m}^{-1} \sum_{1 \le i_1 < \dots < i_m \le n} h(X_{i_1}, \dots, X_{i_m}) \]

docs.title: 4.1 Implications of the Rao-Blackwell Construction
docs.text:
The identity above provides a finite-sample explanation of why "complete averaging" is the canonical estimator.

  1. Unbiasedness:

    \[ E U_n = E\{E(A|T)\} = E A = \theta \]

  2. Variance reduction relative to a single subsample:

    \[ Var(U_n) = Var\{E(A|T)\} \le Var(A) \]

  3. Connection to UMVU theory: In parametric models, if \(T\) is complete and sufficient, then by the Lehmann-Scheffé theorem, the same conditional expectation is the uniformly minimum variance unbiased estimator (UMVU).

What remains nontrivial: The terms in the sum of \(U_n\) are dependent due to overlap between different subsamples. The subsequent sections of this chapter develop projection and overlap tools to quantify this dependence.

docs.title: 5.1 Example: Deriving sample variance via Rao-Blackwellization
docs.text:
For \(\theta = \sigma^2\), the unbiased estimator based on two observations is:

\[ A = \frac{(X_1 - X_2)^2}{2}, \quad E A = \frac{1}{2} E(X_1 - X_2)^2 = \sigma^2 \]

Conditioning on the unordered sample \(T\) yields:

\[ E(A|T) = \binom{n}{2}^{-1} \sum_{1 \le i < j \le n} \frac{(X_i - X_j)^2}{2} = \frac{1}{n-1} \sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar{X}_n)^2 \]

Thus, the familiar unbiased sample variance is the Rao-Blackwellized version of the naive two-point estimator.

Note: The formula with denominator \(n-1\) is not an empirical correction trick; it is a natural consequence of averaging over all data pairs.

docs.title: 5.2 Example: Removing the diagonal bias
docs.text:
Fix \(t \in \mathbb{R}\) and let \(p = F(t)\). The parameter \(p^2\) has the following unbiased two-sample kernel:

\[ h(x_1, x_2) = \mathbb{I}(x_1 \le t)\mathbb{I}(x_2 \le t) \]

The corresponding U-statistic is:

\[ U_n(t) = \frac{1}{n(n-1)} \sum_{i \ne j} \mathbb{I}(X_i \le t)\mathbb{I}(X_j \le t) \]

If we let \(N_t = \sum_{i=1}^n \mathbb{I}(X_i \le t)\), then:

\[ U_n(t) = \frac{N_t(N_t - 1)}{n(n-1)}, \quad E U_n(t) = p^2 \]

In contrast, the traditional plug-in estimator includes the diagonal terms and satisfies:

\[ F_n(t)^2 = (N_t / n)^2 \] \[ E F_n(t)^2 = p^2 + \frac{p(1-p)}{n} \]

(with a bias of \(O(1/n)\)).

docs.title: 6. From Intuition to Asymptotic Theory
docs.text:
The Rao-Blackwell picture explains the construction of U-statistics; the projection picture will explain their asymptotic properties.

  • Reveals how the conditional expectation of the kernel changes with one observation (first-order effect):

    \[ h_1(x) - \theta = E\{h(x, X_2, \dots, X_m)\} - \theta \]

    If the variance of this first-order effect is positive, then many weakly dependent overlapping terms sum to a normal limit:

    \[ \sqrt{n}(U_n - \theta) \approx \frac{m}{\sqrt{n}} \sum_{i=1}^n \{h_1(X_i) - \theta\} \]

  • If the first-order effect is zero, the statistic is degenerate, and higher-order interactions determine its convergence rate and limiting distribution.

Summary: U-statistics emerge from sufficiency and Rao-Blackwellization, but their analysis relies primarily on Hoeffding's projection.

docs.title: 7. Formal Definitions: Symmetric Kernels and U-statistics
docs.text:
Assume \(X_1, \dots, X_n \stackrel{iid}{\sim} P\) on a measurable space \((\mathcal{X}, \mathcal{A})\), and fix \(m < n\).

Definition 9.1 (Symmetric kernel)

A measurable function \(h: \mathcal{X}^m \rightarrow \mathbb{R}\) is called a symmetric kernel of order \(m\) if for any permutation \(\pi\) of \(\{1, \dots, m\}\),

\[ h(x_1, \dots, x_m) = h(x_{\pi(1)}, \dots, x_{\pi(m)}) \]

If \(h\) is not symmetric, it can be replaced by its symmetrization:

\[ h^{sym}(x_1, \dots, x_m) = \frac{1}{m!} \sum_{\pi} h(x_{\pi(1)}, \dots, x_{\pi(m)}) \]

If the original statistic averages over unordered subsets, the U-statistic remains unchanged after symmetrization.

Definition 9.2 (U-statistic)

Assume \(E|h(X_1, \dots, X_m)| < \infty\) and define:

\[ \theta = \theta(P) = E h(X_1, \dots, X_m) \]

The U-statistic based on the kernel \(h\) of order \(m\) is defined as:

\[ U_n = \binom{n}{m}^{-1} \sum_{1 \le i_1 < \dots < i_m \le n} h(X_{i_1}, \dots, X_{i_m}) \]

Clearly, \(E U_n = \theta\). The "U" stands for Unbiasedness: the expectation of each term is \(\theta\).

docs.title: 8. Relationship with Plug-in and V-statistics
docs.text:
The empirical distribution can be written as \(P_n = n^{-1} \sum_{i=1}^n \delta_{X_i}\). A natural plug-in estimator is the V-statistic:

\[ V_n = \int h(x_1, \dots, x_m) dP_n(x_1) \dots dP_n(x_m) = \frac{1}{n^m} \sum_{i_1, \dots, i_m = 1}^n h(X_{i_1}, \dots, X_{i_m}) \]
  • \(V_n\) includes repeated indices, so it may be biased for finite \(n\).
  • \(U_n\) removes repeated indices and is strictly unbiased.
  • For fixed \(m\) and regular kernels, the difference between \(U_n\) and \(V_n\) is typically \(O_p(n^{-1})\), but this difference can be important when dealing with degenerate limits.

docs.title: 9. Core Examples in Modern and Classical Statistics
9.1 Rank Example: Kendall's tau
docs.text:
Example 9.3 (Kendall's tau)

For bivariate data \(Z_i = (X_i, Y_i)\), the parameter of interest is:

\[ \tau = E[\text{sign}\{(X_1 - X_2)(Y_1 - Y_2)\}] \]

The corresponding kernel is:

\[ h(z_1, z_2) = \text{sign}\{(x_1 - x_2)(y_1 - y_2)\} \]

The resulting U-statistic estimator is:

\[ \hat{\tau} = \binom{n}{2}^{-1} \sum_{i < j} h(Z_i, Z_j) \]

It is often used to measure monotone association between variables.

docs.title: 9.2 Classic Test: Mann-Whitney and AUC
docs.text:
Example 9.4 (Mann-Whitney parameter and AUC)

For two independent samples \(X_1, \dots, X_n \sim P\) and \(Y_1, \dots, Y_N \sim Q\), the parameter is defined as:

\[ \theta = \mathbb{P}(X > Y) + \frac{1}{2}\mathbb{P}(X = Y) \]

This parameter can be estimated by a two-sample U-statistic:

\[ U_{n,N} = \frac{1}{nN} \sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j=1}^N \left\{ \mathbb{I}(X_i > Y_j) + \frac{1}{2}\mathbb{I}(X_i = Y_j) \right\} \]

In machine learning, this corresponds to the population AUC (Area Under the ROC Curve) for a scoring rule.

docs.title: 9.3 Kernel Two-sample Test: MMD
docs.text:
Let \(X, X' \sim P\) and \(Y, Y' \sim Q\) be independent, and let \(k\) be a positive definite kernel. The squared Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) is defined as:

\[ \text{MMD}^2(P, Q) = E k(X, X') + E k(Y, Y') - 2 E k(X, Y) \]

For paired observations \(Z_i = (X_i, Y_i)\), its unbiased estimator is a second-order U-statistic:

\[ \widehat{\text{MMD}}_u^2 = \binom{n}{2}^{-1} \sum_{i < j} h(Z_i, Z_j) \]

where the symmetric kernel is:

\[ h(z_i, z_j) = k(x_i, x_j) + k(y_i, y_j) - k(x_i, y_j) - k(x_j, y_i) \]
  • Property: Under the null hypothesis \(H_0: P = Q\), the first-order projection of this kernel is zero. Therefore, the statistic is degenerate, and its null limiting distribution is a weighted chi-square type.

docs.title: 9.4 Kernel Independence Test: HSIC
docs.text:
Let \(Z = (X, Y)\), and let \(k\) and \(l\) be kernels on the spaces of \(X\) and \(Y\), respectively. The Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion (HSIC) satisfies: for characteristic kernels,

\[ \text{HSIC}(P_{XY}, k, l) = 0 \quad \text{if and only if } X \text{ and } Y \text{ are independent} \]
  • The unbiased empirical HSIC is a U-statistic of order 4.
  • Under the independence assumption, it is degenerate: its first-order projection vanishes.
  • This explains why its null distribution is not a simple normal limit; in practice, spectral methods, permutation tests, or wild-bootstrap are used for approximation.

Key takeaway: Degenerate U-statistics are not theoretical curiosities; they are at the absolute core of modern kernel tests.

docs.title: 10. Conditional Projections and Hoeffding's Variance Formula
docs.text: To quantify the dependence among cross-terms in a U-statistic, we introduce conditional projection tools.

docs.title: 10.1 Conditional Projections
docs.text:
Assume the kernel has finite second moment: \(E h^2(X_1, \dots, X_m) < \infty\). For \(k = 0, 1, \dots, m\), define the conditional expectation projection:

  • For \(k=0\):
\[ h_0 = \theta \]
  • For \(1 \le k \le m\):
\[ h_k(x_1, \dots, x_k) = E\{h(x_1, \dots, x_k, X_{k+1}, \dots, X_m)\} \]

Note that \(h_m = h\), and the expectation satisfies:

\[ E h_k(X_1, \dots, X_k) = \theta \]

Next, define the centered projection:

\[ \tilde{h}_k(x_1, \dots, x_k) = h_k(x_1, \dots, x_k) - \theta \]

and the corresponding projection variance:

\[ \xi_k = Var\{h_k(X_1, \dots, X_k)\} \]

docs.title: 10.2 Monotonicity of the Projection Variances
docs.text:
By the tower property of conditional expectation:

\[ h_k(X_1, \dots, X_k) = E\{h_{k+1}(X_1, \dots, X_{k+1}) | X_1, \dots, X_k\} \]

Applying Jensen's inequality yields:

\[ \xi_k \le \xi_{k+1} \]

where \(\xi_0 = 0\) and \(\xi_m = Var\{h(X_1, \dots, X_m)\}\).

  • Intuition: For \(k = 0, 1, \dots, m-1\), the projection variance \(\xi_k\) measures how much of the total variation of the kernel is already explained by knowing \(k\) of its \(m\) arguments.

docs.title: 10.3 Hoeffding's Variance Formula
docs.text:
Theorem 9.5 (Hoeffding's variance formula)

If \(E h^2(X_1, \dots, X_m) < \infty\), then the exact variance of the U-statistic is:

\[ Var(U_n) = \binom{n}{m}^{-1} \sum_{k=1}^m \binom{m}{k} \binom{n-m}{m-k} \xi_k \]

Moreover, it satisfies the following important properties:

  • 1. Upper and lower bounds:
\[ \frac{m^2}{n} \xi_1 \le Var(U_n) \le \frac{m}{n} \xi_m \]
  • 2. Monotonicity in sample size:
\[ (n+1)Var(U_{n+1}) \le n Var(U_n) \]
  • 3. Asymptotic variance under degeneracy: If there exists an integer \(r\) such that \(\xi_1 = \dots = \xi_{r-1} = 0\) and \(\xi_r > 0\), then:
\[ Var(U_n) = \frac{r! \binom{m}{r}^2 \xi_r}{n^r} + O(n^{-(r+1)}) \] Proof of Theorem 9.5 (click to expand)

Step 1: Computing covariance by overlap

Let \(\tilde{h} = h - \theta\) be the centered kernel. If index subsets \(I\) and \(J\) have exactly \(k\) common elements (i.e., \(|I \cap J| = k\)), then conditioning on those \(k\) common observations yields:

\[ E\{\tilde{h}(X_I)\tilde{h}(X_J)\} = E \left[ E\{\tilde{h}(X_I) | X_{I \cap J}\} E\{\tilde{h}(X_J) | X_{I \cap J}\} \right] \]

By the definition of projections, this equals:

\[ = E\{\tilde{h}_k(X_1, \dots, X_k)^2\} = \xi_k \]

This is the most crucial step: the covariance depends only on the number \(k\) of shared indices between the two subsets.

Step 2: Counting overlaps

Fix a particular subset \(I\). We need to count how many subsets \(J\) of size \(m\) share exactly \(k\) elements with \(I\). Combinatorially, this is equivalent to choosing \(k\) elements from the \(m\) elements of \(I\), and \(m-k\) elements from the \(n-m\) elements not in \(I\):

\[ \binom{m}{k}\binom{n-m}{m-k} \]

Expanding the variance as a double sum:

\[ Var(U_n) = \binom{n}{m}^{-2} \sum_{I} \sum_{J} Cov\{h(X_I), h(X_J)\} \]

Grouping terms:

\[ = \binom{n}{m}^{-2} \sum_{I} \sum_{k=1}^m \binom{m}{k}\binom{n-m}{m-k} \xi_k \]

The outer sum over \(I\) has \(\binom{n}{m}\) terms, hence:

\[ = \binom{n}{m}^{-1} \sum_{k=1}^m \binom{m}{k}\binom{n-m}{m-k} \xi_k \]

(Note: when \(k=0\), the two subsets are completely independent, covariance is 0, and the corresponding term vanishes.) This completes the proof. \(\square\)

docs.title: 10.4 Rates: Why Degeneracy Matters
docs.text:
Analyzing the coefficients of \(\xi_k\) in the variance formula, we can perform an asymptotic expansion:

\[ \binom{n}{m}^{-1}\binom{m}{k}\binom{n-m}{m-k} = \binom{m}{k}^2 k! n^{-k} + O(n^{-(k+1)}) \]

Thus, the first non-zero projection variance determines the stochastic order of the U-statistic.

If \(\xi_1 = \dots = \xi_{r-1} = 0\) and \(\xi_r > 0\), then the fluctuation is:

\[ U_n - \theta = O_p(n^{-r/2}) \]
  • When \(r = 1\): The U-statistic is non-degenerate, with \(\sqrt{n}\) rate and normal limit distribution.
  • When \(r = 2\): The U-statistic is degenerate of order 2, with a faster convergence rate (\(n^{-1}\)), and the limit distribution is non-Gaussian (typically a weighted sum of infinitely many chi-square random variables).

docs.title: 11. Asymptotic Properties of U-Statistics
docs.text:
In the asymptotic theory of U-statistics, the main challenge is: when \(m > 1\), the U-statistic \(U_n\) is not a simple sum of independent random variables (even though the original sample \(\{X_i\}\) is independent, different subsamples overlap). This prevents direct application of the classical central limit theorem (CLT) for independent random variables.

Solution: Find the projection of \(U_n\) onto the individual observations \(X_1, \dots, X_n\). Specifically, by computing the conditional expectations \(E(U_n|X_i)\) (\(i=1, \dots, n\)), we construct a new statistic:

\[ \tilde{U}_n = EU_n + \sum_{i=1}^n \{E(U_n|X_i) - EU_n\} \]

Since \(X_i\) are independent, \(\tilde{U}_n\) is a sum of i.i.d. random variables, and the CLT can be applied directly. If we can show that the residual term \(U_n - \tilde{U}_n\) is asymptotically negligible, then by Slutsky's theorem, the asymptotic normality of \(U_n\) follows.

docs.title: 11.1 Definition and Lemma for Projection of U-statistics
docs.text:
Definition 9.6 (Projection)

Let \(U_n\) be a U-statistic based on the sample \(\{X_1, \dots, X_n\}\). The projection of \(U_n\) onto \(\{X_1, \dots, X_n\}\) is defined as:

\[ \tilde{U}_n = EU_n + \sum_{i=1}^n \{E(U_n|X_i) - EU_n\} := \theta + \sum_{i=1}^n \{\varphi_n(X_i) - \theta\} \quad \text{--- (9.1)} \]

where \(\varphi_n(X_i) = E(U_n|X_i)\).

If \(\{X_i\}\) are i.i.d. (or independent), then the sequence \(\{\varphi_n(X_i)\}\) is also i.i.d. (or independent). Clearly, by properties of conditional expectation, \(E\tilde{U}_n = \theta\) (if \(h = h_m\), then equals \(EU_n\)).

Based on the covariance property \(cov(U_n, \tilde{U}_n) = var(\tilde{U}_n)\) (see Shao p179), we obtain the following key lemma regarding the variance of the projection error:

Lemma 9.7

Let \(U_n\) be a U-statistic with \(var(U_n) < \infty\) for each \(n\). Then:

\[ E(U_n - \tilde{U}_n)^2 = var(U_n - \tilde{U}_n) = var(U_n) - var(\tilde{U}_n) \]

docs.title: 11.2 Asymptotic Distribution Theorem for U-statistics
docs.text:
Theorem 9.8 (Limit distribution of U-statistics)

Let \(U_n\) be a U-statistic based on i.i.d. sample \(\{X_i\}_{i=1}^n\), and assume \(Eh^2(X_1, \dots, X_m) < \infty\).

  • (i) Non-degenerate case: If the first-order projection variance \(\xi_1 = var(\tilde{h}_1(X)) > 0\), then:
\[ \sqrt{n}(U_n - EU_n) \xrightarrow{d} N(0, m^2\xi_1) \]
  • (ii) First-order degenerate case: If \(\xi_1 = 0\) but \(\xi_2 > 0\), then:
\[ n(U_n - EU_n) \xrightarrow{d} \frac{m(m-1)}{2} \sum_{j=1}^\infty \lambda_j(\chi_{1,j}^2 - 1) \]

where \(\{\chi_{1,j}^2\}_{j \ge 1}\) are i.i.d. \(\chi_1^2\) random variables, and \(\lambda_j\) are constants (eigenvalues) satisfying \(\sum_{j=1}^\infty \lambda_j^2 = \xi_2\).

docs.title: 11.3 Proof of Theorem 9.8 (i) (Non-degenerate case)
docs.text:
Proof of Theorem 9.8 (i) (click to expand)

First, compute the conditional expectation \(E(U_n|X_1)\):

\[ E(U_n|X_1) = \binom{n}{m}^{-1} \sum_{I} E(h(X_{i_1}, \dots, X_{i_m})|X_1) \]

Split it into two parts:

\[ = \binom{n}{m}^{-1} \left\{ \sum_{I_1} E(h(X_{i_1}, \dots, X_{i_m})|X_1) + \sum_{I_2} \theta \right\} \]

where \(I_1\) consists of all combinations \((i_1, \dots, i_m)\) that contain index \(1\), and \(I_2\) consists of the other combinations not containing \(1\). By combinatorial counting:

\[ |I_1| = \binom{n-1}{m-1}, \quad |I_2| = \binom{n-1}{m} \]

Substituting:

\[ E(U_n|X_1) = \frac{m!(n-m)!}{n!} \left[ \frac{(n-1)!}{(m-1)!(n-m)!} h_1(X_1) + \frac{(n-1)!}{m!(n-m-1)!} \theta \right] \]

After simplification:

\[ = \frac{m}{n} h_1(X_1) + \frac{n-m}{n} \theta \]

Next, construct the projection statistic \(\tilde{U}_n\):

\[ \tilde{U}_n = \theta + \sum_{i=1}^n \left\{ \frac{m}{n} h_1(X_i) + \frac{n-m}{n} \theta - \theta \right\} \]

Simplify:

\[ = \theta + \frac{m}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \{h_1(X_i) - \theta\} = \theta + \frac{m}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \tilde{h}_1(X_i) \]

By the CLT for i.i.d. random variables, since \(E\tilde{h}_1^2(X_1) < \infty\):

\[ \sqrt{n}(\tilde{U}_n - \theta) \xrightarrow{d} N(0, m^2\xi_1) \]

provided \(\xi_1 > 0\) (because \(var(\tilde{U}_n) = m^2\xi_1/n\)).

On the other hand, applying Lemma 9.7:

\[ E(U_n - \tilde{U}_n)^2 = var(U_n) - var(\tilde{U}_n) \]

Using the expansion of \(var(U_n)\) from Theorem 9.5:

\[ = \frac{m^2\xi_1}{n} + O(n^{-2}) - \frac{m^2\xi_1}{n} = O(n^{-2}) \]

By Chebyshev's inequality, for any \(\epsilon > 0\):

\[ P(\sqrt{n}|U_n - \tilde{U}_n| > \epsilon) \le \frac{n E(U_n - \tilde{U}_n)^2}{\epsilon^2} = O(n^{-1}) \rightarrow 0 \]

thus \(\sqrt{n}(U_n - \tilde{U}_n) = o_p(1)\). Finally, using the algebraic identity:

\[ \sqrt{n}(U_n - \theta) = \sqrt{n}(\tilde{U}_n - \theta) + \sqrt{n}(U_n - \tilde{U}_n) \]

Applying Slutsky's theorem:

\[ = \sqrt{n}(\tilde{U}_n - \theta) + o_p(1) \xrightarrow{d} N(0, m^2\xi_1) \]

This completes the proof. \(\square\)

docs.title: 11.4 Proof of Theorem 9.8 (ii) (Degenerate case)
docs.text:
Degenerate U-statistics correspond to \(\xi_1 = 0\). In this case, the scaling factor becomes \(n\) instead of \(\sqrt{n}\), and the limiting distribution is a linear combination of infinite chi-square variables.

Proof of Theorem 9.8 (ii) (click to expand)

We now prove the degenerate U-statistic theorem 9.8(ii). Our goal is to show:

\[ n(\hat{U}_n - heta) := rac{m(m-1)}{n-1} \sum_{1 \le i < j \le n} ilde{h}_2(X_i, X_j) \xrightarrow{d} rac{m(m-1)}{2} Y \]

where \(Y = \sum_{j=1}^\infty \lambda_j(W_j^2 - 1)\), and \(W_1^2, W_2^2, \dots\) are independent \(\chi_1^2\) random variables. Let:

\[ T_n = rac{1}{n} \sum_{i e j} ilde{h}_2(X_i, X_j) \]

Then:

\[ n(\hat{U}_n - heta) = rac{m(m-1)}{2} rac{n}{n-1} T_n \]

Therefore, the goal reduces to proving \(T_n \xrightarrow{d} Y\). We will use characteristic functions to prove this, i.e., we need to show for any \(x\):

\[ E_F\{e^{ixT_n}\} ightarrow E\{e^{ixY}\}, \quad n ightarrow \infty \quad ext{--- (9.2)} \]

We will use a special representation of \( ilde{h}_2(x, y)\). Let \(\{\phi_j(\cdot)\}\) be orthonormal eigenfunctions associated with eigenvalues \(\{\lambda_j\}\) corresponding to \( ilde{h}_2\). That is, they satisfy:

\[ E_F\{\phi_j(X)\phi_k(X)\} = egin{cases} 1, & j = k \ 0, & j e k \end{cases} \]

and \( ilde{h}_2(x, y)\) can be expressed as the mean square limit of \(\sum_{k=1}^K \lambda_k \phi_k(x) \phi_k(y)\) as \(K ightarrow \infty\). That is:

\[ \lim_{K ightarrow \infty} E_F\left\{ \left[ ilde{h}_2(X_1, X_2) - \sum_{k=1}^K \lambda_k \phi_k(X_1) \phi_k(X_2) ight]^2 ight\} = 0 \]

In the mean square sense we write:

\[ ilde{h}_2(x, y) = \sum_{k=1}^\infty \lambda_k \phi_k(x) \phi_k(y) \quad ext{--- (9.3)} \]

and correspondingly:

\[ ilde{h}_1(x) = \sum_{k=1}^\infty \lambda_k \phi_k(x) E_F\{\phi_k(X)\} \quad ext{--- (9.4)} \]

Since the degeneracy condition \(\xi_1 = 0\) holds, we must have for all \(k\):

\[ E_F\{\phi_k(X)\} = 0 \quad ext{--- (9.5)} \]

Moreover, by orthogonality:

\[ E_F\left\{ \left[ ilde{h}_2(X_1, X_2) - \sum_{k=1}^K \lambda_k \phi_k(X_1) \phi_k(X_2) ight]^2 ight\} = E_F\{ ilde{h}_2^2(X_1, X_2)\} - \sum_{k=1}^K \lambda_k^2 \]

which implies that the sum of squares of eigenvalues converges:

\[ \sum_{k=1}^\infty \lambda_k^2 = E_F\{ ilde{h}_2^2(X_1, X_2)\} < \infty \]

Substituting the representation into \(T_n\) yields:

\[ T_n = rac{1}{n} \sum_{i e j} \sum_{k=1}^\infty \lambda_k \phi_k(X_i) \phi_k(X_j) \]

Now truncate to the first \(K\) terms and define \(T_{nK}\):

\[ T_{nK} = rac{1}{n} \sum_{i e j} \sum_{k=1}^K \lambda_k \phi_k(X_i) \phi_k(X_j) \]

Using the inequality \(|e^{iz} - 1| \le |z|\) for complex numbers, we can bound the truncation error of the characteristic function:

\[ |E\{e^{ixT_n}\} - E\{e^{ixT_{nK}}\}| \le E|e^{ixT_n} - e^{ixT_{nK}}| \le |x| E|T_n - T_{nK}| \le |x| [E(T_n - T_{nK})^2]^{1/2} \quad ext{--- (9.6)} \]

Observe that \(T_n - T_{nK}\) is itself a U-statistic:

\[ T_n - T_{nK} = rac{2}{n} inom{n}{2} U_{nK} \]

where:

\[ U_{nK} = inom{n}{2}^{-1} \sum_{i < j} g_K(X_i, X_j) \]

with the truncated kernel:

\[ g_K(x, y) = ilde{h}_2(x, y) - \sum_{k=1}^K \lambda_k \phi_k(x) \phi_k(y) \]

It can be verified that this truncated kernel satisfies:

\[ E_F\{g_K(X_1, X_2)\} = 0 \] \[ E_F\{g_K^2(X_1, X_2)\} = \sum_{k=K+1}^\infty \lambda_k^2 \] \[ E_F\{g_K(x, X)\} = 0 \]

Hence \(E(U_{nK}) = 0\), and by Theorem 9.5:

\[ E\{U_{nK}^2\} = inom{n}{2}^{-1} \sum_{k=K+1}^\infty \lambda_k^2 \]

Therefore:

\[ E(T_n - T_{nK})^2 = (n-1)^2 inom{n}{2}^{-1} \sum_{k=K+1}^\infty \lambda_k^2 \le 2 \sum_{k=K+1}^\infty \lambda_k^2 \quad ext{--- (9.7)} \]

Now fix \(x\) and let \(\epsilon > 0\). Choose and fix \(K\) large enough so that:

\[ |x| \left( 2 \sum_{k=K+1}^\infty \lambda_k^2 ight)^{1/2} < \epsilon \]

Combining (9.6) and (9.7), we have established:

\[ |E\{e^{ixT_n}\} - E\{e^{ixT_{nK}}\}| < \epsilon, \quad ext{for all } n \quad ext{--- (9.8)} \]

Next we prove:

\[ T_{nK} \Rightarrow Y_K = \sum_{k=1}^K \lambda_k (W_k^2 - 1) \quad ext{--- (9.9)} \]

We can write \(T_{nK}\) as:

\[ T_{nK} = \sum_{k=1}^K \lambda_k (W_{kn}^2 - Z_{kn}) \]

where \(W_{kn} = n^{-1/2} \sum_{i=1}^n \phi_k(X_i)\) and \(Z_{kn} = n^{-1} \sum_{i=1}^n \phi_k^2(X_i)\). From the earlier conditions, for all \(k\) and \(n\), \(E(W_{kn}) = 0\) and:

\[ Cov\{W_{jn}, W_{kn}\} = egin{cases} 1, & j = k \ 0, & j e k \end{cases} \quad ext{for all } j, k ext{ and } n \]

Thus, by the multivariate Lindeberg-Levy CLT:

\[ (W_{1n}, \dots, W_{Kn}) \xrightarrow{d} N(0, I_{K imes K}) \]

Meanwhile, because \(E_F\{\phi_k^2(X)\} = 1\), the classical strong law of large numbers (SLLN) gives:

\[ (Z_{1n}, \dots, Z_{Kn}) \xrightarrow{wp1} (1, \dots, 1) \]

This proves (9.9), i.e., for sufficiently large \(n\):

\[ |E\{e^{ixT_{nK}}\} - E\{e^{ixY_K}\}| < 2\epsilon \quad ext{--- (9.10)} \]

Finally, we prove:

\[ |E\{e^{ixY_K}\} - E\{e^{ixY}\}| < \epsilon [E(W_1^2 - 1)^2]^{1/2}, \quad ext{for all } n \quad ext{--- (9.11)} \]

To complete this step, we define the random variables \(W_1^2, W_2^2, \dots\) on a common probability space, and express \(Y\) as the mean square limit of \(Y_K\) as \(K ightarrow \infty\). Then:

\[ |E\{e^{ixY_K}\} - E\{e^{ixY}\}| \le |x| [E(Y - Y_K)^2]^{1/2} \] \[ \le |x| [E(W_1^2 - 1)^2]^{1/2} \left[ \sum_{k=K+1}^\infty \lambda_k^2 ight]^{1/2} \]

This yields (9.11). Combining (9.8), (9.10), and (9.11), for any \(x\), any \(\epsilon > 0\), and sufficiently large \(n\), we have:

\[ |E\{e^{ixT_n}\} - E\{e^{ixY}\}| \le \epsilon \{2 + [E(W_1^2 - 1)^2]^{1/2}\} \]

This proves \(T_n \xrightarrow{d} Y\) as \(n ightarrow \infty\), which is the desired result of Theorem 9.8 (ii). \(\square\)

docs.title: 12. Degeneracy and Hypothesis Testing
docs.text:
Many test statistics in practical applications have the following pattern:

  • Non-degenerate under the alternative hypothesis \(H_1\);

  • Degenerate under the null hypothesis \(H_0\).

Classic examples:

  • MMD (Maximum Mean Discrepancy): When \(P \ne Q\), it has a normal limit with \(\sqrt{n}\) rate; under \(P = Q\), it has a degenerate weighted chi-squared limiting distribution.

  • HSIC (Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion): When variables are dependent, it has a normal limit with \(\sqrt{n}\) rate; when variables are independent, it exhibits a degenerate limit.

  • Cramer-von Mises test and integrated squared density test: Their null hypothesis limits typically come from degenerate quadratic forms.

Inference consequence:
