Since \(c\) is the supremum of \(S\), there must be a point \(y \in S\) in \((d, c]\) (otherwise \(d\) would be a smaller upper bound). Because \(y \in S\), the subinterval \([a, y]\) can be covered by finitely many open sets from \(\mathcal{A}\). Taking the union of those finitely many open sets with \(A_0\) gives a finite subcover of \([a, c]\). Hence \(c \in S\).

Claim 2: \(c = b\).

Suppose, for contradiction, that \(c < b\). By Claim 1, \(c \in S\) and \(c \in A_0\). Since \(A_0\) is open and \(c < b\), there exists a point \(e\) with \(c < e \le b\) such that the whole interval \([c, e) \subseteq A_0\). Pick any point \(y'\) in \((c, e)\). Because \([a, c]\) can be covered by finitely many open sets, adding \(A_0\) yields a finite cover of the larger interval \([a, y']\). Thus \(y' \in S\). But this contradicts the fact that \(c\) is the supremum of \(S\) (since \(y' > c\)).

Therefore our assumption is false, and \(c = b\).

Combining Claim 1 and Claim 2, we obtain \(b \in S\), i.e., the whole closed interval \([a, b]\) can be covered by finitely many open sets from \(\mathcal{A}\). This completes the proof. \(\square\)

With this lemma, we can prove the most important compactness theorem in Euclidean spaces.

Theorem 9.2 (Heine–Borel Theorem)

In Euclidean space \(\mathbb{R}^n\) with the standard topology, a subset \(S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n\) is compact if and only if it is closed and bounded.

Proof of Theorem 9.2 (Click to expand)

Sufficiency (closed and bounded \(\implies\) compact):

Suppose \(S\) is bounded. Then it can be enclosed in a sufficiently large \(n\)-dimensional closed cube, i.e., there exists a constant \(M > 0\) such that

\[ S \subseteq [-M, M]^n. \]

By Lemma 9.1, the one-dimensional closed interval \([-M, M]\) is compact. From Chapter 8, the product of finitely many compact spaces (or by Tychonoff's theorem) \([-M, M]^n\) is again compact.

Since \(S\) is closed and is a closed subset of the compact space \([-M, M]^n\), by the property that closed subsets of compact spaces are compact (Theorem 8.1), \(S\) must be compact.

Necessity (compact \(\implies\) closed and bounded):

First, \(\mathbb{R}^n\) is a Hausdorff space. By Theorem 8.2 (compact subsets of Hausdorff spaces are closed), a compact subset \(S\) must be closed.

Next, we show \(S\) is bounded. Consider the following specific open cover of \(\mathbb{R}^n\):

\[ N_k = (-k, k)^n, \quad k \in \mathbb{N}_{\ge 1}. \]

Clearly this family of expanding open cubes covers all of \(\mathbb{R}^n\), and hence covers \(S\).

Because \(S\) is compact, this open cover has a finite subcover. Since the cubes are nested (\(N_1 \subset N_2 \subset \dots\)), the largest among these finitely many open sets contains \(S\).

Thus there exists a positive integer \(K\) such that

\[ S \subseteq N_K = (-K, K)^n. \]

This directly shows \(S\) is bounded. \(\square\)

docs.title: 2. Compactness and Extreme Values of Continuous Functions
docs.text:
In calculus, a continuous function on a closed interval attains its maximum and minimum. Using the language of compactness, we can generalise this to any compact topological space.

Theorem 9.3 (Extreme Value Theorem)

Let \(X\) be a compact space and \(f: X \to \mathbb{R}\) a continuous real‑valued map. Then \(f\) attains both a maximum and a minimum on \(X\). That is, there exist \(c, d \in X\) such that for every \(x \in X\),

\[ f(c) \le f(x) \le f(d). \] Proof of Theorem 9.3 (Click to expand)

Because \(f\) is continuous and \(X\) is compact, by Theorem 8.3 (continuous maps preserve compactness), the image \(f(X)\) is a compact subset of \(\mathbb{R}\).

By the Heine–Borel theorem (Theorem 9.2), a compact set in \(\mathbb{R}\) is closed and bounded.

  • Since \(f(X)\) is bounded, by the completeness of \(\mathbb{R}\), it has a supremum \(\sup f(X)\) and an infimum \(\inf f(X)\).
  • Since \(f(X)\) is closed, it contains all its limit points, hence it contains its supremum and infimum.

Thus there exists \(d \in X\) with \(f(d) = \sup f(X)\), and there exists \(c \in X\) with \(f(c) = \inf f(X)\).

Therefore for every \(x \in X\), we have \(f(c) \le f(x) \le f(d)\). The extreme values are attained. \(\square\)

docs.title: 3. Isolated Points and the Cardinality of Compact Hausdorff Spaces
docs.text:
When examining the point‑set structure of a topological space, isolated points are an important concept.

Definition 9.1 (Isolated Point)

In a topological space \((X, au)\), a point \(x \in X\) is called an isolated point if the singleton set \(\{x\}\) itself is open (i.e., \(\{x\} \in au\)).

A profound topological conclusion is that if a compact Hausdorff space has no isolated points (such spaces are sometimes called “perfect” compact spaces), then it must contain uncountably many points.

Theorem 9.4 (A compact Hausdorff space without isolated points is uncountable)

Let \((X, au)\) be a non‑empty compact Hausdorff space. If \(X\) has no isolated points, then \(X\) is uncountable.

Proof of Theorem 9.4 (Click to expand)

We first prove a key claim.

Claim: For any \(x \in X\) and any open set \(U\) containing \(x\), there exists a non‑empty open set \(V\) such that

\[ ar{V} \subseteq U \quad ext{and} \quad x otin ar{V}. \]

Proof of the claim: Since \(X\) has no isolated points, the open set \(U\) cannot consist only of \(x\) itself. Hence there exists another point \(y \in U \setminus \{x\}\). Because \(X\) is Hausdorff, the distinct points \(x\) and \(y\) can be separated by disjoint open sets: there exist open sets \(W_1\) and \(W_2\) with

\[ x \in W_1,\quad y \in W_2,\quad W_1 \cap W_2 = \emptyset. \]

Define \(V = W_2 \cap U\). Clearly \(y \in V\), so \(V\) is a non‑empty open set. Since \(V \subseteq W_2\), its closure \( ar{V} \subseteq ar{W}_2\). Because \(x \in W_1\) and \(W_1\) is open and disjoint from \(W_2\), we have \(x otin ar{W}_2\), and consequently \(x otin ar{V}\). Moreover, since \(X\) is normal (every compact Hausdorff space is normal, hence regular), we can shrink \(V\) appropriately so that its closure is completely contained in \(U\). This proves the claim.

Now we prove the main theorem by contradiction.

Assume \(X\) is countable. Since \(X\) is non‑empty, we can list all points of \(X\) as a sequence:

\[ X = \{x_1, x_2, x_3, \dots, x_n, \dots\}. \]

Using the claim, we construct an infinite nested sequence of open sets.

  • Step 1: Take \(U_1 = X\). By the claim, for the point \(x_1\) and the open set \(U_1\), there exists a non‑empty open set \(V_1\) such that \( ar{V}_1 \subseteq U_1\) and \(x_1 otin ar{V}_1\).

  • Step 2: Now consider the non‑empty open set \(V_1\) and the next point \(x_2\). If \(x_2 otin V_1\), we arbitrarily choose a non‑empty open set inside \(V_1\) whose closure is contained in \(V_1\) and call it \(V_2\). If \(x_2 \in V_1\), then by the claim there exists a non‑empty open set \(V_2\) such that \( ar{V}_2 \subseteq V_1\) and \(x_2 otin ar{V}_2\).

  • Inductively: Suppose we have constructed a non‑empty open set \(V_{n-1}\). For the point \(x_n\), we can always find a non‑empty open set \(V_n\) satisfying

\[ ar{V}_n \subseteq V_{n-1} \quad ext{and} \quad x_n otin ar{V}_n. \]

Thus we obtain a descending chain of closed sets:

\[ ar{V}_1 \supseteq ar{V}_2 \supseteq ar{V}_3 \supseteq \dots \supseteq ar{V}_n \supseteq \dots \]

Since \(X\) is compact and these closures are non‑empty closed sets, they satisfy the finite intersection property (FIP). In a compact space, the global intersection of any family of closed sets with the FIP must be non‑empty!

Hence there exists a point \(y\) such that

\[ y \in igcap_{n=1}^\infty ar{V}_n. \]

Because \(y \in X\) and we assumed \(X = \{x_1, x_2, \dots\}\), \(y\) must be some point of the sequence, say \(y = x_k\).

But this leads to a contradiction! In the \(k\)‑th step of our construction, we explicitly required

\[ x_k otin ar{V}_k. \]

Therefore \(x_k\) cannot belong to the intersection of all the closures.

This contradiction refutes the assumption that \(X\) is countable. Hence a compact Hausdorff space without isolated points must be uncountable. \(\square\)

docs.title: 4. Nested Closed Set Theorem
docs.text:
At the end of the proof of the previous theorem, we used an important corollary about closed sets in compact spaces. We state it here explicitly as a summary of this chapter.

Corollary 9.5 (Nested Closed Set Theorem in Compact Spaces)

In a compact topological space \((X, \tau)\), let \(\{C_n\}_{n=1}^\infty\) be a descending chain of non‑empty closed sets, i.e.,

\[ C_1 \supseteq C_2 \supseteq C_3 \supseteq \dots \supseteq C_n \supseteq \dots \]

Then the infinite intersection of this chain is non‑empty:

\[ \bigcap_{n=1}^\infty C_n \ne \emptyset. \]

This corollary is essentially a direct application of the finite intersection property (FIP). It plays a central role not only in point‑set topology but also bears a striking resemblance to the “nested ball theorem” in complete metric spaces studied in functional analysis. The key difference is that the nested ball theorem in functional analysis relies on the completeness of the metric and the radii tending to zero, whereas the nested closed set theorem in topology depends purely on compactness.

docs.title: Exercise Set 1 (Homework 01 & 02)
docs.text: This section contains the problems and detailed solutions for the first and second homework assignments of the Point-Set Topology course.

docs.title: Problem 1
docs.text:
Let \(A\) be a non-empty finite set. Let \(\mathcal{P}(A) = \{A' \mid A' \subseteq A\}\) be the power set of \(A\). Let \(2^A\) denote the set of all functions of the form \(f: A \to \{\pm 1\}\).

Prove: There exists a bijection between \(\mathcal{P}(A)\) and \(2^A\), and calculate the cardinality of \(\mathcal{P}(A)\).

Solution

We can construct a bijection by defining an indicator function (characteristic function).

1. Construct the mapping: Define the mapping \(\Phi: \mathcal{P}(A) \to 2^A\). For any subset \(A' \in \mathcal{P}(A)\), its corresponding function \(f_{A'} = \Phi(A')\) is defined as follows:

\[ f_{A'}(x) = \begin{cases} 1, & x \in A' \\ -1, & x \notin A' \end{cases} \]

2. Prove \(\Phi\) is injective: Assume that for \(A_1', A_2' \in \mathcal{P}(A)\), we have \(\Phi(A_1') = \Phi(A_2')\). This means that for all \(x \in A\), \(f_{A_1'}(x) = f_{A_2'}(x)\). According to the definition of \(f_{A'}\): If \(x \in A_1'\), then \(f_{A_1'}(x) = 1\), and thus \(f_{A_2'}(x) = 1\), which by definition implies \(x \in A_2'\). Therefore, \(A_1' \subseteq A_2'\). Similarly, we can obtain \(A_2' \subseteq A_1'\). Therefore \(A_1' = A_2'\), so the mapping is injective.

3. Prove \(\Phi\) is surjective: For any function \(g \in 2^A\), where \(g: A \to \{\pm 1\}\). We can construct the set \(A_g' = \{x \in A \mid g(x) = 1\}\). Clearly \(A_g' \subseteq A\), i.e., \(A_g' \in \mathcal{P}(A)\). By construction, the function generated by \(\Phi(A_g')\) takes \(1\) when \(x \in A_g'\), and \(-1\) otherwise, which is exactly consistent with the values of \(g\). Therefore \(\Phi(A_g') = g\), so the mapping is surjective.

4. Calculate the cardinality: Since a bijection exists, \(|\mathcal{P}(A)| = |2^A|\). For a finite set \(A\), let \(|A| = n\). When constructing the function \(f: A \to \{-1, 1\}\), for every element \(x\) in \(A\), there are \(2\) value choices (\(1\) or \(-1\)). According to the multiplication principle, the total number of functions is:

\[ |2^A| = \underbrace{2 \times 2 \times \dots \times 2}_{n \text{ times}} = 2^n \]

Therefore, the cardinality of the power set is \(|\mathcal{P}(A)| = 2^{|A|}\).

docs.title: Problem 2
docs.text:
Let \(A\) be a non-empty finite set. Let \(\mathcal{F}(A)\) denote the set of all bijections \(f: A \to A\).

Prove: \(\mathcal{F}(A)\) forms a group under the operation of mapping composition \(g \circ f\). Also discuss under what conditions \(\mathcal{F}(A)\) is an abelian group.

Solution

To prove that \((\mathcal{F}(A), \circ)\) forms a group, we need to verify the four group axioms:

1. Closure: If \(f, g \in \mathcal{F}(A)\), then \(f\) and \(g\) are both bijections. Since the composition of two bijections remains a bijection, \(g \circ f: A \to A\) belongs to \(\mathcal{F}(A)\).

2. Associativity: For any \(f, g, h \in \mathcal{F}(A)\), according to the properties of mapping composition, for any \(x \in A\):

\[ [h \circ (g \circ f)](x) = h((g \circ f)(x)) = h(g(f(x))) \] \[ [(h \circ g) \circ f](x) = (h \circ g)(f(x)) = h(g(f(x))) \]

Therefore \(h \circ (g \circ f) = (h \circ g) \circ f\).

3. Identity Element: There exists an identity mapping \(id_A: A \to A\), defined as \(id_A(x) = x\). Clearly, \(id_A\) is a bijection and belongs to \(\mathcal{F}(A)\). For any \(f \in \mathcal{F}(A)\), we have \(f \circ id_A = id_A \circ f = f\).

4. Inverse Element: For any \(f \in \mathcal{F}(A)\), since \(f\) is a bijection, according to the inverse mapping theorem, there exists a unique inverse mapping \(f^{-1}: A \to A\) and \(f^{-1}\) is also a bijection. Therefore \(f^{-1} \in \mathcal{F}(A)\), and it satisfies \(f \circ f^{-1} = f^{-1} \circ f = id_A\).

5. Discussion on Abelian Group: \(\mathcal{F}(A)\) is an abelian group if and only if \(|A| \le 2\).

  • If \(|A| = 1\), \(\mathcal{F}(A)\) contains only the identity element and is an abelian group.

  • If \(|A| = 2\), let \(A = \{a, b\}\), \(\mathcal{F}(A)\) contains \(id_A\) and the transposition \((a, b)\); its order is \(2\), and the commutative law holds.

  • If \(|A| \ge 3\), \(\mathcal{F}(A)\) is the symmetric group \(S_n\) (\(n \ge 3\)). In this case, we can take the transpositions \(f = (1, 2)\) and \(g = (2, 3)\). Then \((g \circ f)(1) = g(2) = 3\), whereas \((f \circ g)(1) = f(1) = 2\). The two are not equal, so it is not an abelian group.

docs.title: Problem 3
docs.text:
Let \(p_n\) be the \(n\)-th prime number arranged in ascending order (e.g., \(p_1=2, p_2=3, p_3=5\)). Prove by mathematical induction or other methods: for every \(n\), \(p_n < 2^{2^n}\).

Solution

We will use mathematical induction based on the estimation properties of the number of prime numbers.

1. Base Case: When \(n = 1\), \(p_1 = 2\). The right side is \(2^{2^1} = 2^2 = 4\). Clearly \(2 < 4\), so the proposition holds for \(n=1\).

2. Inductive Hypothesis: Assume the proposition holds for \(n \le k\), i.e., for all \(1 \le i \le k\), we have \(p_i < 2^{2^i}\).

3. Inductive Step: Based on Euclid's proof idea for the infinitude of primes, the \((k+1)\)-th prime \(p_{k+1}\) satisfies the following inequality:

\[ p_{k+1} \le (p_1 p_2 \dots p_k) + 1 \]

Substituting the inductive hypothesis:

\[ p_{k+1} \le (2^{2^1} \cdot 2^{2^2} \cdot \dots \cdot 2^{2^k}) + 1 \]

According to the rules of exponents, the exponent part inside the parentheses is the sum of a geometric progression:

\[ 2^1 + 2^2 + \dots + 2^k = 2(2^k - 1) = 2^{k+1} - 2 \]

Therefore:

\[ p_{k+1} \le 2^{2^{k+1} - 2} + 1 \]

Since for \(k \ge 1\), we have \(2^{k+1} - 2 < 2^{k+1}\). And when \(x \ge 2\), \(2^{x-2} + 1 < 2^x\) clearly holds. Specifically, for \(k \ge 1\):

\[ 2^{2^{k+1} - 2} + 1 \le 2^{2^{k+1} - 1} < 2^{2^{k+1}} \]

Hence \(p_{k+1} < 2^{2^{k+1}}\). In summary, by mathematical induction, the proposition holds for all \(n \in \mathbb{N}_{\ge 1}\).

docs.title: Problem 4
docs.text:
Let \(S\) and \(S'\) be the following subsets of \(\mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R}\): \(S = \{(x, y) \mid y = x+1 \text{ and } 0 < x < 3\}\) \(S' = \{(x, y) \mid y - x \in \mathbb{Z}\}\)

  • (i) Prove that \(S'\) is an equivalence relation on \(\mathbb{R}\). Describe the equivalence classes of \(S'\).

  • (ii) Let \(\{R_i\}_{i \in I}\) be a family of equivalence relations on \(\mathbb{R}\). Prove that \(\bigcap_{i \in I} R_i\) is also an equivalence relation on \(\mathbb{R}\).

  • (iii) Describe the equivalence relation \(T\) on \(\mathbb{R}\), which is the intersection of all equivalence relations containing \(S\). Describe the equivalence classes of \(T\).

Solution

Solution (i): Prove \(S'\) is an equivalence relation

  • Reflexivity: For any \(x \in \mathbb{R}\), \(x - x = 0\). Since \(0 \in \mathbb{Z}\), we have \((x, x) \in S'\).

  • Symmetry: If \((x, y) \in S'\), then \(y - x = k \in \mathbb{Z}\). Then \(x - y = -k\). Since \(-k\) is also an integer, \((y, x) \in S'\).

  • Transitivity: If \((x, y) \in S'\) and \((y, z) \in S'\), then \(y - x = k_1 \in \mathbb{Z}\) and \(z - y = k_2 \in \mathbb{Z}\). Then \(z - x = (z - y) + (y - x) = k_2 + k_1\). Since the sum of integers is still an integer, \((x, z) \in S'\).

  • Description of equivalence classes: For any \(x \in \mathbb{R}\), its equivalence class is \([x]_{S'} = \{x + k \mid k \in \mathbb{Z}\}\). This essentially discretizes the real number line by integer spans.

Solution (ii): Prove the intersection of equivalence relations is still an equivalence relation Let \(R = \bigcap_{i \in I} R_i\).

  • Reflexivity: For any \(x \in \mathbb{R}\), since each \(R_i\) is an equivalence relation, we have \(\forall i \in I, (x, x) \in R_i\). Therefore \((x, x) \in R\).

  • Symmetry: If \((x, y) \in R\), then for all \(i \in I\), \((x, y) \in R_i\). By the symmetry of \(R_i\), we know \((y, x) \in R_i\). Therefore \((y, x) \in R\).

  • Transitivity: If \((x, y) \in R\) and \((y, z) \in R\), then for all \(i \in I\), \((x, y) \in R_i\) and \((y, z) \in R_i\). By the transitivity of \(R_i\), we know \((x, z) \in R_i\). Therefore \((x, z) \in R\).

Solution (iii): Describe the equivalence relation \(T\) According to the conclusion of (ii), \(T\) is the smallest equivalence relation containing \(S\). The equivalence relation \(T\) is generated by the reflexive, symmetric, and transitive closure of \(S\). \(S\) describes a connection relation with an interval of \(1\) where \(x \in (0, 3)\).

  • Description of equivalence classes:

  • If \(x \in (0, 1]\), it can establish an equivalence relation with subsequent points by continuously adding \(1\); its equivalence class is \([x]_T = \{x, x+1, x+2, x+3\}\) (Note: when \(x\) approaches \(1\), \(x+3\) approaches \(4\)).

  • If \(x \in (1, 4)\) and does not belong to the points in the above generation method, its equivalence class overlaps with the above (i.e., it belongs to a sequence whose starting point is in \((0,1]\)).

  • If \(x \in (-\infty, 0] \cup [4, +\infty)\), it is not "connected" to any other points by the relation \(S\), therefore \([x]_T = \{x\}\).

docs.title: Problem 5
docs.text:
A real number \(x \in \mathbb{R}\) is called an algebraic number if it satisfies a polynomial equation of positive degree with rational coefficients:

\[ x^n + a_{n-1}x^{n-1} + \dots + a_1x + a_0 = 0 \]

where \(a_i \in \mathbb{Q}\); otherwise, it is called a transcendental number. Assume that each such polynomial equation has only a finite number of roots in \(\mathbb{R}\).

Prove: The set of all real algebraic numbers \(\mathcal{A} \subseteq \mathbb{R}\) is countable. And from this, deduce that the set of all real transcendental numbers \(\mathbb{R} - \mathcal{A}\) is uncountable.

Solution

Step 1: Prove the set of polynomials with rational coefficients is countable For each specific degree \(n \ge 1\), a monic polynomial with rational coefficients is uniquely determined by its coefficient sequence \((a_{n-1}, a_{n-2}, \dots, a_0) \in \mathbb{Q}^n\). Because the set of rational numbers \(\mathbb{Q}\) is countable, the Cartesian product of a finite number of countable sets \(\mathbb{Q}^n\) is also countable. The set of all polynomials of positive degree with rational coefficients can be expressed as the union of sets of polynomials of fixed degrees:

\[ \mathcal{P} = \bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty} \mathbb{Q}^n \]

Since the union of countably many countable sets remains countable, the set \(\mathcal{P}\) of all polynomials with rational coefficients is countable.

Step 2: Prove the set of algebraic numbers \(\mathcal{A}\) is countable For each polynomial \(P \in \mathcal{P}\), let \(R(P)\) be the set of all roots of the polynomial \(P\) in \(\mathbb{R}\). According to the problem's assumption, \(R(P)\) is a finite set. The set of all real algebraic numbers \(\mathcal{A}\) can be expressed as the union of the root sets of all polynomials with rational coefficients:

\[ \mathcal{A} = \bigcup_{P \in \mathcal{P}} R(P) \]

Since \(\mathcal{P}\) is countable and each \(R(P)\) is a finite set, according to the theorem that "the union of countably many countable (or finite) sets is still a countable set," \(\mathcal{A}\) is countable.

Step 3: Deduce the uncountability of the set of transcendental numbers We already know that the set of real numbers \(\mathbb{R}\) is uncountable. Since \(\mathbb{R} = \mathcal{A} \cup (\mathbb{R} - \mathcal{A})\), if the set of transcendental numbers \(\mathbb{R} - \mathcal{A}\) were countable, then the union of two countable sets, \(\mathbb{R}\), should also be countable. This contradicts the uncountability of the set of real numbers. Therefore, the set of real transcendental numbers \(\mathbb{R} - \mathcal{A}\) must be uncountable.

docs.title: Problem 6
docs.text:
Let \(X := \{0, 1\}\). Let \(X^{\mathbb{N}}\) be the set of all mappings \(f: \mathbb{N} \to X\). For \(f \in X^{\mathbb{N}}\), define the support of \(f\) as:

\[ supp(f) = f^{-1}(\{1\}) \]

Consider the subset \(X_0^{\mathbb{N}} = \{f \in X^{\mathbb{N}} \mid supp(f) \text{ is a finite set} \}\).

Question: Is \(X_0^{\mathbb{N}}\) countable or uncountable? Please provide your reasoning.

Solution

Conclusion: \(X_0^{\mathbb{N}}\) is a countable set.

Reasoning as follows: Every function \(f \in X_0^{\mathbb{N}}\) is uniquely determined by its support set \(supp(f)\). This is because \(f(n)=1\) if and only if \(n \in supp(f)\), otherwise \(f(n)=0\). Therefore, there exists a natural bijection between \(X_0^{\mathbb{N}}\) and the set \(\mathcal{P}_{fin}(\mathbb{N})\) of all finite subsets of the natural numbers \(\mathbb{N}\).

We can partition \(\mathcal{P}_{fin}(\mathbb{N})\) into a family of subsets categorized by size:

\[ \mathcal{P}_{fin}(\mathbb{N}) = \bigcup_{n=0}^{\infty} \mathcal{P}_n(\mathbb{N}) \]

where \(\mathcal{P}_n(\mathbb{N})\) represents the set consisting of all subsets of natural numbers of exact size \(n\).

  • For \(n=0\), \(\mathcal{P}_0(\mathbb{N}) = \{\emptyset\}\), which is a finite set.

  • For \(n \ge 1\), every subset containing \(n\) elements can be mapped injectively to an ordered \(n\)-tuple \((k_1, k_2, \dots, k_n) \in \mathbb{N}^n\) (for example, arranged in ascending order). Since \(\mathbb{N}^n\) is a countable set, its subset \(\mathcal{P}_n(\mathbb{N})\) must also be countable.

Because \(\mathcal{P}_{fin}(\mathbb{N})\) is the union of countably many countable sets, it is countable. Consequently, \(X_0^{\mathbb{N}}\) is a countable set.

Definition 0.1 (Pseudo-metric space)

A pseudo-metric space is a pair \((S, d)\), where \(S\) is a non-empty set, and \(d: S \times S \to \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\) is a function (called a pseudo-metric on \(S\)) satisfying the following properties: (1) \(d(x, x) = 0\) (2) For all \(x, y \in S\), \(d(x, y) = d(y, x)\) (3) For all \(x, y, z \in S\), the triangle inequality holds: \(d(x, z) \le d(x, y) + d(y, z)\)

Note: If it additionally satisfies the condition "if \(d(x, y) = 0\) then it must be \(x = y\)", then it becomes a strict metric space.

(The following problems 7, 8, and 9 are based on the related concepts of metrics and pseudo-metrics)

docs.title: Problem 7
docs.text:
Let \((S, d)\) be a pseudo-metric space. We define a relation \(\sim\) on \(S\) as follows: if \(d(x, y) = 0\), then we say \(x \sim y\).

Prove: (i) \(\sim\) is an equivalence relation on \(S\) (let the quotient set formed by its equivalence classes be denoted as \(S^*\)); (ii) For every \([x], [y] \in S^*\), defining the function \(d^*([x], [y]) = d(x, y)\), prove that it gives a well-defined metric on \(S^*\).

Solution

(i) Prove it is an equivalence relation

  • Reflexivity: From pseudo-metric definition (1), \(d(x, x) = 0\), so \(x \sim x\).

  • Symmetry: If \(x \sim y\), then \(d(x, y) = 0\). From pseudo-metric definition (2), \(d(y, x) = d(x, y) = 0\), so \(y \sim x\).

  • Transitivity: If \(x \sim y\) and \(y \sim z\), then \(d(x, y) = 0\) and \(d(y, z) = 0\). By the triangle inequality: \(0 \le d(x, z) \le d(x, y) + d(y, z) = 0 + 0 = 0\)

Thus \(d(x, z) = 0\), which means \(x \sim z\).

(ii) Prove \(d^*\) is a well-defined metric

  • 1. Well-definedness: We need to prove that the value of \(d^*([x], [y])\) does not depend on the choice of the representative elements of the equivalence classes. Let \(x \sim x'\) and \(y \sim y'\), i.e., \(d(x, x') = 0\) and \(d(y, y') = 0\). According to the triangle inequality: \(d(x, y) \le d(x, x') + d(x', y') + d(y', y) = 0 + d(x', y') + 0 = d(x', y')\)

Similarly, applying the triangle inequality in reverse yields \(d(x', y') \le d(x, y)\). Therefore, \(d(x, y) = d(x', y')\), the value is independent of the representatives, hence well-defined.

  • 2. Verify metric axioms:

  • Non-negativity and Reflexivity: \(d^*([x], [y]) = d(x, y) \ge 0\). And \(d^*([x], [x]) = d(x, x) = 0\).

  • Strict Positivity: If \(d^*([x], [y]) = 0\), then \(d(x, y) = 0\). According to the definition of \(\sim\), this means \(x \sim y\), i.e., \([x] = [y]\).

  • Symmetry: \(d^*([x], [y]) = d(x, y) = d(y, x) = d^*([y], [x])\).

  • Triangle Inequality:

    \[ d^*([x], [z]) = d(x, z) \le d(x, y) + d(y, z) = d^*([x], [y]) + d^*([y], [z]) \]

Thus \(d^*\) is indeed a metric on \(S^*\).

docs.title: Problem 8
docs.text:
Let \(n \in \mathbb{N}_{\ge 1}\). Consider the function \(d_n: \mathbb{R}^2 \times \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\) defined on \(\mathbb{R}^2 \times \mathbb{R}^2\), whose formula is:

\[ d_n(x, y) := (|x_1 - y_1| + |x_2 - y_2|)^n \]

where \(x = (x_1, x_2), y = (y_1, y_2) \in \mathbb{R}^2\). Determine all values of \(n\) that make \((\mathbb{R}^2, d_n)\) a metric space.

Solution

Conclusion: The only value of \(n\) that makes \((\mathbb{R}^2, d_n)\) a metric space is \(1\).

Analysis and Proof: For \(d_n\) to be a metric, it must satisfy the triangle inequality for all points: \(d_n(x, z) \le d_n(x, y) + d_n(y, z)\).

Case 1: When \(n = 1\)

\[ d_1(x, y) = |x_1 - y_1| + |x_2 - y_2| \]

This is exactly the Manhattan metric (\(L_1\) metric) on \(\mathbb{R}^2\). According to the triangle inequality for absolute values of real numbers:

\[ |x_1 - z_1| + |x_2 - z_2| \le (|x_1 - y_1| + |y_1 - z_1|) + (|x_2 - y_2| + |y_2 - z_2|) \]

Rearranging this yields \(d_1(x, z) \le d_1(x, y) + d_1(y, z)\). Non-negativity, strict positivity, and symmetry clearly hold. Therefore, \(n=1\) is a solution.

Case 2: When \(n \ge 2\) We try to find a counterexample that violates the triangle inequality. Take three points in \(\mathbb{R}^2\): \(x = (0, 0)\), \(y = (1, 0)\), \(z = (1, 1)\).

We calculate the distances between these three points pairwise:

\[ d_n(x, y) = (|0 - 1| + |0 - 0|)^n = 1^n = 1 \] \[ d_n(y, z) = (|1 - 1| + |0 - 1|)^n = 1^n = 1 \] \[ d_n(x, z) = (|0 - 1| + |0 - 1|)^n = (1 + 1)^n = 2^n \]

To satisfy the triangle inequality, we must have:

\[ d_n(x, z) \le d_n(x, y) + d_n(y, z) \implies 2^n \le 1 + 1 = 2 \]

Since we are in the case of \(n \ge 2\) (and \(n\) is an integer), \(2^n \ge 4 > 2\). This clearly contradicts the triangle inequality! Therefore, when \(n \ge 2\), \(d_n\) cannot constitute a metric.

In conclusion, the only \(n\) satisfying the condition is \(1\).

docs.title: Problem 9
docs.text:
Let \((S, d)\) be a metric space. Are we always able to define a metric \(d'\) on the power set \(\mathcal{P}(S)\) of \(S\), such that for any \(x, y \in S\), we have \(d'(\{x\}, \{y\}) = d(x, y)\)? Please prove or provide your reasoning.

Solution

Conclusion: Yes, we can always construct such a metric \(d'\).

Construction and Proof: The core of this problem lies in: viewing singletons as copies of \(S\), how can we legitimately "extend" the metric defined on the subset of singletons to the entire power set \(\mathcal{P}(S)\) containing non-singletons, without breaking the three metric axioms (especially the triangle inequality).

  • Trivial case: If \(S = \emptyset\), then \(\mathcal{P}(S) = \{\emptyset\}\). Defining the trivial metric \(d'(\emptyset, \emptyset) = 0\) on this singleton set is sufficient.

  • General case: Let \(S\) be non-empty. We fix any arbitrary point \(x_0 \in S\). For any two sets \(A\) and \(B\) in \(\mathcal{P}(S)\), we define the metric \(d'(A, B)\) as follows:

  • If \(A = B\), define \(d'(A, B) = 0\).

  • If \(A = \{x\}\) and \(B = \{y\}\) (i.e., both are singletons, and \(x eq y\)), define \(d'(A, B) = d(x, y)\).

  • If \(A = \{x\}\) is a singleton, and \(B\) is not a singleton, define \(d'(A, B) = d(x, x_0) + 1\). By symmetry, if \(A\) is not a singleton and \(B=\{y\}\), then define \(d'(B, A) = d'(A, B) = d(y, x_0) + 1\).

  • If both \(A\) and \(B\) are not singletons (and \(A eq B\)), define \(d'(A, B) = 2\).

Next, we verify that this is indeed a valid metric:

  • Strict Positivity and Symmetry: Because \(d(x,y)>0\) (when \(x eq y\)), and \(d(x, x_0)+1 \ge 1 > 0\) as well as \(2 > 0\), we have \(d'(A,B)=0\) if and only if \(A=B\). Symmetry is directly guaranteed by definition.

  • Verification of the Triangle Inequality \(d'(A, C) \le d'(A, B) + d'(B, C)\) (assuming \(A, B, C\) are pairwise distinct):

  • All are singletons (\(A=\{x\}, B=\{y\}, C=\{z\}\)): \(d(x,z) \le d(x,y) + d(y,z)\), guaranteed by the triangle inequality of the original metric \(d\).

  • Two singletons, one non-singleton (\(A=\{x\}, B=\{y\}\), \(C\) non-singleton): We need to prove \(d'(A,C) \le d'(A,B) + d'(B,C)\). That is, to prove \(d(x, x_0) + 1 \le d(x, y) + d(y, x_0) + 1\). Canceling the 1 yields \(d(x, x_0) \le d(x, y) + d(y, x_0)\), which is guaranteed by the original metric \(d\) and thus holds. Similarly, we need to prove \(d'(A,B) \le d'(A,C) + d'(C,B)\). That is, to prove \(d(x,y) \le d(x, x_0) + 1 + d(y, x_0) + 1\). This obviously holds because \(d(x,y) \le d(x, x_0) + d(y, x_0) \le d(x, x_0) + d(y, x_0) + 2\).

  • One singleton, two non-singletons (\(A=\{x\}\), \(B\) non-singleton, \(C\) non-singleton): We need to prove \(d'(A,C) \le d'(A,B) + d'(B,C)\). That is, to prove \(d(x, x_0) + 1 \le d(x, x_0) + 1 + 2\), which obviously holds. Similarly, we need to prove \(d'(B,C) \le d'(B,A) + d'(A,C)\). That is, to prove \(2 \le d(x, x_0) + 1 + d(x, x_0) + 1 = 2d(x, x_0) + 2\). Since distance is non-negative (\(d(x,x_0) \ge 0\)), the right side of the inequality is at least 2, which clearly holds.

  • All non-singletons: We need to prove \(2 \le 2 + 2\), which obviously holds.

All metric axioms are satisfied, and according to the definition, when \(A=\{x\}, B=\{y\}\), \(d'(A,B) = d(x,y)\). Therefore, such a metric \(d'\) always exists.

docs.title: Exercise Set 2 (Homework 03 & 04)
docs.text: This section contains exercises related to the third and fourth homework assignments of the Point-Set Topology course.

docs.title: Problem 1
docs.text:
Let \(S\) be a non-empty set.

(i) Consider the discrete metric \(d: S imes S o \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\), defined as: \(d(x, y)=0\) when \(x=y\); and \(d(x, y)=1\) when \(x eq y\). Prove that the topology \(\mathcal{T}_d\) induced by this metric is exactly the power set \(\mathcal{P}(S)\), i.e., every subset of \(S\) is an open set in the metric space \((S, d)\).

(ii) Is it always possible to find a metric on \(S\) such that the topology it induces is the trivial topology (i.e., \(\{ \emptyset, S \}\))?

Solution

(i) Prove that the discrete metric induces the discrete topology

To prove \(\mathcal{T}_d = \mathcal{P}(S)\), it is sufficient to prove that every singleton set \(\{x\}\) in \(S\) is an open set.

For any \(x \in S\), consider the open ball centered at \(x\) with radius \(\epsilon = 1/2\):

\[ B(x, 1/2) = \{ y \in S \mid d(y, x) < 1/2 \} \]

According to the definition of the discrete metric, when \(y eq x\), \(d(y, x) = 1 > 1/2\); only when \(y = x\), \(d(y, x) = 0 < 1/2\). Therefore, \(B(x, 1/2) = \{x\}\).

Since an open ball in a metric space must be an open set, \(\{x\}\) is an open set. Because any subset \(A\) of \(S\) can be expressed as the union of singleton sets:

\[ A = igcup_{x \in A} \{x\} \]

and the topology is closed under arbitrary union operations, \(A\) must be an open set. Thus, \(\mathcal{T}_d = \mathcal{P}(S)\).

(ii) Discussion on the metrizability of the trivial topology

Conclusion: It is possible when \(|S| \le 1\); it does not exist when \(|S| \ge 2\).

Reasoning: Assume \(S\) contains at least two distinct points \(x\) and \(y\). If there exists a metric \(d\) inducing the trivial topology, then \(d(x, y) = \epsilon > 0\). Consider the open ball \(B(x, \epsilon) = \{ z \in S \mid d(z, x) < \epsilon \}\).

Since \(d(x, x) = 0 < \epsilon\), then \(x \in B(x, \epsilon)\). Since \(d(y, x) = \epsilon ot< \epsilon\), then \(y otin B(x, \epsilon)\).

This means \(B(x, \epsilon)\) is neither the empty set (it contains \(x\)) nor the entire space \(S\) (it does not contain \(y\)). However, in the trivial topology, the only open sets are \(\emptyset\) and \(S\). This creates a contradiction. Therefore, if \(|S| \ge 2\), there is no metric that induces the trivial topology.

docs.title: Problem 2
docs.text:
Prove that \(\mathcal{B} := \{ (a, b) \mid a < b \text{ and } a, b \in \mathbb{Q} \}\) is a basis for the standard topology on \(\mathbb{R}\) (induced by the metric \(d(x, y) = |x - y|\)). Also prove that \(\text{Card}(\mathcal{B}) = \aleph_0\).

Solution

1. Prove that \(\mathcal{B}\) is a basis for the standard topology

Let \(\mathcal{T}\) be the standard topology on \(\mathbb{R}\). To prove that \(\mathcal{B}\) is a basis, we need to prove that for any open set \(U \in \mathcal{T}\) and any point \(x \in U\), there exists \(B \in \mathcal{B}\) such that \(x \in B \subseteq U\).

Given that \(U\) is an open set, there exists \(\epsilon > 0\) such that \((x - \epsilon, x + \epsilon) \subseteq U\). According to the Density of rational numbers in real numbers: In the interval \((x - \epsilon, x)\), there must exist a rational number \(a\); In the interval \((x, x + \epsilon)\), there must exist a rational number \(b\).

Thus we obtain \(a < x < b\), and \(a, b \in \mathbb{Q}\). Clearly \((a, b) \in \mathcal{B}\). And because \(x - \epsilon < a\) and \(b < x + \epsilon\), we have:

\[ x \in (a, b) \subseteq (x - \epsilon, x + \epsilon) \subseteq U \]

Proof complete.

2. Calculate the cardinality of the basis

Each element of the set \(\mathcal{B}\) is uniquely determined by an ordered pair of rational numbers \((a, b)\) satisfying \(a < b\). Therefore, there exists an injection \(\Psi: \mathcal{B} \to \mathbb{Q} \times \mathbb{Q}\). Since \(\mathbb{Q}\) is a countable set, its Cartesian product \(\mathbb{Q} \times \mathbb{Q}\) is also a countable set (i.e., its cardinality is \(\aleph_0\)). Because \(\mathcal{B}\) is an infinite set (e.g., containing all \((0, n), n \in \mathbb{Q}^+\)), and its cardinality is not greater than \(\aleph_0\), by the Cantor-Bernstein Theorem:

\[ \text{Card}(\mathcal{B}) = \aleph_0 \]

docs.title: Problem 3
docs.text:
For \(n \in \mathbb{N}_{\ge 1}\), consider a finite set \(X_n := \{1, 2, \dots, n\}\) of size \(n\). How many topologies are there on \(X_n\)? Furthermore, consider the set \(\Omega\) of all topologies on \(X_n\). Define \(\mathcal{T}_i < \mathcal{T}_j\) as \(\mathcal{T}_i \subsetneq \mathcal{T}_j\). Under what conditions does \((\Omega, <)\) form a linear order relation?

Solution

1. Number of Topologies

There is no simple general formula for the number of topologies on a finite set, usually denoted as \(T(n)\). For the first few \(n\), the values are:

  • \(n=1: T(1) = 1\) (only the trivial topology)
  • \(n=2: T(2) = 4\) (trivial, discrete, and two Sierpinski topologies)
  • \(n=3: T(3) = 29\)

2. Discussion on the Linear Order Relation

Conclusion: \((\Omega, <)\) forms a linear order relation if and only if \(n=1\).

Reasoning: A linear order requires that for any two elements \(\mathcal{T}_i, \mathcal{T}_j\) in \(\Omega\), it must hold that \(\mathcal{T}_i \subseteq \mathcal{T}_j\) or \(\mathcal{T}_j \subseteq \mathcal{T}_i\).

When \(n \ge 2\), we can construct two incomparable topologies. Suppose \(X_n\) contains distinct elements \(a\) and \(b\). Define topology \(\mathcal{T}_1 = \{ \emptyset, X_n, \{a\} \}\); Define topology \(\mathcal{T}_2 = \{ \emptyset, X_n, \{b\} \}\).

Clearly \(\{a\} otin \mathcal{T}_2\) and \(\{b\} otin \mathcal{T}_1\). Thus \(\mathcal{T}_1 ot\subseteq \mathcal{T}_2\) and \(\mathcal{T}_2 ot\subseteq \mathcal{T}_1\). Therefore, when \(n \ge 2\), \((\Omega, <)\) is not a linear order.

docs.title: Problem 4
docs.text:
Let \(S\) be a set.

(i) Prove: If \(\{ \mathcal{T}_i \}_{i \in I}\) is a family of topologies on \(S\), then their intersection \(\bigcap_{i \in I} \mathcal{T}_i\) is also a topology on \(S\). (ii) Give an example of two topologies \(\mathcal{T}_1\) and \(\mathcal{T}_2\) such that \(\mathcal{T}_1 \cup \mathcal{T}_2\) is not a topology. Find the unique smallest topology containing \(\mathcal{T}_1 \cup \mathcal{T}_2\).

Solution

(i) Prove that the intersection is a topology

Denote \(\mathcal{T} = \bigcap_{i \in I} \mathcal{T}_i\).

  1. Contains the empty set and the whole space: Since for all \(i \in I\), \(\emptyset, S \in \mathcal{T}_i\) holds, then \(\emptyset, S \in \mathcal{T}\).
  2. Closed under arbitrary unions: Let \(\{ U_\alpha \}_{\alpha \in A} \subseteq \mathcal{T}\). Then for each \(i \in I\), \(\{ U_\alpha \} \subseteq \mathcal{T}_i\). Since \(\mathcal{T}_i\) is a topology, \(\bigcup U_\alpha \in \mathcal{T}_i\). Therefore \(\bigcup U_\alpha \in \bigcap \mathcal{T}_i = \mathcal{T}\).
  3. Closed under finite intersections: Let \(U_1, \dots, U_k \in \mathcal{T}\). Then for each \(i \in I\), \(U_1, \dots, U_k \in \mathcal{T}_i\), so \(\bigcap_{j=1}^k U_j \in \mathcal{T}_i\). Therefore, the finite intersection belongs to \(\mathcal{T}\).

(ii) Counterexample where the union is not a topology

Let \(S = \{a, b, c\}\). Take \(\mathcal{T}_1 = \{ \emptyset, S, \{a\} \}\) and \(\mathcal{T}_2 = \{ \emptyset, S, \{b\} \}\). Then \(\mathcal{T}_1 \cup \mathcal{T}_2 = \{ \emptyset, S, \{a\}, \{b\} \}\).

However, \(\{a\} \cup \{b\} = \{a, b\}\), but \(\{a, b\} \notin \mathcal{T}_1 \cup \mathcal{T}_2\). This violates the axiom of closure under union operations, so the union is not a topology.

Smallest Topology: The unique smallest topology containing \(\mathcal{T}_1 \cup \mathcal{T}_2\) is the topology generated by this union as a subbasis. In this example, the topology is:

\[ \mathcal{T}_{min} = \{ \emptyset, S, \{a\}, \{b\}, \{a, b\} \} \]

docs.title: Problem 5
docs.text:
A subset of \(\mathbb{R}^2\) is called radially open if it contains an open line segment in every direction at each of its points. Let \(\mathcal{T}_{ro}\) denote the family of all radially open sets.

Prove that \(\mathcal{T}_{ro}\) is a topology on \(\mathbb{R}^2\). What is its relationship with the standard topology \(\mathcal{T}_{std}\)?

Solution

1. Prove it is a topology

The key lies in proving closure under finite intersections. Let \(A, B \in \mathcal{T}_{ro}\). For any point \(x \in A \cap B\):

  • Since \(x \in A\), there exists an open line segment \(I_A(\theta) \subseteq A\) in direction \(\theta\);
  • Since \(x \in B\), there exists an open line segment \(I_B(\theta) \subseteq B\) in direction \(\theta\).

Take the intersection of these two segments \(I_A \cap I_B\). Since they share the same center and are on the same ray, their intersection is still an open line segment containing \(x\), and \(I_A \cap I_B \subseteq A \cap B\). Therefore \(A \cap B\) is also radially open. Combining with the obvious inclusion of \(\emptyset, S\) and the properties of union operations, \(\mathcal{T}_{ro}\) is a topology.

2. Relationship with the standard topology

Conclusion: \(\mathcal{T}_{std} \subsetneq \mathcal{T}_{ro}\).

  • Inclusion relation: Points in a standard open set contain an open ball \(B(x, \epsilon)\). This ball clearly contains an open line segment of length \(2\epsilon\) in any direction. Thus, a standard open set must be a radially open set.
  • Strictness (Counterexample): There exist radially open sets that are not standard open sets. Construct a set: \(U = \{ (r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta) \mid 0 \le r < f(\theta) \}\), where \(f(\theta)\) is a positive function that approaches 0 rapidly as the polar angle approaches certain values. For example, if \(f(\theta)\) is made extremely "sharp" near the origin, the origin contains segments in every direction but cannot contain any full disk. Such a set is radially open at the origin, but the origin is not an interior point under the standard topology.

docs.title: Problem 6
docs.text:
Let \(X = \mathbb{R}^2\) endowed with the standard topology. Consider its subset (Topologist's Sine Curve):

\[ A = \{ (x, \sin(1/x)) : x \in (0, 1] \} \subset X \]

Calculate the following four sets: \(A^o\), \(LP(A)\), \(\overline{A}\), and \(\overline{A} \cap \overline{\mathbb{R}^2 - A}\).

Solution

1. Interior \(A^o\)

Since \(A\) is the graph of the continuous function \(y = \sin(1/x)\) on the interval \((0, 1]\), it is a curve in \(\mathbb{R}^2\). For any point \(P\) in \(A\), any of its open neighborhoods (open disks) will contain points not belonging to the curve (i.e., points whose y-coordinates do not satisfy \(y = \sin(1/x)\)). Therefore, \(A\) does not contain any non-empty open balls. Thus:

\[ A^o = \emptyset \]

2. Limit Point Set \(LP(A)\) and Closure \(\overline{A}\)

As \(x \to 0^+\), the function \(\sin(1/x)\) oscillates infinitely many times between \(-1\) and \(1\). Therefore, every point in the segment \(\{0\} \times [-1, 1]\) on the y-axis is a limit point of \(A\). The points of set \(A\) itself are obviously also its limit points. Therefore:

\[ LP(A) = A \cup ( \{0\} \times [-1, 1] ) \]

Since the closure \(\overline{A} = A \cup LP(A)\), we can conclude:

\[ \overline{A} = A \cup ( \{0\} \times [-1, 1] ) \]

3. Intersection \(\overline{A} \cap \overline{\mathbb{R}^2 - A}\)

Since \(A^o = \emptyset\), every point in the whole space belongs either to the interior of \(\mathbb{R}^2 - A\) or to the boundary of \(A\). Since \(\overline{\mathbb{R}^2 - A} = \mathbb{R}^2 - A^o = \mathbb{R}^2 - \emptyset = \mathbb{R}^2\). Therefore:

\[ \overline{A} \cap \overline{\mathbb{R}^2 - A} = \overline{A} \cap \mathbb{R}^2 = \overline{A} \]

docs.title: Problem 7
docs.text:
Let \(X\) be a set, and \(f: \mathcal{P}(X) \to \mathcal{P}(X)\) be a function satisfying the following properties (for any \(A, B \subseteq X\)): (i) \(f(\emptyset) = \emptyset\); (ii) \(A \subseteq f(A)\); (iii) \(f(A) = f(f(A))\); (iv) \(f(A \cup B) = f(A) \cup f(B)\).

Prove: (1) The set \(\mathcal{T}_f := \{ X - A : A \in \mathcal{P}(X) \text{ and } f(A) = A \}\) is a topology on \(X\); (2) The closure \(\overline{A}\) of any subset \(A \subseteq X\) with respect to the topology \(\mathcal{T}_f\) is exactly \(f(A)\).

Solution

(1) Prove that \(\mathcal{T}_f\) is a topology

  • Empty set and Whole space: From property (i), \(f(\emptyset) = \emptyset\), thus \(X - \emptyset = X \in \mathcal{T}_f\). From property (ii), \(X \subseteq f(X)\), while \(f(X) \subseteq X\) obviously holds, so \(f(X) = X\). Therefore \(X - X = \emptyset \in \mathcal{T}_f\).

  • Arbitrary Union Operation: Let \(\{ U_\alpha \}_{\alpha \in I}\) be a family of open sets in \(\mathcal{T}_f\), where \(U_\alpha = X - A_\alpha\) and \(f(A_\alpha) = A_\alpha\). Their union \(\bigcup U_\alpha = X - \bigcap A_\alpha\). From property (iv), it can be deduced that \(f\) is monotonic: if \(A \subseteq B\), then \(f(A) \subseteq f(B)\). Since \(\bigcap A_\alpha \subseteq A_\alpha\), then \(f(\bigcap A_\alpha) \subseteq f(A_\alpha) = A_\alpha\). Thus \(f(\bigcap A_\alpha) \subseteq \bigcap A_\alpha\). Combining with the reverse inclusion in property (ii), we get \(f(\bigcap A_\alpha) = \bigcap A_\alpha\). Therefore \(\bigcup U_\alpha \in \mathcal{T}_f\).

  • Finite Intersection Operation: Let \(U_1, U_2 \in \mathcal{T}_f\), then \(U_1 \cap U_2 = X - (A_1 \cup A_2)\). From property (iv), \(f(A_1 \cup A_2) = f(A_1) \cup f(A_2) = A_1 \cup A_2\). Therefore \(U_1 \cap U_2 \in \mathcal{T}_f\).

(2) Prove the closure \(\overline{A} = f(A)\)

According to the definition of closure, \(\overline{A}\) is the intersection of all closed sets containing \(A\). Under this topology, a closed set \(C\) satisfies \(f(C) = C\).

  • First, from property (iii), \(f(f(A)) = f(A)\), so \(f(A)\) itself is a closed set. Also, from property (ii), \(A \subseteq f(A)\). Thus \(f(A)\) is a closed set containing \(A\), so \(\overline{A} \subseteq f(A)\).

  • Second, let \(C\) be any closed set containing \(A\) (i.e., \(A \subseteq C\) and \(f(C) = C\)). From the monotonicity of \(f\), we have \(f(A) \subseteq f(C) = C\). This means \(f(A)\) is contained in every closed set containing \(A\), therefore \(f(A) \subseteq \bigcap C = \overline{A}\).

In summary, \(\overline{A} = f(A)\).

docs.title: Problem 8
docs.text:
Consider the function \(f: [0, 1) \to S^1\), defined as \(f(t) = (\cos(2\pi t), \sin(2\pi t))\). Prove that \(f\) is not a homeomorphism with respect to the standard subspace topology. Is it possible to find a homeomorphism between \([0, 1)\) and \(S^1\)?

Solution

1. Prove \(f\) is not a homeomorphism

Although \(f\) is a continuous bijection, its inverse \(f^{-1}\) is discontinuous at point \((1, 0)\). We can provide a more rigorous proof from the perspective of topological invariants:

  • Method 1: Compactness Under the standard Euclidean topology, \(S^1\) is a bounded closed set in \(\mathbb{R}^2\), and therefore it is compact. However, \([0, 1)\) is not a closed set in \(\mathbb{R}\), and therefore it is not compact. Since a homeomorphism must preserve compactness, \(f\) cannot be a homeomorphism.

  • Method 2: Cut point (Connectedness) If \(f\) is a homeomorphism, then the connectedness of the space after removing a point should remain unchanged. For \(S^1\), removing any point \(p\) leaves the remaining space \(S^1 - \{p\}\) still connected (homeomorphic to an open interval). For \([0, 1)\), if we remove point \(t = 1/2\), the remaining space \([0, 1/2) \cup (1/2, 1)\) is disconnected. Therefore, these two spaces do not have the same local connected structure, so \(f\) is not a homeomorphism.

2. Conclusion

Impossible. Based on the reasons of compactness and cut points above, no homeomorphism exists between \([0, 1)\) and \(S^1\).

docs.title: Problem 9
docs.text:
A subset \(A \subseteq X\) is called regularly open if \(A = (\overline{A})^o\).

(i) Give an example of an open set in \(\mathbb{R}\) that is not regularly open. Can you characterize regularly open sets in \(\mathbb{R}\)? (ii) Prove that for any \(A \subseteq X\), the set \((\overline{A})^o\) is a regularly open set.

Solution

(i) Example and Characterization

  • Counterexample: Take \(A = (0, 1) \cup (1, 2)\). Then \(\overline{A} = [0, 2]\), and \((\overline{A})^o = (0, 2)\). Clearly \(A \neq (\overline{A})^o\), so \(A\) is not a regularly open set. The reason is that \(A\) is missing a point \(\{1\}\) from the interior of the closure.

  • Characterization: Regularly open sets in \(\mathbb{R}\) are those open sets "without extra gaps". That is, they cannot be obtained by removing some isolated points or boundary points from a larger open set.

(ii) Prove \((\overline{A})^o\) is regularly open

Let \(U = (\overline{A})^o\). We want to prove \(U = (\overline{U})^o\).

  • According to the definition \(U \subseteq \overline{U}\), since \(U\) is an open set, \(U = U^o \subseteq (\overline{U})^o\).

  • On the other hand, since \(U = (\overline{A})^o \subseteq \overline{A}\), and the closure operation is monotonic and idempotent: It follows that \(\overline{U} \subseteq \overline{(\overline{A})} = \overline{A}\). Taking the interior of both sides gives \((\overline{U})^o \subseteq (\overline{A})^o = U\).

In summary, \(U = (\overline{U})^o\), i.e., \((\overline{A})^o\) is a regularly open set.

docs.title: Problem 10
docs.text:
Let \(A\) be a subset of a topological space \(X\). Prove the equation \(\overline{A} = A \cup LP(A)\).

Solution

1. Prove \(A \cup LP(A) \subseteq \overline{A}\)

  • It is obvious that \(A \subseteq \overline{A}\).

  • Let \(x \in LP(A)\). According to the definition of limit point, for any open neighborhood \(U\) of \(x\), \(U \cap (A - \{x\}) eq \emptyset\). This means \(U \cap A eq \emptyset\) holds for all open neighborhoods. According to the characterization of closure by neighborhoods, this is exactly the necessary and sufficient condition for \(x \in \overline{A}\). Thus \(LP(A) \subseteq \overline{A}\).

Therefore \(A \cup LP(A) \subseteq \overline{A}\).

2. Prove \(\overline{A} \subseteq A \cup LP(A)\)

Let \(x \in \overline{A}\).

  • If \(x \in A\), then the conclusion obviously holds.

  • If \(x otin A\), since \(x \in \overline{A}\), for any open neighborhood \(U\) of \(x\), \(U \cap A eq \emptyset\). Because \(x otin A\), the points in the set \(U \cap A\) must not be \(x\). That is, \(U \cap (A - \{x\}) eq \emptyset\). This satisfies the definition of a limit point, so \(x \in LP(A)\).

Therefore \(x \in A \cup LP(A)\).

In summary, \(\overline{A} = A \cup LP(A)\).

docs.title: Exercise Set 3 (Homework 05 & 06)
docs.text: This section contains the fifth and sixth assignments for the Point Set Topology course and related supplementary exercises. Topics include the equivalence of metric spaces, infinite product spaces, connectivity and path-connectivity, fixed-point theorems, and the compactness of the finite-complement topology.

docs.title: Problem 1
docs.text:
Let \((X, d)\) be a metric space, and let \(\mathcal{T}\) be the topology induced by \(d\). Define a function:

\[ d^*(x, y) = \min\{d(x, y), 1\} \]

for every pair \(x, y \in X\).

Prove:

(i) \(d^*\) is a metric on \(X\). (ii) The topology \(\mathcal{T}^*\) induced by \(d^*\) is equal to \(\mathcal{T}\). (iii) Is it always possible to find a constant \(A \in \mathbb{R}_{>0}\) such that for all \(x, y \in X\), \(A \cdot d(x, y) \le d^*(x, y)\)?

Solution

(i) Proving \(d^*\) is a metric

  1. Non-negativity and Positivity: Since \(d(x, y) \ge 0\), then \(d^*(x, y) = \min\{d, 1\} \ge 0\). Furthermore, \(d^*(x, y) = 0 \iff \min\{d, 1\} = 0 \iff d(x, y) = 0 \iff x = y\).

  2. Symmetry: \(d^*(x, y) = \min\{d(x, y), 1\} = \min\{d(y, x), 1\} = d^*(y, x)\).

  3. Triangle Inequality: We need to prove \(d^*(x, z) \le d^*(x, y) + d^*(y, z)\).

  4. If \(d^*(x, y) + d^*(y, z) \ge 1\), since \(d^*(x, z) \le 1\), the inequality holds trivially.

  5. If \(d^*(x, y) + d^*(y, z) < 1\), since \(d^* \le d\), this implies \(d^*(x, y) = d(x, y)\) and \(d^*(y, z) = d(y, z)\). According to the triangle inequality of the original metric \(d\): \(d(x, z) \le d(x, y) + d(y, z) < 1\). Therefore, \(d^*(x, z) = \min\{d(x, z), 1\} = d(x, z)\). Thus, \(d^*(x, z) \le d(x, y) + d(y, z) = d^*(x, y) + d^*(y, z)\).

(ii) Proving \(\mathcal{T}^* = \mathcal{T}\)

To prove that two metrics induce the same topology, it suffices to show that their open balls can contain each other.

  • For any \(\epsilon > 0\), let \(\epsilon' = \min\{\epsilon, 1\}\). Then \(B_{d^*}(x, \epsilon') \subseteq B_d(x, \epsilon)\). Because if \(d^*(x, y) < \epsilon' \le 1\), then \(d(x, y) = d^*(x, y) < \epsilon' \le \epsilon\).

  • Conversely, for any \(\epsilon > 0\), let \(\epsilon' = \min\{\epsilon, 1/2\}\). Then \(B_d(x, \epsilon') \subseteq B_{d^*}(x, \epsilon)\). Because if \(d(x, y) < \epsilon' \le 1/2\), then \(d^*(x, y) = d(x, y) < \epsilon' \le \epsilon\).

Since the open balls contain each other, the topologies generated by the two metrics are identical.

(iii) Discussion on Constant \(A\)

Conclusion: Not necessarily.

Reason: If the metric \(d\) is unbounded (for example, in Euclidean space \(\mathbb{R}^n\)), for any \(A > 0\), we can always find two points \(x, y\) far enough apart such that \(d(x, y) > 1/A\). In this case:

\[ A \cdot d(x, y) > 1 \]

However, by definition \(d^*(x, y) \le 1\) always holds. This leads to \(A \cdot d(x, y) > d^*(x, y)\), which contradicts the requirement. This \(A\) can only be found if the original metric space itself is bounded.

docs.title: Problem 2
docs.text:
Consider the Cartesian product space:

\[ \mathbb{R}^\omega := \prod_{i \in \mathbb{N}} \mathbb{R} = \{ (x_i)_{i \in \mathbb{N}} \mid x_i \in \mathbb{R} \} \]

Let \(R_{ez}^\omega \subseteq \mathbb{R}^\omega\) be the subset of all "eventually zero" sequences (i.e., only finitely many components are non-zero).

Please calculate the interior and closure of \(R_{ez}^\omega\) under the Product Topology \(\mathcal{T}_p\) and the Box Topology \(\mathcal{T}_b\), respectively.

Solution

1. Under the Product Topology \(\mathcal{T}_p\)

  • Interior \((R_{ez}^\omega)^\circ\): Any non-empty open set \(U\) must contain a basis element \(\prod U_i\) (where almost all \(U_i = \mathbb{R}\)). Since infinitely many components can take any real value, this open set must contain sequences with infinitely many non-zero components. Therefore, \(U \not\subseteq R_{ez}^\omega\), so the interior is empty: \((R_{ez}^\omega)^\circ = \emptyset\).

  • Closure \(\overline{R_{ez}^\omega}\): For any sequence \(x = (x_i) \in \mathbb{R}^\omega\) and any open neighborhood \(U\), we can choose a sufficiently large \(N\) such that \(U_i = \mathbb{R}\) for all \(i > N\). Construct the sequence \(y = (x_1, x_2, \dots, x_N, 0, 0, \dots)\). Clearly \(y \in R_{ez}^\omega\) and \(y \in U\). This means every point is a limit point, so the closure is the entire space: \(\overline{R_{ez}^\omega} = \mathbb{R}^\omega\).

2. Under the Box Topology \(\mathcal{T}_b\)

  • Interior \((R_{ez}^\omega)^\circ\): Similarly, any non-empty basic open element in the box topology still allows components to take values freely within an interval. As long as \(U_i\) is not a singleton \(\{0\}\), we can always construct a sequence with infinitely many non-zero terms that falls into this neighborhood. Thus, the interior remains empty: \((R_{ez}^\omega)^\circ = \emptyset\).

  • Closure \(\overline{R_{ez}^\omega}\): Basis elements of the box topology take the form \(\prod U_i\), where every component can be restricted. Let \(x\) be a sequence with infinitely many non-zero components (i.e., \(x \notin R_{ez}^\omega\)). For each non-zero component \(x_i\), we can choose an open interval \(U_i = (x_i - \frac{|x_i|}{2}, x_i + \frac{|x_i|}{2})\) that does not contain \(0\). For components that are \(0\), we take any neighborhood. The box open set \(\prod U_i\) constructed this way has an empty intersection with \(R_{ez}^\omega\). Therefore, points not in \(R_{ez}^\omega\) are not limit points, making it a closed set: \(\overline{R_{ez}^\omega} = R_{ez}^\omega\).

docs.title: Problem 3
docs.text:
(i) Is the topological space \((\mathbb{R}^\omega, \mathcal{T}_p)\) a metrizable space? (ii) Is it connected?

(Hint: For metrizability, consider the function \(d^\omega(x, y) = \sup \{ \frac{d^*(x_i, y_i)}{i+1} : i \in \mathbb{N} \}\), where \(d\) is the standard metric on \(\mathbb{R}\).)

Solution

(i) Metrizability

Conclusion: It is metrizable.

Reason: Using the metric in the hint:

\[ d^\omega(x, y) = \sup_{i \in \mathbb{N}} \frac{\min\{|x_i - y_i|, 1\}}{i+1} \]

Since the denominator \(i+1\) approaches infinity as the dimension increases, this ensures the metric is very loose on far-end coordinates and very strict on near-end coordinates. This decay characteristic perfectly corresponds to the "only constraints on finite coordinates" structure of the product topology. Through rigorous verification of ball inclusions, it can be proven that the topology induced by this metric is exactly equal to the product topology \(\mathcal{T}_p\).

(ii) Connectivity

Conclusion: It is connected.

Reason: The real line \(\mathbb{R}\) is a connected space under the standard topology. According to a famous theorem in topology: Any Cartesian product of connected spaces (under the product topology) remains connected. Since \(\mathbb{R}^\omega\) is a product of countably many connected spaces, it is connected under the product topology.

docs.title: Problem 4
docs.text:
Consider the topological space \((\mathbb{R}^\omega, \mathcal{T}_b)\). Let \(U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^\omega\) be the subset consisting of all bounded sequences, i.e.:

\[ U = \{ x = (x_i) \mid \exists C_x, \text{ such that for all } i, |x_i| \le C_x \} \]

Prove that \(U\) and \(\mathbb{R}^\omega - U\) form a non-trivial separation of the space, and deduce whether \((\mathbb{R}^\omega, \mathcal{T}_b)\) is connected.

Solution

1. Prove \(U\) is an open set

For any bounded sequence \(x = (x_i) \in U\), every term satisfies \(|x_i| \le C_x\). Consider the box open set:

\[ V = \prod_{i \in \mathbb{N}} (x_i - 1, x_i + 1) \]

For any element \(y = (y_i)\) in \(V\):

\[ |y_i| \le |x_i| + 1 \le C_x + 1 \]

Thus \(y\) is also a bounded sequence, meaning \(V \subseteq U\). Since every point has an open neighborhood entirely contained in \(U\), \(U\) is an open set.

2. Prove \(\mathbb{R}^\omega - U\) is an open set

For any unbounded sequence \(z = (z_i) \in \mathbb{R}^\omega - U\), consider the same form of box open set:

\[ W = \prod_{i \in \mathbb{N}} (z_i - 1, z_i + 1) \]

If there exists some \(y \in W\) that is bounded (i.e., \(|y_i| \le M\)), then based on the distance relationship:

\[ |z_i| \le |y_i| + 1 \le M + 1 \]

This would mean \(z\) is also a bounded sequence, contradicting the premise. Therefore, all sequences in \(W\) must be unbounded, i.e., \(W \subseteq \mathbb{R}^\omega - U\). Thus \(\mathbb{R}^\omega - U\) is also an open set.

3. Conclusion

Since both \(U\) and \(\mathbb{R}^\omega - U\) are non-empty open sets, they are disjoint, and their union is the entire space. This constitutes a non-trivial separation of the space. Therefore, the box topology space \((\mathbb{R}^\omega, \mathcal{T}_b)\) is disconnected.

docs.title: Problem 5
docs.text:
Consider the following subset in \(\mathbb{R}^2\) endowed with the standard subspace topology:

\[ X = \{(x, 0) : x \in \mathbb{R}\} \cup \{(x, 1/x) : x \in \mathbb{R}_{>0}\} \]

Question: Is the space \(X\) connected? Please provide a proof.

Solution

Conclusion: \(X\) is disconnected.

Proof:

We split \(X\) into two natural geometric parts:

\[ A = \{(x, 0) \mid x \in \mathbb{R}\} \quad (\text{the } x\text{-axis}) \] \[ B = \{(x, 1/x) \mid x \in \mathbb{R}_{>0}\} \quad (\text{the hyperbola branch in the first quadrant}) \]

Clearly \(A\) and \(B\) are non-empty sets, \(A \cap B = \emptyset\), and \(X = A \cup B\). To prove \(X\) is disconnected, we only need to show that \(A\) and \(B\) are both closed sets in the subspace \(X\) (thereby forming a non-trivial separation).

  • Proving \(A\) is closed: \(A\) is a complete line, which is a closed set in the standard topology of the entire space \(\mathbb{R}^2\). By the properties of subspace topology, \(A = A \cap X\), so \(A\) must be closed in the subspace \(X\).

  • Proving \(B\) is closed: We need to examine the limit points of \(B\) in the entire space \(\mathbb{R}^2\). Suppose there is a sequence \((x_n, 1/x_n) \in B\) that converges to some point \((x_0, y_0)\) in \(\mathbb{R}^2\).

  • If \(x_0 > 0\), since \(f(x) = 1/x\) is continuous, then \(y_0 = 1/x_0\), and the limit point \((x_0, y_0)\) is still in \(B\).

  • If \(x_0 = 0\), as \(x_n \to 0^+\), \(1/x_n \to +\infty\). Since the \(y\)-coordinate diverges, the sequence does not converge in \(\mathbb{R}^2\), and no limit point exists.
  • If \(x_0 < 0\), since \(x_n > 0\) in the sequence, it cannot converge to a negative number.

This shows that \(B\) contains all its limit points in \(\mathbb{R}^2\), so \(B\) is itself a closed set in \(\mathbb{R}^2\). Consequently, in the subspace \(X\), \(B = B \cap X\) is also closed.

Since \(X = A \cup B\), and \(A, B\) are non-empty, disjoint closed sets, they constitute a non-trivial separation of \(X\). Therefore, the topological space \(X\) is disconnected.

docs.title: Problem 6
docs.text:
Prove that the following subspace of \(\mathbb{R}^2\) (a variation of the Topologist's Sine Curve) is not path-connected:

\[ X = \{ (0,0) \} \cup \{ (x, \sin(1/x)) : x \in \mathbb{R}_{>0} \} \] Solution

We use proof by contradiction. Suppose \(X\) is path-connected.

1. Construct a path:

Since \(X\) is path-connected, there must exist a continuous mapping \(\gamma: [0, 1] \to X\) between the origin \((0,0)\) and a point on the curve \((1/\pi, 0)\) such that:

\[ \gamma(0) = (0,0) \quad \text{and} \quad \gamma(1) = (1/\pi, 0) \]

2. Consider component functions:

Let \(\gamma(t) = (x(t), y(t))\). Since \(\gamma\) is a continuous mapping, its coordinate component functions \(x(t)\) and \(y(t)\) must be real-valued continuous functions on the closed interval \([0, 1]\).

Consider the set \(T = \{ t \in [0, 1] \mid x(t) = 0 \}\). Because the singleton \(\{0\}\) is closed and \(x(t)\) is continuous, \(T\) is a closed subset of \([0, 1]\). Let \(t_0 = \sup T\). Since we know \(x(1) = 1/\pi > 0\), it must be that \(t_0 < 1\).

By the properties of the supremum, to the right of \(t_0\) (i.e., for \(t \in (t_0, 1]\)), we have \(x(t) > 0\).

3. Derive a contradiction:

As \(t\) approaches \(t_0\) from the right (\(t \to t_0^+\)), we have \(x(t) \to 0^+\). Since \(\gamma\) lies in \(X\), when \(x(t) > 0\), it must satisfy:

\[ y(t) = \sin\left(\frac{1}{x(t)}\right) \]

Since \(y(t)\) is also a continuous function, its right-hand limit at \(t_0\) must exist and equal \(y(t_0)\), i.e., \(y(t_0) = 0\). However, as \(x(t) \to 0^+\), the variable \(1/x(t) \to +\infty\). The sine function \(\sin(1/x(t))\) will oscillate infinitely many times between \([-1, 1]\), and no limit exists.

This creates an irreconcilable contradiction with the requirement that \(y(t)\) must be continuous at \(t_0\). Therefore, no such continuous path \(\gamma\) exists. Thus \(X\) is not path-connected.

docs.title: Problem 7
docs.text:
Prove that the three spaces \((0, 1)\), \((0, 1]\), and \([0, 1]\) are not homeomorphic to each other.

Solution

We distinguish these three subspaces using topological invariants (compactness and cut-point properties):

1. Distinguishing \([0, 1]\) from the others

Under the standard topology, the closed interval \([0, 1]\) is a bounded closed set in the real line. According to the Heine-Borel Theorem, \([0, 1]\) is a compact space. In contrast, the open interval \((0, 1)\) and the semi-open interval \((0, 1]\) are not closed sets, so they are not compact. Since homeomorphism must preserve compactness, \([0, 1]\) is not homeomorphic to either \((0, 1)\) or \((0, 1]\).

2. Distinguishing \((0, 1)\) from \((0, 1]\)

We use the number of cut points for topological differentiation.

  • For \((0, 1]\), there exists a special point (the endpoint \(1\)). If we remove this point, the remaining space \((0, 1] \setminus \{1\} = (0, 1)\) is still a connected interval. Thus, \((0, 1]\) has a non-cut point.
  • For \((0, 1)\), every point is a cut point. Regardless of which point \(c \in (0, 1)\) is removed, the space breaks into two disjoint non-empty open sets \((0, c) \cup (c, 1)\), making it disconnected.

A homeomorphism must preserve the topological structure of cut points and non-cut points. Since their cut-point properties are fundamentally different, \((0, 1)\) and \((0, 1]\) are not homeomorphic.

In conclusion, these three spaces are pairwise non-homeomorphic.

docs.title: Problem 8
docs.text:
(i) Prove that every continuous function \(f: [0, 1] \to [0, 1]\) has at least one fixed point \(x \in [0, 1]\), i.e., \(f(x) = x\). (ii) If \([0, 1]\) is replaced by \((0, 1)\) or \((0, 1]\), does the above conclusion still hold? Please provide reasons.

Solution

(i) Proving the existence of a fixed point

We construct an auxiliary function \(g(x) = f(x) - x\). Since \(f(x)\) is continuous and the identity map \(x\) is also continuous, \(g(x)\) is a continuous function on the closed interval \([0, 1]\).

Examine the values at the endpoints:

  • If \(f(0) = 0\) or \(f(1) = 1\), then a fixed point is already found.
  • Otherwise, it must be that \(f(0) > 0\) (since the range of \(f\) is in \([0, 1]\)) and \(f(1) < 1\).
  • Substituting into the auxiliary function gives \(g(0) = f(0) - 0 > 0\) and \(g(1) = f(1) - 1 < 0\).

According to the Intermediate Value Theorem for continuous real functions, since the function values have opposite signs at the endpoints, there must exist a point \(x_0\) in the interior \((0, 1)\) such that:

\[ g(x_0) = 0 \]

Which means \(f(x_0) - x_0 = 0 \implies f(x_0) = x_0\). Thus \(f\) must have at least one fixed point on \([0, 1]\).

(ii) Discussion on other intervals

Conclusion: For \((0, 1)\) and \((0, 1]\), the conclusion does not hold.

  • Counter-example for \((0, 1)\): Construct the continuous function \(f(x) = x^2\). It maps \((0, 1)\) to \((0, 1)\). Solving \(x^2 = x\) yields \(x=0\) or \(x=1\), but neither point is in the open interval \((0, 1)\). Therefore, this function has no fixed point. (Or take \(f(x) = (x+1)/2\), where the solution \(x=1\) is not in the interval).

  • Counter-example for \((0, 1]\): Construct the continuous function \(f(x) = x/2\). It maps \((0, 1]\) to \((0, 1/2] \subseteq (0, 1]\). Solving \(x/2 = x\), the only solution is \(x=0\), which is not inside the interval \((0, 1]\). Thus, there is no fixed point.

docs.title: Problem 9
docs.text:
Let \((X, \mathcal{T})\) be a topological space. An open neighborhood basis of a point \(x \in X\) is a collection of open sets \(\{B_i\}_{i \in I}\) satisfying:

  1. For all \(i\), \(x \in B_i\);
  2. For any open set \(U\) containing \(x\), there exists some \(B_i\) such that \(B_i \subseteq U\).

If every point in a topological space \(X\) has an open neighborhood basis consisting of path-connected sets, we say \(X\) is locally path-connected.

Prove: If \(X\) is connected and locally path-connected, then \(X\) must be path-connected. (Hint: Fix \(x \in X\), and consider the set \(S_x\) of all points in \(X\) that can be connected to \(x\) by a path. Prove that \(S_x\) is both open and closed.)

Solution

1. Construct the path-component set \(S_x\)

Fix any point \(x \in X\). We define the set \(S_x\) as the set of points that can be connected to \(x\) by a path:

\[ S_x = \{ y \in X \mid \text{there exists a path } \gamma: [0, 1] \to X, \text{ such that } \gamma(0) = x \text{ and } \gamma(1) = y \} \]

A constant path (identically equal to \(x\)) clearly connects \(x\) to itself, so \(x \in S_x\), making \(S_x\) a non-empty set.

2. Prove \(S_x\) is an open set

Take any \(y \in S_x\). Since \(X\) is locally path-connected, for point \(y\) and the space \(X\), there must exist a path-connected open set \(B_y\) from \(y\)'s neighborhood basis such that \(y \in B_y \subseteq X\).

Examine any point \(z\) in \(B_y\):

  • Since \(y \in S_x\), there is a path from \(x\) to \(y\).
  • Since \(B_y\) is path-connected, there is a path from \(y\) to \(z\).

Concatenating these two paths gives a path from \(x\) to \(z\), implying \(z \in S_x\). Since \(z \in S_x\) for every \(z \in B_y\), then \(B_y \subseteq S_x\). This means every point in \(S_x\) has an open neighborhood entirely contained within \(S_x\), so \(S_x\) is an open set.

3. Prove \(S_x\) is a closed set

We need to show that its complement \(X \setminus S_x\) is open.

Take any \(w \in X \setminus S_x\). Similarly, by local path-connectivity, \(w\) must have a path-connected open neighborhood \(B_w\). If this neighborhood \(B_w\) intersects \(S_x\), suppose there is a point \(v \in B_w \cap S_x\):

  • \(v \in S_x\) implies there is a path from \(x\) to \(v\).
  • \(B_w\) being path-connected implies there is a path from \(v\) to \(w\).

Concatenating the paths would imply \(w \in S_x\), which contradicts \(w \in X \setminus S_x\)! Thus, \(B_w \cap S_x = \emptyset\), meaning \(B_w \subseteq X \setminus S_x\). Since every point in the complement has an open neighborhood in the complement, \(X \setminus S_x\) is open, so \(S_x\) is closed.

4. Conclusion

In summary, \(S_x\) is a non-empty, both open and closed set in the topological space \(X\). Since the space \(X\) is connected, the only non-empty set that is both open and closed must be \(X\) itself. Therefore:

\[ S_x = X \]

This indicates that every point in the space can be connected to \(x\) by a path, so \(X\) must be path-connected.

docs.title: Problem 10
docs.text:
Consider the finite-complement topology on \(\mathbb{R}\): \(\mathcal{T} = \{ \emptyset \} \cup \{ \mathbb{R} \setminus A : A \text{ is a finite set} \}\).

Prove: Every subset \(X \subseteq \mathbb{R}\) (endowed with the subspace topology) is compact.

Solution

Proof:

Let \(\{U_i\}_{i \in I}\) be an arbitrary open cover of the subspace \(X\).

  1. If \(X\) is an empty set, it is trivially compact.

  2. If \(X\) is non-empty, we can pick any non-empty open set from the cover, say \(U_{i_0}\).

  3. According to the definitions of subspace topology and finite-complement topology, \(U_{i_0}\) must take the form \(U_{i_0} = X \cap (\mathbb{R} \setminus A)\), where \(A\) is some finite set in \(\mathbb{R}\).

  4. Now, we examine the remaining part of \(X\) not yet covered by \(U_{i_0}\): \(X \setminus U_{i_0} = X \setminus (X \cap (\mathbb{R} \setminus A)) = X \cap A\). Since \(A\) is a finite set, the intersection \(X \cap A\) must also be a finite set. This means there are only finitely many points in \(X\) not covered by \(U_{i_0}\); let's call them \(\{x_1, x_2, \dots, x_k\}\).

  5. Since \(\{U_i\}_{i \in I}\) covers \(X\), for each remaining point \(x_j\) (\(j = 1, \dots, k\)), there must exist some open set \(U_{i_j}\) in the cover such that \(x_j \in U_{i_j}\).

  6. Thus, we only need to take the initially chosen \(U_{i_0}\) plus these \(k\) extra open sets to form a collection: \(\{U_{i_0}, U_{i_1}, \dots, U_{i_k}\}\).

Clearly, this is a finite subcollection of open sets that completely covers \(X\).

Since every open cover of \(X\) has a finite subcover, by the definition of compactness, the subspace \(X\) must be compact.

docs.title: Exercise 4 (Homework 07 & 08 & 09)
docs.text: This section contains the seventh homework assignment of the Topology course and its related proofs. It covers the separation of Hausdorff spaces and compact sets, the cardinality of connected metric spaces, a special case of the Baire category theorem, topological properties of the Cantor set, and the minimality of compact topological spaces.

docs.title: Problem 1
docs.text:
Let \((X, \mathcal{T})\) be a Hausdorff space. Let \(A, B \subseteq X\) be two disjoint compact subsets.

Prove that there exist disjoint open sets \(U, V\) in \(X\) such that \(A \subseteq U\) and \(B \subseteq V\).

Solution

Proof:

First fix an arbitrary point \(a \in A\).

For every point \(b \in B\), since \(A \cap B = \emptyset\), we necessarily have \(a \ne b\).

Since \(X\) is Hausdorff, for distinct points \(a\) and \(b\), there exist disjoint open sets \(U_{a,b}\) and \(V_{a,b}\) in \(X\) such that \(a \in U_{a,b}\) and \(b \in V_{a,b}\).

As \(b\) ranges over the whole set \(B\), the family of open sets \(\{V_{a,b}\}_{b \in B}\) forms an open cover of the compact set \(B\).

By compactness, there is a finite subcover; that is, there exist finitely many points \(b_1, b_2, \dots, b_n \in B\) such that:

\[ B \subseteq \bigcup_{i=1}^n V_{a,b_i} \]

For these finitely many points, define:

\[ U_a = \bigcap_{i=1}^n U_{a,b_i} \quad \text{and} \quad V_a = \bigcup_{i=1}^n V_{a,b_i} \]

Clearly \(U_a\) is a finite intersection of open sets, hence open; \(V_a\) is a union of open sets, hence also open. Moreover, since \(U_{a,b_i} \cap V_{a,b_i} = \emptyset\) for all \(i\), we deduce \(U_a \cap V_a = \emptyset\). At this point, \(a \in U_a\) and \(B \subseteq V_a\).

Now let \(a\) range over the whole set \(A\). The family of open sets \(\{U_a\}_{a \in A}\) forms an open cover of the compact set \(A\).

Similarly, there exist finitely many points \(a_1, a_2, \dots, a_m \in A\) such that the finite subcover holds:

\[ A \subseteq \bigcup_{j=1}^m U_{a_j} \]

Finally, define:

\[ U = \bigcup_{j=1}^m U_{a_j} \quad \text{and} \quad V = \bigcap_{j=1}^m V_{a_j} \]

Clearly \(U\) and \(V\) are open sets and satisfy \(A \subseteq U\) and \(B \subseteq V\).

Check that they are disjoint:

\[ U \cap V = \left( \bigcup_{j=1}^m U_{a_j} \right) \cap V = \bigcup_{j=1}^m (U_{a_j} \cap V) \subseteq \bigcup_{j=1}^m (U_{a_j} \cap V_{a_j}) = \emptyset \]

Therefore, we have found disjoint open sets \(U\) and \(V\) satisfying the required conditions.

docs.title: Problem 2
docs.text:
Prove that a connected metric space \((X, d)\) containing more than one point must be uncountable.

(Hint: Pick \(a \in X\) and consider the function \(d_a: X \to \mathbb{R}\), defined by \(d_a(x) := d(a, x)\). Think about the connectedness of countable subsets of \(\mathbb{R}\).)

Solution

Proof:

Since the space \(X\) contains more than one point, there exist two points \(a, b \in X\) such that \(a \ne b\). By positivity of the metric, we have:

\[ d(a, b) > 0 \]

Fix the point \(a\) and define the distance function \(d_a: X \to \mathbb{R}\) by:

\[ d_a(x) = d(a, x) \]

By the triangle inequality, for any \(x, y \in X\), we have \(|d_a(x) - d_a(y)| = |d(a, x) - d(a, y)| \le d(x, y)\). Therefore \(d_a\) is (uniformly) continuous on \(X\).

We know the following important property of topological spaces: the image of a connected space under a continuous map is connected. Since \(X\) is connected, the image \(d_a(X)\) must be a connected subset of the real line \(\mathbb{R}\).

Examine the elements of \(d_a(X)\). Since \(a \in X\) and \(b \in X\), the image must contain:

\[ d_a(a) = 0 \quad \text{and} \quad d_a(b) = d(a, b) > 0 \]

In \(\mathbb{R}\), a connected subset containing both \(0\) and \(d(a,b)\) must be an interval containing the entire closed interval \([0, d(a,b)]\).

Any real interval of positive length is uncountable. Hence the image \(d_a(X)\) is uncountable.

Since the image of a function is uncountable, its domain \(X\) must also be uncountable.

docs.title: Problem 3
docs.text:
(A special case of the Baire category theorem) Let \((X, \mathcal{T})\) be a compact Hausdorff space. Let \(\{A_i : i \in \mathbb{N}\}\) be a family of closed subsets of \(X\), and suppose that for each \(i\), its interior is empty, i.e. \((A_i)^\circ = \emptyset\).

Prove that the interior of the union is empty, i.e. \(\left( \bigcup_{i=1}^\infty A_i \right)^\circ = \emptyset\).

Solution

Proof:

We argue by contradiction. Suppose the interior of the union is nonempty. Then there exists a nonempty open set \(V_0\) such that:

\[ V_0 \subseteq \bigcup_{i=1}^\infty A_i \]

Consider the set \(A_1\). Since \(A_1\) is closed and has empty interior (that is, it contains no nonempty open set), the open set \(V_0\) can never be completely contained in \(A_1\). Therefore, the set \(V_0 \setminus A_1\) is a nonempty open set.

A compact Hausdorff space is necessarily a regular space. In a regular space, every nonempty open set contains the closure of some nonempty open set. Hence there exists a nonempty open set \(V_1\) satisfying:

\[ \overline{V_1} \subseteq V_0 \setminus A_1 \]

Next consider \(A_2\). Similarly, since \(A_2\) has empty interior, \(V_1\) cannot be completely contained in \(A_2\), so \(V_1 \setminus A_2\) is also nonempty open. By regularity, we can find a nonempty open set \(V_2\) satisfying:

\[ \overline{V_2} \subseteq V_1 \setminus A_2 \subseteq \overline{V_1} \]

Repeating this process indefinitely, we construct a sequence of open sets \(\{V_n\}\) such that for every \(k \ge 1\):

\[ \overline{V_k} \subseteq V_{k-1} \setminus A_k \subseteq \overline{V_{k-1}} \]

Thus we obtain a nested decreasing sequence of nonempty closed sets:

\[ \overline{V_1} \supseteq \overline{V_2} \supseteq \overline{V_3} \supseteq \dots \]

Since \(X\) is compact and this family of closed sets has the finite intersection property, the intersection of the entire decreasing sequence must be nonempty:

\[ \bigcap_{k=1}^\infty \overline{V_k} \ne \emptyset \]

Let \(x \in \bigcap_{k=1}^\infty \overline{V_k}\). Since all the \(\overline{V_k}\) are contained in \(V_0\), we have \(x \in V_0\). By the initial assumption \(V_0 \subseteq \bigcup A_i\), there exists some integer \(m\) such that \(x \in A_m\).

However, by the construction of the sequence, \(x \in \overline{V_m}\). And by the recursive construction:

\[ \overline{V_m} \subseteq V_{m-1} \setminus A_m \]

This implies \(x \notin A_m\), which contradicts the conclusion in step 8 that \(x \in A_m\).

This contradiction shows that the initial assumption was false. Therefore the union cannot contain any nonempty open set, i.e. \(\left( \bigcup_{i=1}^\infty A_i \right)^\circ = \emptyset\).

docs.title: Problem 4
docs.text:
(The Cantor set) Let \(A_0 = [0, 1]\), and for each \(n \in \mathbb{N}\), define recursively:

\[ A_n = A_{n-1} \setminus \bigcup_{k=0}^{3^{n-1}-1} \left( \frac{1+3k}{3^n}, \frac{2+3k}{3^n} \right) \]

Let \(C := \bigcap_{n \ge 0} A_n\), endowed with the standard subspace topology inherited from \(\mathbb{R}\).

Prove the following: (i) \(C\) is totally disconnected (i.e. every connected component of \(C\) is a singleton). (ii) \(C\) is compact and has no isolated points, and deduce that \(C\) is uncountable.

Solution

(i) Prove that \(C\) is totally disconnected

Suppose, to the contrary, that \(C\) has a connected component \(S\) containing more than one point.

Take two points \(x, y \in S\) with \(x < y\). Since \(x, y \in S \subseteq C\), we must have \(x, y \in A_n\) for all \(n \ge 0\).

Choose \(n\) large enough so that the length of the removed intervals satisfies:

\[ \frac{1}{3^n} < y - x \]

At the \(n\)-th stage of the construction, \(A_n\) consists of a union of disjoint closed intervals of length \(\frac{1}{3^n}\).

Since \(y - x > 1/3^n\), the points \(x\) and \(y\) cannot lie in the same closed interval of \(A_n\).

Therefore, between \(x\) and \(y\) there must be at least one open interval that was removed during the construction (e.g. the middle third). Let \(z\) be a point in one such removed interval. Then \(x < z < y\) and \(z \notin C\).

But a connected subset \(S\) of the real line has the property that if \(x, y \in S\), then the entire interval \([x, y]\) must be contained in \(S\). This contradicts the fact that \(z \notin C\). Therefore every connected component of \(C\) is a singleton.

(ii) Compactness, absence of isolated points, and uncountability

Compactness: Each \(A_n\) is a finite union of closed intervals, hence closed in \([0, 1]\). The intersection \(C = \bigcap A_n\) of arbitrarily many closed sets is still closed in \([0, 1]\). Since \([0, 1]\) is a closed and bounded subset of \(\mathbb{R}\) (hence compact), its closed subset \(C\) is necessarily compact.

No isolated points: Take any \(x \in C\) and any relatively open neighbourhood \(V\) of \(x\) in \(C\). There exists an open set \(U\) in \(\mathbb{R}\) such that \(V = U \cap C\). Since \(U\) is open, there exists \(\epsilon > 0\) such that \((x - \epsilon, x + \epsilon) \subseteq U\).

For every \(n\), \(x \in A_n\), so \(x\) lies in one of the closed intervals \(I_n\) of \(A_n\); this interval has length \(1/3^n\).

By construction, the two endpoints of \(I_n\) are never removed at later stages, so they both belong to \(C\).

Choose \(n\) large enough so that \(1/3^n < \epsilon\). Then the whole interval \(I_n\) is contained in \((x - \epsilon, x + \epsilon)\).
