The two endpoints of \(I_n\) belong to \(V\). Even if \(x\) happens to be one of these endpoints, the other endpoint is distinct from \(x\) and belongs to \(V\). This shows that every neighbourhood of \(x\) contains a point of \(C\) different from \(x\). Hence \(x\) is not an isolated point (i.e. \(C\) is perfect).

Uncountability: We have shown that \(C\) is compact (hence a complete metric space) with no isolated points. By the Baire category theorem, since a countable union of nowhere dense singleton sets cannot constitute a complete space, \(C\) must be uncountable.

docs.title: Problem 5
docs.text:
Fix a compact topological space \((X, \mathcal{T})\). Prove that the following two statements are equivalent:

(i) With respect to \(\mathcal{T}\), every compact subset of \(X\) is closed in \(X\); (ii) For any topology \(\mathcal{T}'\) strictly finer than \(\mathcal{T}\), the space \((X, \mathcal{T}')\) is non-compact.

Also, give an example of a space \((X, \mathcal{T})\) satisfying the above (equivalent) conditions.

Solution

Proof of (i) \(\implies\) (ii)

Let \(\mathcal{T}'\) be a topology strictly finer than \(\mathcal{T}\) (i.e. \(\mathcal{T}' \supsetneq \mathcal{T}\)).

Because the topology is finer, there exists an open set \(U \in \mathcal{T}' \setminus \mathcal{T}\).

Let \(K = X \setminus U\). Clearly \(K\) is closed in \(\mathcal{T}'\), but not closed in \(\mathcal{T}\).

We argue by contradiction. Suppose the space \((X, \mathcal{T}')\) is still compact.

Since \(K\) is a closed subset of the compact space \((X, \mathcal{T}')\), by standard topological properties \(K\) is compact in \((X, \mathcal{T}')\).

Consider the identity map \(id: (X, \mathcal{T}') \to (X, \mathcal{T})\). Since \(\mathcal{T}'\) contains \(\mathcal{T}\), this map is continuous.

The continuous image of a compact set is compact. Therefore \(K\) must also be compact in \((X, \mathcal{T})\).

By assumption (i), every compact subset of \((X, \mathcal{T})\) must be closed. Thus \(K\) must be closed in \(\mathcal{T}\).

This contradicts the conclusion in step 3 that \(K\) is not closed in \(\mathcal{T}\). Therefore \((X, \mathcal{T}')\) cannot be compact.

Proof of (ii) \(\implies\) (i)

Again we argue by contradiction. Suppose condition (i) is false; that is, there exists a compact subset \(K\) of \(X\) which is not closed in \(\mathcal{T}\).

Since \(K\) is not closed, its complement \(X \setminus K\) is not open in \(\mathcal{T}\).

We construct a new topology \(\mathcal{T}'\) by adding \(X \setminus K\) to the family of open sets. Let its subbasis be \(\mathcal{T} \cup \{X \setminus K\}\). Since \(X \setminus K \notin \mathcal{T}\), the new topology \(\mathcal{T}'\) is strictly finer than \(\mathcal{T}\).

We now show that under this finer topology, \((X, \mathcal{T}')\) is still compact.

Let \(\{U_\alpha\} \cup \{V_\beta \setminus K\}\) be an arbitrary open cover of \(X\) in the new topology \(\mathcal{T}'\), where \(U_\alpha, V_\beta \in \mathcal{T}\).

Since sets of the form \(V_\beta \setminus K\) cannot cover any point of \(K\), the subset \(K\) must be entirely covered by the original open sets \(\{U_\alpha\}\).

Since \(K\) is compact in \(\mathcal{T}\), there exists a finite subcover \(\{U_{\alpha_1}, \dots, U_{\alpha_n}\}\) covering \(K\).

Let \(W = \bigcup_{i=1}^n U_{\alpha_i}\). Then \(W\) is a \(\mathcal{T}\)-open set containing \(K\).

Consider the remaining uncovered part \(X \setminus W\). It is \(\mathcal{T}\)-closed and contained in the compact space \(X\). Hence \(X \setminus W\) is \(\mathcal{T}\)-compact.

Also note that \(X \setminus W \subseteq X \setminus K\), so it is covered by the remaining sets in the cover. Using the finite subcover property, only finitely many of these sets are needed to cover \(X \setminus W\).

Hence we have extracted a finite subcover of the whole space \(X\), proving that \((X, \mathcal{T}')\) is compact.

But this contradicts condition (ii), which says every strictly finer topology must be non-compact. Therefore the assumption is false and condition (i) must hold.

Example of a space satisfying the conditions

Any compact Hausdorff space satisfies these conditions.

A concrete example: the closed interval \([0, 1]\) with the standard topology.

Reason: in a Hausdorff space, every compact subset is necessarily closed, so it satisfies condition (i) and therefore equivalently condition (ii).

docs.title: Problem 6
docs.text:
Determine whether the following two spaces are locally compact:

(i) The rational numbers \(\mathbb{Q}\) with the standard topology; (ii) The real line \((\mathbb{R}, \mathcal{T})\) with the topology generated by the basis \(\mathcal{B} = \{(a, b] : a, b \in \mathbb{R}, a < b\}\).

Justify your answers.

Solution

(i) \(\mathbb{Q}\) with the standard topology is not locally compact

Proof: We argue by contradiction. Suppose \(\mathbb{Q}\) is locally compact. Then for any point \(x \in \mathbb{Q}\), there must exist a compact neighbourhood \(K\) of \(x\) in \(\mathbb{Q}\).

Since \(K\) is a neighbourhood of \(x\), there exists \(\epsilon > 0\) such that the open set \(U = (x - \epsilon, x + \epsilon) \cap \mathbb{Q}\) satisfies:

\[ x \in U \subseteq K \]

Since \(\mathbb{Q}\) is a metric space, its compact subset \(K\) must be sequentially compact.

Now choose an irrational number \(y\) in the interval \((x - \epsilon, x + \epsilon)\) (such irrationals exist because they are dense in \(\mathbb{R}\)). By the density of the rationals, we can construct a sequence of rationals \(\{x_n\} \subset U \subseteq K\) such that \(x_n \to y\) in the usual metric on \(\mathbb{R}\).

Since \(K\) is sequentially compact, the sequence \(\{x_n\}\) must have a convergent subsequence within \(K\) (hence within \(\mathbb{Q}\)). However, in \(\mathbb{R}\) the sequence converges uniquely to the irrational number \(y \notin \mathbb{Q}\), so in \(\mathbb{Q}\) the sequence has no limit point. This is a fundamental contradiction to the sequential compactness of \(K\). Hence \(\mathbb{Q}\) is not locally compact.

(ii) \((\mathbb{R}, \mathcal{T})\) with the upper limit topology is not locally compact

Proof: The basic open sets of this topology are left-open right-closed intervals \((a, b]\). We again argue by contradiction. Suppose this space is locally compact. Then any point \(x \in \mathbb{R}\) must have a compact neighbourhood \(K\) containing \(x\).

By definition of neighbourhood, there exists a basis element \((a, x]\) such that:

\[ x \in (a, x] \subseteq K \]

Notice that in the upper limit topology, the set \((a, x]\) is both open and closed (its complement \((-\infty, a] \cup (x, \infty)\) can be written as a union of basis elements and is open). A closed subset of a compact set \(K\) must also be compact, so \((a, x]\) must be compact, and thus must be limit point compact.

We construct a sequence in \((a, x]\) that decreases strictly to \(a\), for example:

\[ x_n = a + \frac{x - a}{n} \quad (n \ge 1) \]

Clearly \(x_n \in (a, x]\) for all \(n\). For any point \(y \in (a, x]\), we may choose a neighbourhood of the form \((c, y]\) in the upper limit topology. Since the sequence \(x_n\) decreases strictly to \(a < y\), for sufficiently large \(n\) we have \(x_n < c < y\), meaning that this neighbourhood \((c, y]\) contains only finitely many points of the sequence.

Therefore this sequence has no limit point in \((a, x]\). This contradicts the fact that \((a, x]\), being compact, must be limit point compact. Hence this space is not locally compact.

docs.title: Problem 7
docs.text:
Prove that the product space \(\left(\prod_{i=1}^{\infty} A_i, \mathcal{T}_p\right)\) is compact in the product topology, where each \(A_i\) is a nonempty finite set with the discrete topology.

(Hint: Review the conclusion from Homework 5; consider sequential compactness and metrizability.)

Solution

Proof:

First, since each \(A_i\) is finite and discrete, it is a metrizable space. The product of countably many metrizable spaces is metrizable in the product topology. For metric spaces, compactness is equivalent to sequential compactness. Therefore, it suffices to prove that the product space is sequentially compact.

Let \(\{x^{(n)}\}_{n=1}^{\infty}\) be an arbitrary sequence in the product space \(\prod_{i=1}^{\infty} A_i\). We will use the Cantor diagonal argument to extract a convergent subsequence.

Consider the sequence of first coordinates \(\{x_1^{(n)}\}_{n=1}^{\infty}\). Since \(A_1\) is finite and the sequence has infinitely many terms, by the pigeonhole principle there is some element of \(A_1\) that is taken infinitely many times. Hence we can extract a subsequence \(\{x^{(n, 1)}\}\) from the original sequence such that its first coordinate is constant.

Next, consider the second coordinates of the subsequence \(\{x^{(n, 1)}\}\). Since \(A_2\) is finite, we can extract from \(\{x^{(n, 1)}\}\) a further subsequence \(\{x^{(n, 2)}\}\) whose second coordinate is also constant (now both the first and second coordinates are fixed).

Continuing inductively, suppose we have extracted the \(k\)-th subsequence \(\{x^{(n, k)}\}\). Since \(A_{k+1}\) is finite, we can always extract the \((k+1)\)-th subsequence \(\{x^{(n, k+1)}\}\) whose first \(k+1\) coordinates are all constant.

Now construct the diagonal sequence:

\[ y^{(m)} = x^{(m, m)} \]

Consider this diagonal sequence \(y^{(m)}\). For any fixed coordinate position \(k\), when \(m \ge k\), \(y^{(m)}\) belongs to the \(k\)-th subsequence (or a later subsequence), so its \(k\)-th coordinate is a fixed constant.

In the product topology, convergence of a sequence is equivalent to coordinate-wise convergence. Hence for every fixed \(k\), the \(k\)-th coordinate of the diagonal sequence \(y^{(m)}\) is eventually constant, so it converges in the \(k\)-th coordinate.

Therefore the diagonal sequence \(y^{(m)}\) converges in the product topology to some point of the space. This shows that every sequence has a convergent subsequence, so the product space is sequentially compact, and therefore compact.

docs.title: Problem 8
docs.text:
(\(p\)-adic integers) Fix a prime number \(p\). For each \(i \in \mathbb{N}_{\ge 1}\), we have the quotient ring \(\mathbb{Z}/p^i\mathbb{Z}\) induced by the equivalence relation. Consider the following set:

\[ \mathbb{Z}_p := \left\{ (a_i)_{i \in \mathbb{N}_{\ge 1}} : a_i \in \mathbb{Z}/p^i\mathbb{Z} \text{ and for all } i, \phi_{i+1}(a_{i+1}) = a_i \right\} \subseteq \prod_{i=1}^{\infty} (\mathbb{Z}/p^i\mathbb{Z}) \]

where \(\phi_i: \mathbb{Z}/p^i\mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z}/p^{i-1}\mathbb{Z}\) is the natural surjection. Give each \(\mathbb{Z}/p^i\mathbb{Z}\) the discrete topology, and give the product space the product topology.

(i) Prove that \(\mathbb{Z}_p\) is closed in the product space \(\prod_{i=1}^{\infty} (\mathbb{Z}/p^i\mathbb{Z})\), and is compact. (ii) For each \(i \ge 1\), let \(f_i: \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z}/p^i\mathbb{Z}\) be the standard quotient map. Consider the embedding \(f: \mathbb{Z} \hookrightarrow \mathbb{Z}_p\), defined by \(f(a) = (f_i(a))_{i \ge 1}\). Prove that \(f(\mathbb{Z})\) is dense in \(\mathbb{Z}_p\).

Solution

(i) Prove that \(\mathbb{Z}_p\) is closed and compact

For any fixed \(i \ge 1\), define the map \(\psi_i: \prod_{k=1}^{\infty} (\mathbb{Z}/p^k\mathbb{Z}) \to \mathbb{Z}/p^i\mathbb{Z}\) by:

\[ \psi_i((a_k)_{k=1}^{\infty}) = \phi_{i+1}(a_{i+1}) - a_i \]

This map \(\psi_i\) depends only on the \(i\)-th and \((i+1)\)-th coordinates of the product space. Since projection maps are continuous and algebraic operations on finitely many coordinates are continuous in the discrete topology, \(\psi_i\) must be continuous.

Let \(E_i\) be the set defined by the \(i\)-th compatibility condition:

\[ E_i = \{ (a_k) \in \prod (\mathbb{Z}/p^k\mathbb{Z}) : \phi_{i+1}(a_{i+1}) = a_i \} = \psi_i^{-1}(\{0\}) \]

Since the singleton \(\{0\}\) is closed in the discrete topology and \(\psi_i\) is continuous, the preimage \(E_i\) is closed in the product topology.

The space \(\mathbb{Z}_p\) of \(p\)-adic integers is the intersection of all compatibility sets:

\[ \mathbb{Z}_p = \bigcap_{i=1}^{\infty} E_i \]

An arbitrary intersection of closed sets is closed, hence \(\mathbb{Z}_p\) is closed.

On the other hand, each coordinate space \(\mathbb{Z}/p^i\mathbb{Z}\) is finite and hence compact in the discrete topology. By the Tychonoff theorem, the product space \(\prod_{i=1}^{\infty} (\mathbb{Z}/p^i\mathbb{Z})\) is compact.

A closed subset of a compact space is compact. Since \(\mathbb{Z}_p\) is closed in the compact product space, \(\mathbb{Z}_p\) itself is compact.

(ii) Prove that \(f(\mathbb{Z})\) is dense

To prove density, it suffices to show that for every nonempty basic open set \(U\) in the subspace topology of \(\mathbb{Z}_p\), we have \(U \cap f(\mathbb{Z}) \ne \emptyset\).

Under the product topology, a basic open set \(U\) in \(\mathbb{Z}_p\) is determined by finitely many coordinate restrictions. Because of the compatibility conditions \(\phi_{i+1}(a_{i+1}) = a_i\) in \(\mathbb{Z}_p\), higher-order coordinates completely determine the lower-order coordinates.

Hence every nonempty basic open set in \(\mathbb{Z}_p\) can be represented by a restriction on one sufficiently large \(N\)-th coordinate: there exists a positive integer \(N\) and a constant \(c \in \mathbb{Z}/p^N\mathbb{Z}\) such that:

\[ U = \{ (x_i)_{i=1}^{\infty} \in \mathbb{Z}_p : x_N = c \} \]

Since \(c\) is an equivalence class in the quotient ring \(\mathbb{Z}/p^N\mathbb{Z}\), we can choose a representative \(a \in \mathbb{Z}\) such that:

\[ a \equiv c \pmod{p^N} \]

Consider the image \(f(a) = (f_i(a))_{i \ge 1}\) of the integer \(a\) under the map \(f\). By construction, its \(N\)-th coordinate is exactly \(f_N(a) = c\).

Therefore \(f(a) \in U\). This shows that \(U \cap f(\mathbb{Z})\) is nonempty. Since every nonempty open set contains a point of \(f(\mathbb{Z})\), we have \(\overline{f(\mathbb{Z})} = \mathbb{Z}_p\), i.e. \(f(\mathbb{Z})\) is dense in \(\mathbb{Z}_p\).

docs.title: Problem 9
docs.text:
Consider the subspace \(Y = \{0\} \cup \{1/n : n \in \mathbb{N}_{\ge 1}\}\) of the real line \(\mathbb{R}\). Is \(Y\) homeomorphic to the one-point compactification \(X = (\mathbb{N}_{\ge 1} \cup \{\infty\}, \mathcal{T}')\) of the natural numbers \(\mathbb{N}_{\ge 1}\) with the discrete topology? Justify your answer.

Solution

Conclusion: Yes, they are homeomorphic.

Proof:

We first construct a bijection \(f: X \to Y\) as follows:

\[ f(n) = \frac{1}{n} \quad (\text{for } n \in \mathbb{N}_{\ge 1}) \] \[ f(\infty) = 0 \]

This is clearly a bijection.

We now prove that \(f\) is continuous. We need to check that the preimage under \(f\) of every open set in \(Y\) is open in \(X\).

Let \(V\) be an arbitrary open set in \(Y\). Consider two cases:

  • Case 1: \(0 \notin V\). Then \(V\) consists entirely of isolated points of the form \(1/n\). Its preimage \(f^{-1}(V)\) is a subset of \(\mathbb{N}_{\ge 1}\) and does not contain \(\infty\). Since \(\mathbb{N}_{\ge 1}\) is discrete, in its one-point compactification \(X\), every subset not containing \(\infty\) is open. Hence \(f^{-1}(V)\) is open in \(X\).

  • Case 2: \(0 \in V\). Since \(V\) is open in the subspace \(Y\) of \(\mathbb{R}\), there exists \(\epsilon > 0\) such that \((-\epsilon, \epsilon) \cap Y \subseteq V\). This means that for all \(n > 1/\epsilon\), the points \(1/n\) belong to \(V\). In other words, \(V\) misses only finitely many points of \(Y\) of the form \(1/n\). Consider its preimage \(f^{-1}(V)\): it contains the point \(\infty\), and its complement in \(\mathbb{N}_{\ge 1}\) is finite. By the definition of the one-point compactification, a set containing the point at infinity and having finite complement is exactly an open neighbourhood in the compactification space \(X\). Hence \(f^{-1}(V)\) is again open.

This proves that \(f\) is continuous.

Finally, we use an important theorem in general topology: a continuous bijection from a compact space to a Hausdorff space is necessarily a homeomorphism.

  • The space \(X\) is a one-point compactification, which by definition is a compact space.
  • The space \(Y\) is a subspace of the metric space \(\mathbb{R}\), hence a Hausdorff space.

Since \(f: X \to Y\) is a continuous bijection satisfying the “compact domain to Hausdorff codomain” condition, \(f\) must be a homeomorphism.

docs.title: Problem 10
docs.text:
Prove that the product topological space \((\mathbb{R}^\omega, \mathcal{T}_p)\) has no one-point compactification.

(Hint: Is \(\mathbb{R}^\omega\) locally compact?)

Solution

Proof:

According to the fundamental theory of topology, a space \(X\) has a Hausdorff one-point compactification if and only if \(X\) itself is locally compact, Hausdorff, and non-compact. The product space \(\mathbb{R}^\omega\) is clearly Hausdorff (since it is a product of Hausdorff spaces \(\mathbb{R}\)). We will prove that it is not locally compact, so it cannot have a one-point compactification.

We argue by contradiction. Suppose \((\mathbb{R}^\omega, \mathcal{T}_p)\) is locally compact.

Consider the origin \(\mathbf{0} = (0, 0, \dots) \in \mathbb{R}^\omega\). By local compactness, the origin must have a compact neighbourhood \(K\).

By definition of the product topology basis, since \(K\) is a neighbourhood of \(\mathbf{0}\), there exists a basic open set \(U\) such that:

\[ \mathbf{0} \in U \subseteq K \]

In the product topology, a basic open set \(U\) can restrict only finitely many coordinates. That is, there exists a positive integer \(N\) such that:

\[ U = U_1 \times U_2 \times \dots \times U_N \times \mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R} \times \dots \]

where the first \(N\) sets \(U_i\) are open intervals in \(\mathbb{R}\), and from the \((N+1)\)-th coordinate onward, all factors must be the whole space \(\mathbb{R}\).

Now consider the projection onto the \((N+1)\)-th coordinate \(\pi_{N+1}: \mathbb{R}^\omega \to \mathbb{R}\). In the product topology the projection map is always continuous.

Since \(K\) is compact and continuous maps send compact sets to compact sets, the projection \(\pi_{N+1}(K)\) must be a compact subset of \(\mathbb{R}\).

However, from the inclusion \(U \subseteq K\), we obtain the corresponding inclusion of projections:

\[ \pi_{N+1}(U) \subseteq \pi_{N+1}(K) \]

By the structure of the basic open set \(U\), the projection onto the \((N+1)\)-th coordinate is the whole real line:

\[ \pi_{N+1}(U) = \mathbb{R} \]

Combining steps 8 and 9, we get \(\mathbb{R} \subseteq \pi_{N+1}(K)\). Thus the compact set \(\pi_{N+1}(K)\) must equal the whole space \(\mathbb{R}\).

But we know that the real line \(\mathbb{R}\) is unbounded, and therefore not compact! This is an irreconcilable contradiction.

The contradiction shows that our assumption was false, i.e. \(\mathbb{R}^\omega\) is not locally compact. Lacking local compactness, it cannot admit a one-point compactification.

This section contains the ninth homework assignment of the point-set topology course and its related proofs. It covers separability of product spaces, the equivalence of second countability/Lindelöf/separability in metric spaces, the \(T_0\) separation property of pseudometric-generated topologies, properties of \(T_3\) and \(T_4\) spaces, and the regularity of locally compact Hausdorff spaces.

docs.title: Problem 11
docs.text:
Prove that if \(X_i\) is separable for every \(i \in \mathbb{N}\), then the product space \(\left(\prod_{i \in \mathbb{N}} X_i, \mathcal{T}_p\right)\) is also separable.

Solution

Proof:

Since each \(X_i\) is separable, for each \(i \in \mathbb{N}\) there exists a countable dense subset \(A_i \subseteq X_i\).

In the product space \(\prod X_i\), fix a “base point” \(x^* = (x_1^*, x_2^*, \dots)\).

For each \(n \in \mathbb{N}\), define the set \(D_n\) to be the set of sequences whose first \(n\) coordinates belong to \(A_i\) and whose remaining coordinates coincide with the base point:

\[ D_n = \{ (x_i) \in \prod X_i \mid x_i \in A_i \text{ for } i \le n, \text{ and } x_i = x_i^* \text{ for } i > n \} \]

Clearly each \(D_n\) is in bijection with the finite product \(A_1 \times A_2 \times \dots \times A_n\). Since a finite product of countable sets is countable, each \(D_n\) is countable.

Let \(D = \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty D_n\). As a countable union of countable sets, \(D\) must be countable.

We now prove that \(D\) is dense in the product topology. Take an arbitrary nonempty basic open set \(U = \prod_{i=1}^\infty U_i\) in the product space.

By definition of the product topology, only finitely many coordinates have \(U_i\) not equal to the whole space. That is, there exists a positive integer \(N\) such that for all \(i > N\), \(U_i = X_i\).

For \(i \le N\), since \(U_i\) is a nonempty open set in \(X_i\) and \(A_i\) is dense in \(X_i\), there exists a point \(y_i \in U_i \cap A_i\).

Construct a sequence \(y = (y_1, y_2, \dots) \in \prod X_i\), where the first \(N\) coordinates are the chosen points \(y_i\), and all coordinates after \(N\) are the base point coordinates \(x_i^*\).

By definition, since only the first \(N\) coordinates of \(y\) may differ from \(x^*\) and these \(N\) coordinates all belong to \(A_i\), we have \(y \in D_N \subseteq D\).

Also, for \(i \le N\), \(y_i \in U_i\); for \(i > N\), \(y_i = x_i^* \in X_i = U_i\). Hence \(y \in U\).

This shows \(U \cap D \ne \emptyset\). Since every basic open set contains a point of \(D\), \(D\) is dense. Having found a countable dense subset, the product space is separable.

docs.title: Problem 12
docs.text:
Let \((X, d)\) be a metric space. Prove that the following three properties are equivalent:

(i) \(X\) is second countable; (ii) \(X\) is a Lindelöf space; (iii) \(X\) is separable.

(Hint: For (ii) \(\Rightarrow\) (iii), consider the open cover \(\{B(x, 1/n) : x \in X, n \in \mathbb{N}\}\), fix \(n\) and first use the Lindelöf property.)

Solution

Proof:

Proof of (i) \(\Rightarrow\) (ii): Second countable \(\Rightarrow\) Lindelöf

Let \(\mathcal{B}\) be a countable basis for \(X\) and let \(\mathcal{U}\) be an arbitrary open cover of \(X\).

For any point \(x \in X\), since \(\mathcal{U}\) covers \(X\), there exists an open set \(U_x \in \mathcal{U}\) such that \(x \in U_x\).

Since \(\mathcal{B}\) is a basis, there exists a basis element \(B_x \in \mathcal{B}\) such that \(x \in B_x \subseteq U_x\).

Consider the collection \(\mathcal{B}' = \{B_x \mid x \in X\}\) of all chosen basis elements. Since \(\mathcal{B}\) is countable, the subset \(\mathcal{B}'\) must also be countable.

For each basis element in \(\mathcal{B}'\), choose one open set in \(\mathcal{U}\) that contains it. The selected family is a subcollection of \(\mathcal{U}\) and is at most countable.

This countable family still covers all of \(X\). Therefore every open cover has a countable subcover, so \(X\) is Lindelöf.

Proof of (ii) \(\Rightarrow\) (iii): Lindelöf \(\Rightarrow\) separable

For any fixed positive integer \(n\), consider the family of open balls of radius \(1/n\) centered at every point of \(X\):

\[ \mathcal{U}_n = \left\{ B\left(x, \frac{1}{n}\right) : x \in X \right\} \]

Clearly \(\mathcal{U}_n\) is an open cover of \(X\). Since \(X\) is Lindelöf, there exists a countable subcover.

That is, there exist countably many points \(x_1^{(n)}, x_2^{(n)}, \dots \in X\) such that the corresponding open balls cover \(X\):

\[ X \subseteq \bigcup_{i=1}^\infty B\left(x_i^{(n)}, \frac{1}{n}\right) \]

Let \(D_n = \{x_i^{(n)} \mid i \in \mathbb{N}\}\) be the set of these countably many centers. \(D_n\) is countable.

Let \(D = \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty D_n\). A countable union of countable sets is still countable.

We prove that \(D\) is dense in \(X\). Take any \(y \in X\) and any \(\epsilon > 0\). There exists a positive integer \(n\) such that \(1/n < \epsilon\).

Since the balls with centers in \(D_n\) cover \(X\), there exists some \(x_k^{(n)} \in D_n \subseteq D\) such that \(y \in B(x_k^{(n)}, 1/n)\).

This means \(d(y, x_k^{(n)}) < 1/n < \epsilon\), so \(x_k^{(n)} \in B(y, \epsilon)\). Thus \(D\) intersects every open neighbourhood of \(y\). Hence \(D\) is dense in \(X\), and \(X\) is separable.

Proof of (iii) \(\Rightarrow\) (i): Separable \(\Rightarrow\) second countable

Suppose \(X\) is separable, so there exists a countable dense subset \(D\).

Construct the family of open balls:

\[ \mathcal{B} = \left\{ B\left(x, \frac{1}{n}\right) : x \in D, n \in \mathbb{N} \right\} \]

Since \(D\) and \(\mathbb{N}\) are countable, \(\mathcal{B}\) is a countable family. We claim that \(\mathcal{B}\) is a basis for \(X\).

Take an arbitrary open set \(U\) in \(X\) and a point \(y \in U\). Since \(U\) is open, there exists \(\epsilon > 0\) such that \(B(y, \epsilon) \subseteq U\).

Choose an integer \(n\) large enough so that \(1/n < \epsilon / 2\).

Since \(D\) is dense in \(X\), there exists a point \(x \in D\) inside the open ball \(B(y, 1/n)\). That is, \(d(y, x) < 1/n\).

Now the basis element \(B(x, 1/n) \in \mathcal{B}\) contains \(y\), because \(d(y, x) < 1/n\).

For any \(z \in B(x, 1/n)\), by the triangle inequality:

\[ d(z, y) \le d(z, x) + d(x, y) < \frac{1}{n} + \frac{1}{n} = \frac{2}{n} < \epsilon \]

Hence \(B(x, 1/n) \subseteq B(y, \epsilon) \subseteq U\). Since every open set can be approximated by elements of \(\mathcal{B}\), \(\mathcal{B}\) is indeed a countable basis for the space. Hence \(X\) is second countable.

docs.title: Problem 13
docs.text:
Let \((X, d)\) be a pseudometric space. Let \(\mathcal{T}_d\) be the topology on \(X\) generated by the open balls

\[ \left\{ B(x, \epsilon) : x \in X, \epsilon \in \mathbb{R}_{>0} ight\} \]

where \(B(x, \epsilon) := \{y \in X : d(x, y) < \epsilon\}\). Prove that the topological space \((X, \mathcal{T}_d)\) is a \(T_0\) space if and only if \(d\) is a metric.

Solution

Proof of necessity (\(\Rightarrow\)):

Suppose \((X, \mathcal{T}_d)\) is a \(T_0\) space. To prove that \(d\) is a metric, it suffices to prove that for all \(x e y\), \(d(x, y) > 0\) (since a pseudometric already satisfies symmetry, triangle inequality, and nonnegativity).

For \(x e y\), since the space is \(T_0\), there exists an open set \(U\) containing one of the points but not the other. Suppose, without loss of generality, that \(x \in U\) and \(y otin U\).

Since \(\mathcal{T}_d\) is generated by open balls (in fact, the open balls themselves form a basis for the pseudometric topology), there exists an open ball \(B(p, r)\) such that:

\[ x \in B(p, r) \subseteq U \]

Since \(y otin U\), we must have \(y otin B(p, r)\).

By the definition of open balls, \(d(p, x) < r\) and \(d(p, y) \ge r\).

Using the triangle inequality for pseudometrics, \(d(p, y) \le d(p, x) + d(x, y)\), hence:

\[ d(x, y) \ge d(p, y) - d(p, x) > r - r = 0 \]

Since \(d(x, y) > 0\) for all \(x e y\), \(d\) satisfies the positivity condition and is therefore a genuine metric.

Proof of sufficiency (\(\Leftarrow\)):

Suppose \(d\) is a metric. Take any two distinct points \(x e y\) in \(X\).

Since the metric satisfies positivity, we have \(d(x, y) = r > 0\).

Choose \(\epsilon = r / 2 > 0\) and consider the open ball \(B(x, \epsilon)\).

Clearly \(x \in B(x, \epsilon)\).

If \(y \in B(x, \epsilon)\), then by definition \(d(x, y) < \epsilon = r / 2\), contradicting \(d(x, y) = r\).

Hence \(y otin B(x, \epsilon)\).

We have found an open set \(B(x, \epsilon)\) that contains \(x\) but not \(y\). Thus the space satisfies the \(T_0\) separation axiom.

docs.title: Problem 14
docs.text:
For a topological space \((X, \mathcal{T})\), prove the following statements:

(i) If \(X\) is a \(T_3\) space, then for any distinct \(x, y \in X\), there exist open sets \(U, V\) such that \(x \in U\), \(y \in V\), and \(\overline{U} \cap \overline{V} = \emptyset\). (ii) If \(X\) is a \(T_4\) space, then for any disjoint closed sets \(A, B \subseteq X\), there exist open sets \(U, V\) such that \(A \subseteq U\), \(B \subseteq V\), and \(\overline{U} \cap \overline{V} = \emptyset\).

Solution

(i) Proof for \(T_3\) spaces

Suppose \(X\) is a \(T_3\) space, i.e. it is regular and satisfies the \(T_1\) separation axiom. For any distinct \(x, y \in X\), by the \(T_1\) property the singleton \(\{y\}\) is closed.

Since \(x \notin \{y\}\) and \(\{y\}\) is closed, by regularity there exist disjoint open sets \(U_1\) and \(W_1\) such that:

\[ x \in U_1 \quad \text{and} \quad y \in W_1 \]

Since \(U_1 \cap W_1 = \emptyset\), we have \(U_1 \subseteq X \setminus W_1\). Because \(W_1\) is open, \(X \setminus W_1\) is closed.

Since \(U_1\) is contained in the closed set \(X \setminus W_1\), its closure must also be contained in it:

\[ \overline{U_1} \subseteq X \setminus W_1 \]

This means \(\overline{U_1} \cap W_1 = \emptyset\), hence \(y \notin \overline{U_1}\).

Now we have the point \(y\) and the closed set \(\overline{U_1}\) not containing \(y\). Applying regularity again, there exist disjoint open sets \(V\) and \(W_2\) such that:

\[ y \in V \quad \text{and} \quad \overline{U_1} \subseteq W_2 \]

Similarly, since \(V \cap W_2 = \emptyset\), we deduce \(\overline{V} \subseteq X \setminus W_2\).

Combining \(\overline{U_1} \subseteq W_2\), we obtain \(\overline{U_1} \subseteq X \setminus \overline{V}\), i.e.:

\[ \overline{U_1} \cap \overline{V} = \emptyset \]

Let \(U = U_1\). We have found open sets \(U\) and \(V\) such that \(x \in U\), \(y \in V\), and \(\overline{U} \cap \overline{V} = \emptyset\).

(ii) Proof for \(T_4\) spaces

Suppose \(X\) is a \(T_4\) space, i.e. it is normal and satisfies the \(T_1\) separation axiom. Let \(A, B\) be two disjoint closed sets.

By normality, there exist disjoint open sets \(U_1\) and \(W_1\) such that:

\[ A \subseteq U_1 \quad \text{and} \quad B \subseteq W_1 \]

As before, since \(U_1 \cap W_1 = \emptyset\), we have \(U_1 \subseteq X \setminus W_1\), and taking closures:

\[ \overline{U_1} \subseteq X \setminus W_1 \]

Since \(B \subseteq W_1\), we get \(\overline{U_1} \cap B = \emptyset\).

Now we have two new disjoint closed sets: \(\overline{U_1}\) and \(B\). Applying normality again, there exist disjoint open sets \(U_2\) and \(V\) such that:

\[ \overline{U_1} \subseteq U_2 \quad \text{and} \quad B \subseteq V \]

Since \(U_2 \cap V = \emptyset\), similarly we deduce \(\overline{V} \subseteq X \setminus U_2\).

Because \(\overline{U_1} \subseteq U_2\), this immediately implies:

\[ \overline{U_1} \cap \overline{V} = \emptyset \]

Let \(U = U_1\). We clearly have \(A \subseteq U\) (by step 2) and \(B \subseteq V\) (by step 5), and the closures are disjoint: \(\overline{U} \cap \overline{V} = \emptyset\). This completes the proof.

docs.title: Problem 15
docs.text:
Prove that every locally compact Hausdorff space is regular, i.e. “locally compact + \(T_2 \Rightarrow T_3\)”.

Solution

Proof:

Let \(X\) be a locally compact Hausdorff space. Since \(X\) is Hausdorff (i.e. \(T_2\)), it satisfies the \(T_1\) separation axiom. To prove regularity, it suffices to show that for every closed set \(A \subseteq X\) and every point \(x otin A\), there exist disjoint open sets separating them.

Since \(X\) is locally compact, the point \(x\) has a compact neighbourhood \(K\) containing \(x\).

By the definition of neighbourhood, there exists an open set \(W\) such that:

\[ x \in W \subseteq K \]

Since compact subsets of Hausdorff spaces are closed, \(K\) is closed.

Define \(C = A \cap K\). Since both \(A\) and \(K\) are closed, \(C\) is a closed subset of \(K\). A closed subset of a compact set is compact, so \(C\) is compact.

Since \(x otin A\), clearly \(x otin C\). Now we need to separate the point \(x\) from the compact set \(C\) in the Hausdorff space \(X\).

For each \(y \in C\), since \(x e y\) and \(X\) is Hausdorff, there exist disjoint open sets \(U_y\) and \(V_y\) such that:

\[ x \in U_y \quad ext{and} \quad y \in V_y \]

The family \(\{V_y \mid y \in C\}\) is an open cover of the compact set \(C\). By compactness, there exist finitely many points \(y_1, y_2, \dots, y_n \in C\) such that:

\[ C \subseteq igcup_{i=1}^n V_{y_i} \]

Now define:

\[ V = igcup_{i=1}^n V_{y_i} \quad ext{and} \quad U = igcap_{i=1}^n U_{y_i} \]

Clearly \(U\) and \(V\) are disjoint open sets and satisfy \(x \in U\) and \(C \subseteq V\).

Now use \(U, V\) to construct two new open sets \(O_1\) and \(O_2\) separating \(x\) from the original closed set \(A\):

\[ O_1 = U \cap W \] \[ O_2 = V \cup (X \setminus K) \]

Check that \(O_1, O_2\) are open and contain the desired sets:

  • Since \(U\) and \(W\) are open, \(O_1\) is open. Also \(x \in U\) and \(x \in W\), so \(x \in O_1\).

  • Since \(V\) is open and \(K\) is closed (so \(X \setminus K\) is open), \(O_2\) is open.

  • For any \(a \in A\): if \(a \in K\), then \(a \in A \cap K = C\), hence \(a \in V \subseteq O_2\); if \(a otin K\), then \(a \in X \setminus K \subseteq O_2\). In either case \(A \subseteq O_2\).

Check that \(O_1\) and \(O_2\) are disjoint:

\[ O_1 \cap O_2 = (U \cap W) \cap (V \cup (X \setminus K)) = (U \cap W \cap V) \cup (U \cap W \cap (X \setminus K)) \]

  • The first part is empty because \(U \cap V = \emptyset\), so \(U \cap W \cap V = \emptyset\).

  • The second part is empty because \(W \subseteq K\), so \(W \cap (X \setminus K) = \emptyset\).

  • Hence \(O_1 \cap O_2 = \emptyset\).

In summary, we have found two disjoint open sets \(O_1\) and \(O_2\) containing \(x\) and the closed set \(A\) respectively. Therefore the space is regular (\(T_3\)).

docs.title: ♾️ Advanced Mathematical Analysis
docs.text: This module covers the core topological and analytical theorems of multivariate calculus and function sequences, with a focus on hard analysis tools closely related to real variable functions and functional analysis.

docs.title: I. Multivariate Differential Calculus and the Implicit Function Theorem
docs.text:
Multivariate Total Differential and Continuous Differentiability

Let \(f: U \subset \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m\) be a mapping. If at the point \(x_0 \in U\) there exists a linear mapping \(L: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m\) such that

\[ \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{\|f(x_0 + h) - f(x_0) - L(h)\|}{\|h\|} = 0 \]

then \(f\) is said to be differentiable at \(x_0\), and we write \(L = Df(x_0)\) (the Jacobian matrix). If \(Df(x)\) exists and is continuous on the whole set \(U\), then \(f\) is said to be \(C^1\) continuously differentiable.

Implicit Function Theorem

Let \(F: \mathbb{R}^n \times \mathbb{R}^m \to \mathbb{R}^m\) be \(C^1\) on an open set \(U\). Suppose that at a point \((x_0, y_0) \in U\) we have:

  1. \(F(x_0, y_0) = 0\)

  2. The Jacobian matrix with respect to \(y\) is locally invertible, i.e., \(\det \left( \frac{\partial F}{\partial y} (x_0, y_0) \right) \neq 0\)

Then there exists a neighborhood \(V \subset \mathbb{R}^n\) of \(x_0\) and a unique \(C^1\) mapping \(g: V \to \mathbb{R}^m\) satisfying \(g(x_0) = y_0\), such that for every \(x \in V\),

\[ F(x, g(x)) = 0 \]

Moreover, the derivative (sensitivity) of the implicit function can be obtained directly via the chain rule:

\[ Dg(x) = - \left( \frac{\partial F}{\partial y}(x, g(x)) \right)^{-1} \frac{\partial F}{\partial x}(x, g(x)) \]

docs.title: II. Uniform Convergence of Function Sequences and Series
docs.text:
Definition of Uniform Convergence

A sequence of functions \(\{f_n\}\) defined on an interval \(I\) converges uniformly to a limit function \(f\) if for every \(\epsilon > 0\) there exists an integer \(N\) (independent of the variable \(x\)) such that for all \(n > N\) and all \(x \in I\),

\[ |f_n(x) - f(x)| < \epsilon \]
  • Functional analysis perspective: This is equivalent to convergence of \(\{f_n\}\) in the supremum norm on \(I\): \(\lim_{n \to \infty} \|f_n - f\|_\infty = 0\).

Continuity Preservation under Uniform Convergence (Foundation for Completeness of \(C^k[a, b]\))

If the sequence \(\{f_n\}\) converges uniformly to \(f\) on \([a, b]\), and each \(f_n\) is continuous on \([a, b]\), then the limit function \(f\) is also continuous on \([a, b]\).

Extension: Connection to Completeness of the Function Space \(C^k[a, b]\)

In functional analysis, the norm on the Banach space \(C^k[a, b]\) is defined by

\[ \|f\|_{C^k} = \sum_{j=0}^k \max_{t \in [a, b]} |f^{(j)}(t)| \]

Proving that this space is complete – i.e., that every Cauchy sequence converges to an element inside the space – relies on the uniform convergence theorem for derivatives in mathematical analysis:

If the sequences of derivative functions \(\{f_n^{(j)}\}\) each converge uniformly on \([a, b]\) to \(g_j\), then the limit \(f\) of the original sequence satisfies \(f^{(j)} = g_j\). Consequently, by the continuity preservation theorem above, the resulting limit function \(f \in C^k[a, b]\).

docs.title: III. Interchange of Limits with Integrals and Derivatives
docs.text:
Passing the Limit under the Riemann Integral

Let \(\{f_n\}\) be a sequence of Riemann integrable functions on \([a, b]\). If \(f_n \xrightarrow{\text{uniformly}} f\), then the limit function \(f\) is also Riemann integrable on \([a, b]\), and the limit and integral can be interchanged:

\[ \lim_{n \to \infty} \int_a^b f_n(x) dx = \int_a^b \left( \lim_{n \to \infty} f_n(x) \right) dx = \int_a^b f(x) dx \]

(Note: In real variable theory, when the Riemann integral is upgraded to the Lebesgue integral, this theorem is completely replaced by the more general Lebesgue Dominated Convergence Theorem (LDCT).)

Differentiation under the Riemann Integral (Leibniz Integral Rule)

Let \(f(x, y)\) and its partial derivative \(\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x, y)\) be continuous on the rectangle \([a, b] \times [c, d]\). Define the parameter‑dependent integral \(F(y) = \int_a^b f(x, y) dx\). Then \(F(y)\) is differentiable and satisfies

\[ \frac{d}{dy} \int_a^b f(x, y) dx = \int_a^b \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x, y) dx \]

docs.title: IV. Compactness Theory and the Arzelà–Ascoli Theorem
docs.text:
This is one of the most advanced theorems in mathematical analysis and is closely linked to functional analysis (especially the study of compact operators). It provides a criterion for the compactness of subsets in function spaces.

Uniform Boundedness and Equicontinuity

Let \(\mathcal{F}\) be a family of functions defined on a compact interval \([a, b]\):

  • Uniformly Bounded: There exists a constant \(M > 0\) such that for all \(f \in \mathcal{F}\) and all \(t \in [a, b]\), \(|f(t)| \le M\).

  • Equicontinuous: For every \(\epsilon > 0\), there exists a \(\delta > 0\) depending only on \(\epsilon\) (and not on the particular function \(f\) or point \(t\)) such that whenever \(|t_1 - t_2| < \delta\),

\[ |f(t_1) - f(t_2)| < \epsilon \quad (\forall f \in \mathcal{F}) \]

Arzelà–Ascoli Theorem

Let \(\mathcal{F} \subset C[a, b]\). Then \(\mathcal{F}\) is relatively compact (i.e., every sequence in \(\mathcal{F}\) has a subsequence that converges uniformly) if and only if \(\mathcal{F}\) is uniformly bounded and equicontinuous on \([a, b]\).

docs.title: 🔢 Linear Algebra
docs.text: This module currently focuses on content related to Linear Algebra.

docs.title: 1. Matrix Calculus
docs.text:
Matrix calculus has always been the most challenging topic for me. I encountered it repeatedly in courses like Regression Analysis, Multivariate Statistical Analysis, and Practical Algorithms for Optimization, yet I never organized it systematically. After losing 15 points on a major matrix derivation problem during the Practical Algorithms for Optimization final exam due to time constraints and cumbersome summation notation, I decided to consolidate these methods, specifically focusing on the more elegant Matrix Differential Method.

Layout Convention

This reference sheet consistently adopts the Denominator Layout, which is most common in machine learning and optimization. That is: for a scalar \(f\) with respect to an \(m \times n\) matrix \(X\), the derivative \(\frac{\partial f}{\partial X}\) has the same dimensions as \(X\) (\(m \times n\)).

docs.title: (1) Core Method: Matrix Differential Method
docs.text:
The traditional approach of taking partial derivatives element-wise is prone to errors within complex summation symbols. A more elegant alternative is to use the Total Differential.

Connection Between Differential and Derivative

The total differential \(df\) of a scalar function \(f(X)\) can always be expressed as the trace of the product of a certain matrix and \(dX\):

\[ df = \text{tr}\left( \left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial X}\right)^T dX \right) \]

The Four-Step Method:

  1. Compute the total differential \(df\).
  2. Simplify using trace properties to reach the form \(\text{tr}(M^T dX)\).
  3. Remove the \(\text{tr}\) and \(dX\); the remaining matrix \(M\) is the derivative \(\frac{\partial f}{\partial X}\).
Basic Rules of Matrix Differentials
  • Addition/Subtraction: \(d(X \pm Y) = dX \pm dY\)
  • Product Rule: \(d(XY) = (dX)Y + X(dY)\)
  • Transpose: \(d(X^T) = (dX)^T\)
  • Trace: \(d(\text{tr}(X)) = \text{tr}(dX)\)
  • Cyclic Property of Trace: \(\text{tr}(ABC) = \text{tr}(CAB) = \text{tr}(BCA)\)
  • Invariance under Transpose: \(\text{tr}(A) = \text{tr}(A^T)\)

docs.title: (2) Trace Derivatives
docs.text:
Trace derivatives are frequently required when deriving OLS (Ordinary Least Squares) or constructing loss functions.

Common Trace Derivative Formulas

Let \(X\) be the variable matrix, and \(A, B\) be constant matrices:

  1. \[\frac{\partial \text{tr}(AX)}{\partial X} = A^T\]
  2. \[\frac{\partial \text{tr}(AXB)}{\partial X} = A^T B^T\]
  3. \[\frac{\partial \text{tr}(X^TAX)}{\partial X} = (A + A^T)X\]

(Special Case: If \(A\) is symmetric, the result simplifies to \(2AX\))

Derivation: \(\frac{\partial \text{tr}(AX)}{\partial X}\)

Let \(f = \text{tr}(AX)\). Compute the differential:

\[ df = d(\text{tr}(AX)) = \text{tr}(d(AX)) = \text{tr}(A dX) \]

To match the form \(\text{tr}(M^T dX)\), observe that \(\text{tr}(A dX) = \text{tr}((A^T)^T dX)\). Thus, \(M^T = A \implies M = A^T\).

Therefore: \(\frac{\partial f}{\partial X} = A^T\).

Derivation: \(\frac{\partial \text{tr}(X^TAX)}{\partial X}\)

Let \(f = \text{tr}(X^TAX)\). Compute the differential (using the product rule \(d(UV) = (dU)V + U(dV)\)):

\[ df = \text{tr}(d(X^T) AX + X^T d(AX)) = \text{tr}((dX)^T AX) + \text{tr}(X^T A dX) \]

Using the transpose invariance \(\text{tr}(M) = \text{tr}(M^T)\) for the first term:

\[ \text{tr}((dX)^T AX) = \text{tr}(((dX)^T AX)^T) = \text{tr}(X^T A^T dX) \]

Combining the terms:

\[ df = \text{tr}(X^T A^T dX) + \text{tr}(X^T A dX) = \text{tr}((X^T A^T + X^T A) dX) \]

Factorizing and using the cyclic property to match \(\text{tr}(M^T dX)\):

\[ df = \text{tr}( (X^T(A^T + A)) dX ) = \text{tr}( ((A^T + A)^T X)^T dX ) \]

Thus, \(M = (A^T + A)^T X = (A + A^T)X\).

docs.title: (3) Determinant and Inverse Matrix Derivatives
docs.text:
In Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE), especially involving the covariance matrix \(\Sigma\) of a multivariate normal distribution, derivatives of determinants and inverses are essential.

Inverse and Determinant Derivative Formulas

Let \(X\) be an invertible square matrix:

  1. Inverse Matrix Differential: \(d(X^{-1}) = -X^{-1} (dX) X^{-1}\)

  2. Determinant Differential (Jacobi's Formula): \(d|X| = |X| \text{tr}(X^{-1} dX)\)

  3. Derivative of the Determinant: \(\frac{\partial |X|}{\partial X} = |X| (X^{-1})^T\)

  4. Derivative of the Log-Determinant: \(\frac{\partial \ln |X|}{\partial X} = (X^{-1})^T\)

Derivation: Differential of the Inverse \(d(X^{-1})\)

Starting from the identity \(XX^{-1} = I\), take the differential of both sides:

\[ d(XX^{-1}) = d(I) \implies (dX)X^{-1} + X d(X^{-1}) = 0 \]

Rearranging and left-multiplying by \(X^{-1}\):

\[ X d(X^{-1}) = -(dX)X^{-1} \implies d(X^{-1}) = -X^{-1}(dX)X^{-1} \] Determinant Derivative \(d|X|\) (Cofactor Summation Method)

This derivation bridges the gap between scalar summation, the adjugate matrix, and the matrix trace.

1. Element-wise derivative: \(\frac{\partial |X|}{\partial x_{ij}} = C_{ij}\) According to the Laplace Expansion, expanding along the \(i\)-th row:

\[|X| = \sum_{k=1}^n x_{ik} C_{ik}\]

Since the calculation of the cofactor \(C_{ik}\) does not include any elements from the \(i\)-th row, \(C_{ik}\) is treated as a constant with respect to \(x_{ij}\). Taking the derivative:

\[\frac{\partial |X|}{\partial x_{ij}} = \frac{\partial}{\partial x_{ij}} (x_{i1}C_{i1} + \dots + x_{ij}C_{ij} + \dots + x_{in}C_{in}) = C_{ij}\]

Conclusion: The partial derivative of the determinant with respect to an element is its corresponding cofactor.

2. Converting Differential to Trace: \(d|X| = \text{tr}(X^* dX)\) Using the definition of the total differential and the adjugate matrix \(X^*\) (where \((X^*)_{ji} = C_{ij}\)):

\[ d|X| = \sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j=1}^n \frac{\partial |X|}{\partial x_{ij}} dx_{ij} = \sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j=1}^n C_{ij} dx_{ij} \]

Rewriting this as the sum of the diagonal elements of a matrix product:

\[ d|X| = \sum_{j=1}^n \left( \sum_{i=1}^n (X^*)_{ji} (dX)_{ij} \right) = \text{tr}(X^* dX) \]

3. Deriving Jacobi's Formula: \(d|X| = |X| \text{tr}(X^{-1} dX)\) Substituting the relationship \(X^* = |X| X^{-1}\):

\[d|X| = \text{tr}(|X| X^{-1} dX) = |X| \text{tr}(X^{-1} dX)\]

This is Jacobi's Formula, relating the rate of change of the determinant to the inverse and trace of the matrix.

4. Gradient of the Log-Determinant \(\frac{\partial \ln |X|}{\partial X}\) Compute the total differential for \(f = \ln |X|\) and substitute Jacobi's Formula:

\[df = d(\ln |X|) = \frac{1}{|X|} d|X| = \text{tr}(X^{-1} dX)\]

Comparing this to the standard form \(df = \text{tr}\left( \left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial X}\right)^T dX \right)\):

$\(\left( \frac{\partial \ln |X|}{\partial X} \right)^T = X^{-1} \implies \frac{\partial \ln |X|}{\partial X} = (X^{-1})^T\)$.

(Note: If \(X\) is symmetric, the result simplifies to \(X^{-1}\))

Determinant Derivative \(d|X|\) (Matrix Differential Method)

This derivation is entirely independent of element-wise Laplace expansion, utilizing only the multiplicative properties of determinants and the linearity of the trace.

Core Lemma (Infinitesimal around Identity): For an infinitesimal perturbation \(dE\) to the identity matrix \(I\):

\[|I + dE| = 1 + \text{tr}(dE) + o(\|dE\|)\]

Intuition: If \(dE\) has eigenvalues \(\lambda_i\), then \(|I+dE| = \prod (1+\lambda_i) = 1 + \sum \lambda_i + \dots = 1 + \text{tr}(dE)\).

General Case Derivation for \(X\): To calculate \(d|X| = |X + dX| - |X|\), we factor out \(X\) to construct the identity form:

\[ \begin{aligned} |X + dX| &= |X(I + X^{-1}dX)| \\ &= |X| \cdot |I + X^{-1}dX| \end{aligned} \]

Substituting the lemma with \(dE = X^{-1}dX\):

\[ \begin{aligned} |X + dX| &= |X| \cdot (1 + \text{tr}(X^{-1}dX)) \\ &= |X| + |X|\text{tr}(X^{-1}dX) \end{aligned} \]

By the definition of the differential \(d|X| = |X + dX| - |X|\), we immediately obtain:

\[d|X| = |X|\text{tr}(X^{-1}dX)\] Derivation: Gradient of the Determinant \(\frac{\partial |X|}{\partial X}\)

Let \(f = |X|\). According to Jacobi's Formula, the differential is:

\[ df = |X| \text{tr}(X^{-1} dX) \]

Rewriting this into the inner product form of the trace:

\[ df = \text{tr}(|X| X^{-1} dX) = \text{tr}( (|X| (X^{-1})^T)^T dX ) \]

Comparing to \(df = \text{tr}(M^T dX)\), we obtain:

\[ \frac{\partial |X|}{\partial X} = |X| (X^{-1})^T \]

docs.title: (4) Eigenvalue Derivatives
docs.text:
Highly important for deriving Principal Component Analysis (PCA) or studying perturbations of covariance matrices.

Eigenvalue Derivative Formula

Let \(X\) be a square matrix with a non-zero eigenvalue \(\lambda\), its corresponding right eigenvector \(u\) (\(Xu = \lambda u\)), and its left eigenvector \(v\) (\(v^T X = \lambda v^T\)).

Assuming the eigenvectors are normalized such that \(v^T u = 1\), the derivative of the eigenvalue \(\lambda\) with respect to \(X\) is:

\[ \frac{\partial \lambda}{\partial X} = v u^T \]

(Note: If \(X\) is a real symmetric matrix, the left and right eigenvectors are identical (\(u=v\)), and the derivative is \(uu^T\))

Derivation: \(\frac{\partial \lambda}{\partial X}\)

Start from the definition of the right eigenvector:

\[ Xu = \lambda u \]

Take the total differential of both sides:

\[ (dX)u + X(du) = (d\lambda)u + \lambda(du) \]

Left-multiply both sides by the left eigenvector \(v^T\):

\[ v^T(dX)u + v^TX(du) = v^T(d\lambda)u + v^T\lambda(du) \]

Since \(v^T\) is the left eigenvector (\(v^TX = \lambda v^T\)), substitute this into the second term on the left:

\[ v^T(dX)u + \lambda v^T(du) = d\lambda (v^Tu) + \lambda v^T(du) \]

The terms \(\lambda v^T(du)\) on both sides cancel out:

\[ v^T(dX)u = d\lambda (v^Tu) \implies d\lambda = \frac{v^T(dX)u}{v^Tu} \]

Since the trace of a scalar is itself, we can apply \(\text{tr}\) and the cyclic property:

\[ d\lambda = \text{tr}\left( \frac{v^T(dX)u}{v^Tu} \right) = \text{tr}\left( \frac{u v^T}{v^Tu} dX \right) \]

Extracting the scalar \(v^T u\) and comparing to the standard form \(df = \text{tr}(M^T dX)\):

\[ M^T = \frac{u v^T}{v^Tu} \implies M = \frac{v u^T}{v^Tu} \]

Given the normalization \(v^Tu = 1\), the final result is:

\[ \frac{\partial \lambda}{\partial X} = v u^T \]

docs.title: 📏 Measure Theory Basics
docs.text: This module covers the core content of set theory and measure theory, including Lebesgue measure, measurable functions, Lebesgue integral theory, and the three major convergence theorems.

docs.title: I. Set Algebras and Cardinality
docs.text:
Equipotence and Cardinality

If there exists a bijection between sets \(A\) and \(B\), then \(A\) and \(B\) are said to be equipotent, denoted \(A \sim B\).

  • Countable set: A set equipotent to the positive integers \(\mathbb{N}\) is called a countable set, and its cardinality is denoted \(\aleph_0\).

  • Continuum cardinality: The cardinality of a set equipotent to the real numbers \(\mathbb{R}\) is denoted \(\mathfrak{c}\). It is known that \(\mathfrak{c} = 2^{\aleph_0}\).

Bernstein's Theorem

Let \(A\) and \(B\) be two sets. If there exists an injection from \(A\) to \(B\), and also an injection from \(B\) to \(A\), then \(A \sim B\).

Open Sets, Closed Sets, and the Cantor Set

  • Structure of open sets: Any non‑empty open set in \(\mathbb{R}\) can be uniquely represented as a union of at most countably many disjoint open intervals.

  • Cantor ternary set (\(C\)): Constructed by repeatedly removing the middle third open interval from the closed interval \([0, 1]\).

    • Properties: \(C\) is a compact, perfect, nowhere dense set; its cardinality is \(\mathfrak{c}\), but its Lebesgue measure is 0.

docs.title: II. Lebesgue Measure Theory
docs.text:
Outer Measure

For any subset \(E\) of \(\mathbb{R}^n\), the Lebesgue outer measure \(m^*(E)\) is defined as:

\[ m^*(E) = \inf \left\{ \sum_{i=1}^\infty |I_i| \ \middle|\ E \subset \bigcup_{i=1}^\infty I_i \right\} \]

where \(\{I_i\}\) is an at most countable sequence of open rectangles covering \(E\), and \(|I_i|\) denotes the volume of the rectangle.

Carathéodory's Definition of Measurability

A set \(E \subset \mathbb{R}^n\) is called Lebesgue measurable if for every “test set” \(T \subset \mathbb{R}^n\),

\[ m^*(T) = m^*(T \cap E) + m^*(T \cap E^c) \]

holds. In this case, its outer measure is called the Lebesgue measure, denoted \(m(E) = m^*(E)\). The collection of all measurable sets forms a \(\sigma\)-algebra.

Continuity of Measure
  1. Continuity of increasing sequence: If \(E_1 \subset E_2 \subset \dots \subset E_n \subset \dots\) are all measurable, then
\[ m\left( \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty E_n \right) = \lim_{n \to \infty} m(E_n) \]
  1. Continuity of decreasing sequence: If \(E_1 \supset E_2 \supset \dots \supset E_n \supset \dots\) are all measurable and \(m(E_1) < \infty\), then
\[ m\left( \bigcap_{n=1}^\infty E_n \right) = \lim_{n \to \infty} m(E_n) \]

docs.title: III. Measurable Functions and Their Convergence
docs.text:
Definition of Measurable Function

Let \(E \subset \mathbb{R}^n\) be a measurable set, and let \(f\) be an extended real‑valued function defined on \(E\). If for every real number \(a\) the set

\[ \{x \in E \mid f(x) > a\} \]

is Lebesgue measurable, then \(f\) is called a measurable function on \(E\).

Almost Everywhere (a.e.)

If a property holds at all points of \(E\) except possibly on a subset of measure zero, then it is said to hold almost everywhere on \(E\).

Relations among Four Types of Convergence

Let \(\{f_n\}\) and \(f\) be finite measurable functions on \(E\).

  1. Almost everywhere convergence (\(f_n \xrightarrow{a.e.} f\)): \(m(\{x \in E \mid \lim_{n\to\infty} f_n(x) \neq f(x)\}) = 0\).

  2. Convergence in measure (\(f_n \xrightarrow{m} f\)): For every \(\epsilon > 0\), \(\lim_{n \to \infty} m(\{x \in E \mid |f_n(x) - f(x)| > \epsilon\}) = 0\).

  3. Implication chain and conversion:

    • If \(m(E) < \infty\), then \(f_n \xrightarrow{a.e.} f \implies f_n \xrightarrow{m} f\) (Egorov’s theorem).

    • If \(f_n \xrightarrow{m} f\), then there exists a subsequence \(\{f_{n_k}\}\) such that \(f_{n_k} \xrightarrow{a.e.} f\) (Riesz’s theorem).

Two Core Theorems (Egorov & Lusin)

  • Egorov’s theorem: Let \(m(E) < \infty\). If \(f_n \xrightarrow{a.e.} f\), then for any \(\delta > 0\) there exists a measurable subset \(E_0 \subset E\) with \(m(E \setminus E_0) < \delta\) such that \(\{f_n\}\) converges uniformly to \(f\) on \(E_0\).

  • Lusin’s theorem: Let \(f\) be a measurable function on \(E\) that is finite almost everywhere. Then for any \(\delta > 0\) there exists a closed set \(F \subset E\) with \(m(E \setminus F) < \delta\) such that the restriction of \(f\) to \(F\) is continuous.

docs.title: IV. Lebesgue Integral and Dominated Convergence Theorems
docs.text:
Integral of Non‑negative Simple Functions

Let \(\phi(x) = \sum_{i=1}^k c_i \chi_{A_i}(x)\) be a non‑negative simple function on \(E\), where the \(A_i\) are pairwise disjoint measurable sets. Its Lebesgue integral is defined as

\[ \int_E \phi(x) dx = \sum_{i=1}^k c_i m(A_i) \]

Lebesgue Integral of General Functions

  • Non‑negative measurable function: Define \(\int_E f(x) dx = \sup \{ \int_E \phi(x) dx \mid 0 \le \phi \le f,\ \phi \text{ is simple} \}\).

  • General measurable function: Introduce the positive part \(f^+ = \max(f, 0)\) and the negative part \(f^- = \max(-f, 0)\). If at least one of \(\int_E f^+ dx\) and \(\int_E f^- dx\) is finite, then define

\[ \int_E f(x) dx = \int_E f^+(x) dx - \int_E f^-(x) dx \]

If both parts are finite, \(f\) is said to be Lebesgue integrable on \(E\).

Three Core Limit Theorems for Integrals
  • 1. Levi’s Monotone Convergence Theorem: If \(0 \le f_1(x) \le f_2(x) \le \dots \le f_n(x) \le \dots\) and \(f_n(x) \xrightarrow{a.e.} f(x)\), then
\[ \lim_{n \to \infty} \int_E f_n(x) dx = \int_E f(x) dx \]
  • 2. Fatou’s Lemma: If \(\{f_n\}\) is a sequence of non‑negative measurable functions on \(E\), then
\[ \int_E \liminf_{n \to \infty} f_n(x) dx \le \liminf_{n \to \infty} \int_E f_n(x) dx \]
  • 3. Lebesgue’s Dominated Convergence Theorem (LDCT): Let \(\{f_n\}\) be a sequence of measurable functions and \(f_n(x) \xrightarrow{a.e.} f(x)\). If there exists a non‑negative integrable function \(F(x)\) such that \(|f_n(x)| \le F(x)\) a.e. for all \(n\), then \(f\) is also integrable, and
\[ \lim_{n \to \infty} \int_E f_n(x) dx = \int_E f(x) dx \]

docs.title: V. Integration Spaces and Differentiation Theory
docs.text:
Differentiation under the Integral Sign and Fubini’s Theorem

  • Fubini’s theorem: If \(f(x, y)\) is non‑negative measurable (or integrable) on the measurable set \(E_X \times E_Y\) in \(\mathbb{R}^p \times \mathbb{R}^q\), then the double integral equals the iterated integrals:
\[ \int_{E_X \times E_Y} f(x, y) dxdy = \int_{E_X} \left( \int_{E_Y} f(x, y) dy \right) dx = \int_{E_Y} \left( \int_{E_X} f(x, y) dx \right) dy \]

Functions of Bounded Variation and Absolutely Continuous Functions

  • Functions of bounded variation (\(BV\)): If the total variation \(V_a^b(f)\) of \(f\) on \([a, b]\) is finite, then \(f\) can be expressed as the difference of two increasing functions (Jordan decomposition), and \(f\) is differentiable almost everywhere.

  • Absolutely continuous functions (\(AC\)): For any \(\epsilon > 0\), there exists \(\delta > 0\) such that for any finite collection of pairwise disjoint open intervals \(\{(a_i, b_i)\}_{i=1}^m\) in \([a, b]\) with \(\sum_{i=1}^m (b_i - a_i) < \delta\), we have

\[ \sum_{i=1}^m |f(b_i) - f(a_i)| < \epsilon \]
  • Necessary and sufficient condition for the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus: The formula \(f(x) - f(a) = \int_a^x f'(t) dt\) holds if and only if \(f(x)\) is absolutely continuous on \([a, b]\).

docs.title: 🎯 Convex Optimization
docs.text: This module covers the core concepts in convex optimization theory, with a focus on Duality Theory and KKT Optimality Conditions.

docs.title: I. Standard Form of a Convex Optimization Problem
docs.text:
Definition of Standard Form

A classic convex optimization problem can be written in the following standard form:

\[ \begin{aligned} \min_{x} \quad & f_0(x) \\ \text{s.t.} \quad & f_i(x) \le 0, \quad i = 1, \dots, m \\ & h_i(x) = 0, \quad i = 1, \dots, p \end{aligned} \]

where the objective function \(f_0(x)\) and inequality constraint functions \(f_i(x)\) must be convex functions; the equality constraint functions \(h_i(x) = a_i^T x - b_i\) must be affine functions (i.e., linear).

docs.title: II. Lagrangian Duality
docs.text:
Lagrangian Function

Construct the function \(L: \mathbb{R}^n imes \mathbb{R}^m imes \mathbb{R}^p o \mathbb{R}\) that incorporates the constraints into the objective:

\[ L(x, \lambda, u) = f_0(x) + \sum_{i=1}^m \lambda_i f_i(x) + \sum_{i=1}^p u_i h_i(x) \]

where \(\lambda_i \ge 0\) are the Lagrange multipliers for the inequality constraints, and \( u_i\) are the Lagrange multipliers for the equality constraints.

Lagrange Dual Function

The dual function \(g(\lambda, u)\) is defined as the infimum of the Lagrangian over the primal variable \(x\):

\[ g(\lambda, u) = \inf_{x \in \mathcal{D}} L(x, \lambda, u) \]
  • Key property: Regardless of whether the primal problem is convex, the dual function \(g(\lambda, u)\) is always a concave function (since it is the pointwise infimum of a family of affine functions in \((\lambda, u)\)).
Weak Duality and Strong Duality (Duality Gap)

Let \(p^*\) be the optimal value of the primal problem, and \(d^*\) the optimal value of the dual problem. The dual problem can be written as \(\max_{\lambda \ge 0, u} g(\lambda, u)\).

  • Weak Duality: For any optimization problem, we always have:
\[ d^* \le p^* \]

  • Strong Duality: We have \(d^* = p^*\) (i.e., the duality gap is zero).

  • Slater's condition (sufficient condition for strong duality): If the primal problem is convex and there exists a strictly feasible point \(x\) such that \(f_i(x) < 0\) for all inequality constraints, then strong duality holds.

docs.title: III. KKT Optimality Conditions (Karush–Kuhn–Tucker Conditions)
docs.text:
Formal Description of KKT Conditions

Assume strong duality holds. Let \(x^*\) be a primal optimal point, and \((\lambda^*, u^*)\) a dual optimal point. If the relevant functions are differentiable, then they must satisfy the following KKT conditions:

  • 1. Stationarity: The gradient of the Lagrangian with respect to \(x\) vanishes at the optimum:
\[ abla f_0(x^*) + \sum_{i=1}^m \lambda_i^* abla f_i(x^*) + \sum_{i=1}^p u_i^* abla h_i(x^*) = 0 \]
  • 2. Complementary Slackness: The multipliers and inequality constraints are tightly coupled:
\[ \lambda_i^* f_i(x^*) = 0, \quad i = 1, \dots, m \]

(Intuition: if a constraint is inactive, i.e., \(f_i(x^*) < 0\), then its multiplier must be zero \(\lambda_i^* = 0\); if a multiplier is positive, then we must have \(f_i(x^*) = 0\).)

  • 3. Primal Feasibility: The optimal point must satisfy all primal constraints:
\[ f_i(x^*) \le 0, \quad h_i(x^*) = 0 \]
  • 4. Dual Feasibility: The Lagrange multipliers for inequality constraints must be non‑negative:
\[ \lambda_i^* \ge 0 \] Necessity and Sufficiency of KKT Conditions

  • Necessity: For any differentiable optimization problem, if strong duality holds, then the optimal primal‑dual pair \((x^*, \lambda^*, u^*)\) must satisfy the KKT conditions.

  • Sufficiency: If the primal problem is convex, then any triple \((x^*, \lambda^*, u^*)\) that satisfies the KKT conditions is automatically a globally optimal primal‑dual pair.

docs.title: 🎲 Probability Theory
docs.text: This module covers core inequalities in probability theory, convergence theory of random variables, and large sample limit theorems.

docs.title: 1. Core Probability Inequalities
docs.text:
Markov's Inequality

For a non-negative random variable \(X \ge 0\) and any \(a > 0\):

\[ P(X \ge a) \le \frac{E[X]}{a} \]

Chebyshev's Inequality

For any random variable \(X\) and \(a > 0\):

\[ P(|X - E[X]| \ge a) \le \frac{Var(X)}{a^2} \]

Kolmogorov's Maximal Inequality

If \(X_1, \dots, X_n\) are independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) with mean 0 and finite variance:

\[ P\left(\max_{1\le k\le n} \left|\sum_{i=1}^k X_i\right| \ge \lambda\right) \le \frac{1}{\lambda^2} \sum_{i=1}^n Var(X_i) \] Borel-Cantelli Lemma

Let the event sequence \(\{A_n\}\) occurring infinitely often (i.o.) be denoted as \(\limsup A_n\):

  1. First Lemma: If \(\sum_{n=1}^\infty P(A_n) < \infty\), then \(P(A_n \text{ i.o.}) = 0\).
  2. Second Lemma: If \(\{A_n\}\) are mutually independent, and \(\sum_{n=1}^\infty P(A_n) = \infty\), then \(P(A_n \text{ i.o.}) = 1\).

docs.title: 2. Convergence of Random Variables
docs.text:
Definitions of Four Modes of Convergence

  1. Convergence in Probability (\(X_n \xrightarrow{P} X\)): For any \(\epsilon > 0\), \(\lim_{n \to \infty} P(|X_n - X| > \epsilon) = 0\).
  2. Almost Sure Convergence (\(X_n \xrightarrow{a.s.} X\)): \(P(\lim_{n \to \infty} X_n = X) = 1\).
  3. Convergence in \(L^p\) (\(X_n \xrightarrow{L^p} X\)): \(\lim_{n \to \infty} E[|X_n - X|^p] = 0\).
  4. Convergence in Distribution (\(X_n \xrightarrow{d} X\)):
    • Definition: For all continuity points \(x\) of the limit distribution function \(F(x)\), \(\lim_{n \to \infty} F_n(x) = F(x)\).
    • Lévy's Continuity Theorem: \(X_n \xrightarrow{d} X\) if and only if its characteristic function \(\phi_{X_n}(t) \to \phi_X(t)\) holds for every \(t\), and \(\phi_X(t)\) is continuous at \(t=0\).
Relationships Between Modes of Convergence (Important!)
  • Implication Chains: \(L^p \implies P \implies d\) and \(a.s. \implies P \implies d\).
  • Reverse Implications (Conditional):
    • \(P \to L^p\): If \(X_n \xrightarrow{P} X\) and \(\{|X_n|^p\}\) is Uniformly Integrable (UI), then \(X_n \xrightarrow{L^p} X\).
    • \(P \to a.s.\): If \(X_n \xrightarrow{P} X\), then there necessarily exists a subsequence \(\{n_k\}\) such that \(X_{n_k} \xrightarrow{a.s.} X\).
    • \(d \to P\): If the limit distribution \(X=c\) is a degenerate constant, then convergence in distribution implies convergence in probability.
  • Slutsky's Theorem: If \(X_n \xrightarrow{d} X\) and \(Y_n \xrightarrow{P} c\) (a constant), then \(X_n Y_n \xrightarrow{d} cX\) and \(X_n + Y_n \xrightarrow{d} X + c\).

docs.title: 3. Law of Large Numbers and Central Limit Theorem
docs.text:
Khinchin's Weak Law of Large Numbers (WLLN)

Let \(X_1, X_2, \dots, X_n\) be a sequence of independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) random variables with finite expectation \(E[X_i] = \mu\) (i.e., \(E[|X_1|] < \infty\)). Then the sample mean converges in probability to \(\mu\):

\[ \bar{X}_n = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i \xrightarrow{P} \mu \quad (n \to \infty) \]

Kolmogorov's Strong Law of Large Numbers (SLLN)

If \(X_i\) are i.i.d., then \(E[|X_1|] < \infty\) is a necessary and sufficient condition for \(\bar{X}_n \xrightarrow{a.s.} E[X]\).

Central Limit Theorem (CLT) and Conditions

For a sequence of independent but not necessarily identically distributed random variables \(X_1, X_2, \dots\), let \(E[X_i]=\mu_i\), \(Var(X_i)=\sigma_i^2\), and \(S_n^2 = \sum_{i=1}^n \sigma_i^2\). The standardized sum is \(Z_n = \frac{1}{S_n} \sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \mu_i)\).

  • Lindeberg's Condition (Necessary and Sufficient): For any \(\epsilon > 0\), it satisfies:
\[ \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{1}{S_n^2} \sum_{i=1}^n E[(X_i - \mu_i)^2 I(|X_i - \mu_i| > \epsilon S_n)] = 0 \]

(Intuition: Ensures that no single random variable's extreme tail values dominate the total variance)

  • Lyapunov's Condition (Sufficient): If there exists a \(\delta > 0\) such that:
\[ \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{1}{S_n^{2+\delta}} \sum_{i=1}^n E[|X_i - \mu_i|^{2+\delta}] = 0 \]

(Note: Lyapunov's condition is often easier to verify because if a higher-order moment exists and satisfies this limit, simple integral bounding directly implies Lindeberg's condition holds, thus \(Z_n \xrightarrow{d} N(0,1)\))

docs.title: V. Change of Variables & PDF Transformation
docs.text:
Univariate Transformation

Let \(X\) have PDF \(f_X(x)\), and let \(Y = g(X)\). If \(g(x)\) is a strictly monotonic and differentiable function with inverse \(x = g^{-1}(y)\), the PDF of \(Y\) is:

\[ f_Y(y) = f_X(g^{-1}(y)) \cdot \left| \frac{d}{dy} g^{-1}(y) \right| \]

Multivariate Transformation & the Jacobian

Let \(\mathbf{X} = (X_1, \dots, X_n)^T\) have a joint PDF \(f_{\mathbf{X}}(\mathbf{x})\), and let \(\mathbf{Y} = \mathbf{g}(\mathbf{X})\) be a one-to-one mapping. Let the inverse be \(\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{h}(\mathbf{y})\) where \(\mathbf{h} = \mathbf{g}^{-1}\). The joint PDF of \(\mathbf{Y}\) is:

\[ f_{\mathbf{Y}}(\mathbf{y}) = f_{\mathbf{X}}(\mathbf{h}(\mathbf{y})) \cdot | \det(J_{\mathbf{h}}(\mathbf{y})) | \]

Where \(J_{\mathbf{h}}(\mathbf{y})\) is the Jacobian Matrix, defined as:

\[ J_{\mathbf{h}}(\mathbf{y}) = \frac{\partial (x_1, \dots, x_n)}{\partial (y_1, \dots, y_n)} = \begin{pmatrix} \frac{\partial x_1}{\partial y_1} & \dots & \frac{\partial x_1}{\partial y_n} \\ \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ \frac{\partial x_n}{\partial y_1} & \dots & \frac{\partial x_n}{\partial y_n} \end{pmatrix} \]

docs.title: 📈 Regression Analysis
docs.text: This module covers the core theory of linear regression models, including Ordinary Least Squares (OLS), the Gauss-Markov theorem, and corrections when model assumptions are violated.

docs.title: I. Multiple Linear Regression Model and OLS Estimation
docs.text:
Matrix Form of the Model

The multiple linear regression model can be expressed as:

\[ Y = X\beta + \varepsilon \]

where \(Y\) is an \(n \times 1\) vector of observations, \(X\) is an \(n \times k\) design matrix of independent variables (including the constant term), \(\beta\) is a \(k \times 1\) vector of unknown parameters, and \(\varepsilon\) is an \(n \times 1\) vector of random errors.

Ordinary Least Squares (OLS)

Estimate the parameters by minimizing the Residual Sum of Squares (RSS):

\[ \min_{\beta} \text{RSS} = \hat{\varepsilon}^T \hat{\varepsilon} = (Y - X\beta)^T (Y - X\beta) \]

Taking the derivative and setting it to zero yields the Normal Equations: \(X^TX\beta = X^TY\). If \(X\) has full column rank, the optimal estimator is:

\[ \hat{\beta} = (X^T X)^{-1} X^T Y \]

docs.title: II. Classical Gauss-Markov Assumptions and Properties
docs.text:
Classical Linear Regression Model (CLRM) Assumptions

  • 1. Linearity: The population model is linear in parameters.

  • 2. Strict Exogeneity: The conditional expectation of the error term is zero, i.e., \(E[\varepsilon \mid X] = 0\).

  • 3. No Perfect Multicollinearity: \(\text{rank}(X) = k < n\), i.e., there is no exact linear relationship among the independent variables.

  • 4. Homoskedasticity and No Autocorrelation: The conditional variance matrix satisfies:

\[ \text{Var}(\varepsilon \mid X) = \sigma^2 I_n \]

Gauss-Markov Theorem

Under the assumptions of the classical linear regression model, the OLS estimator \(\hat{\beta}\) has the smallest variance among all linear unbiased estimators; i.e., \(\hat{\beta}\) is BLUE (Best Linear Unbiased Estimator).

Statistical Properties of the Estimator

  • Unbiasedness: \(E[\hat{\beta}] = \beta\).

  • Covariance matrix: \(\text{Var}(\hat{\beta}) = \sigma^2 (X^T X)^{-1}\).

  • Unbiased estimator of the error variance \(\sigma^2\):

\[ s^2 = \hat{\sigma}^2 = \frac{\text{RSS}}{n - k} \]

docs.title: III. Goodness of Fit and Hypothesis Testing
docs.text:
Decomposition of Sum of Squares (TSS = ESS + RSS)

  • Total Sum of Squares (TSS): \(\sum (y_i - \bar{y})^2\).

  • Explained Sum of Squares (ESS): \(\sum (\hat{y}_i - \bar{y})^2\).

  • Residual Sum of Squares (RSS): \(\sum (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2\).

  • Coefficient of Determination (\(R^2\)): A measure of the model's explanatory power:

\[ R^2 = \frac{\text{ESS}}{\text{TSS}} = 1 - \frac{\text{RSS}}{\text{TSS}} \]

General Linear Constraints and the F-test

Consider \(m\) linear constraints on the parameters \(\beta\), i.e., the null hypothesis \(H_0: R\beta = r\), where \(R\) is an \(m \times k\) matrix with full row rank.

  • \(\text{RSS}_H\): The residual sum of squares under the restricted model that satisfies the null hypothesis \(H_0\) (imposing constraints reduces the model's fit, so \(\text{RSS}_H \ge \text{RSS}\)).

  • \(\text{RSS}\): The residual sum of squares under the unrestricted full model.

Under the null hypothesis \(H_0\) and the assumption of normally distributed errors, since \((\text{RSS}_H - \text{RSS})/\sigma^2 \sim \chi^2(m)\) and \(\text{RSS}/\sigma^2 \sim \chi^2(n - \text{rank}(X))\), and they are independent, the following F-statistic can be constructed:

\[ F = \frac{(\text{RSS}_H - \text{RSS}) / m}{\text{RSS} / (n - \text{rank}(X))} \sim F(m, n - \text{rank}(X)) \]

(Intuition: If the null hypothesis \(H_0\) is true, imposing constraints should not increase the residual sum of squares significantly, so the F-statistic will be small; conversely, if the F-value exceeds the critical value, we reject \(H_0\).)

t-test Commonly Used for Single Coefficient Significance
  • t-test: Tests the significance of a single coefficient \(H_0: \beta_j = 0\):
\[ t = \frac{\hat{\beta}_j}{\text{se}(\hat{\beta}_j)} \sim t(n - k) \]
